en: The Venerable Master Bai Song of the Ming Dynasty, out of compassion for scholars who found it difficult to consult the *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* and its sub-commentaries (*Shuchao*), divided and compiled them;

this may indeed be said to be of great benefit for study and reference. However, as the text of the *Shuchao* had been occasionally altered and edited, the original wording was incomplete and the fundamental intent was sometimes distorted.
Consequently, I have long desired to revise the compilation in order to preserve the original text, though circumstances prevented me from doing so.
Having been hindered by my travels through the air for several years, I have fortunately found this leisure time to finally fulfill my long-cherished aspiration.
Thus, I have carved these words into woodblocks to ensure their wide dissemination.
This is the preface written by the śramaṇa Shikan in the fourth month of summer in the year of Dingmao, the fourth year of the Jōkyō era.
The eight general rules:

the original text consists of one fascicle, the commentary (*sho*) one fascicle, and the sub-commentary (*shō*) three fascicles. In this country, the commentary was expanded into two fascicles and the sub-commentary into six fascicles;
now, both have been restored to their former state. My combined edition, however, has been reorganized into five fascicles.
The title is marked as *The Combined Edition of the Sublime Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*.
The *Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha* originated from the Tathāgata’s two occasions of exposition and was compiled at once by Ānanda.
The *Commentary* (Shu) originated from the oral teachings of Tiantai and was recorded by Zhang’an. The *Sublime Commentary* (Miaozongchao) was composed by Siming.
This edition of the root text was compiled by me.
Although the Baesong edition lists the names of the translators, neither the sub-commentary (*shu*) nor the sub-sub-commentary (*chao*) contain any section identifying the translators;
therefore, they have not been recorded here.
In the original edition of the *Hyakusō-e*, those written in large characters at the top of the page are the *sūtra*; those indented by one character are the *śāstra* (commentary);

and those written in a medium script in the middle are the *vyākhyā* (extract). Now, following the Tripitaka editions, all are written in large characters; however, the *śāstra* and the *vyākhyā* are distinguished from one another by being indented by one character.

Regarding the structural outlines (*ke-wen*) below, there are those that provide an explanatory outline (*shi-ke*), those with a preliminary summary (*xuan-shi*) preceding the sutra text, those where the general outline (*zong-ke*) appears before the text, and those where the sub-outlines (*zi-ke*) continue into the subsequent sections; their forms are not uniform.

I now dare not alter them to follow a single standard as in previous editions, but I shall mark each section—whether preceding or following the main text—with a grid-line at its respective location to facilitate ease of reading.
I am aware of this.

In the *Baesong Hoe-bon* (Baesong Assembly Edition) of the commentaries (*shu*) and sub-commentaries (*chao*), there are instances where passages have been deleted, supplemented, or moved from earlier to later sections, resulting in disordered sequences and loss of structural integrity;
therefore, I have now restored the commentaries and sub-commentaries each to their original form.
In the "Discriminating the Substance" (*biàntǐ*) section of the middle fascicle of the *Chāo*, it says "divided into two," whereas the subsequent text says "three.
Since the section on the "Calligraphers" (*shūjiā*) below clearly explains the substance and virtues (*tǐdé*), Baesong changed the two characters [referring to "two"] to "three.

In the "Initiating the Preface" (*fāqǐxù*) section, it says "three," yet since there is no third subheading (*kēmù*) below, he likewise changed "three" to "two. This is the second explanation within the general outline of the brief commentary (*zǒngkē lüèshì*).
It says "two," whereas the subsequent text says "three. Since the first section follows the topical outline (*ke*) in its commentary on the scripture, it also changes "two" to "three.
These are all erroneous characters; Baesong is correct, and we now follow his view.
Regarding the various editions of the texts of the *Sūtra-śāstra-ṭīkā*, where there are discrepancies as to whether certain characters are correct or not, one should record above them:
"The character 'A' is also written as 'B'.

This *Sūtra-śāstra-ṭīkā* has been printed in the capital and in Wu for a long time; however, its characters and phrases have become corrupted and erroneous, even coming into contradiction with the commentary itself.

Furthermore, because others had arbitrarily added their own interpretations and excised the original text, causing the structural continuity to be lost and the great meaning of the sūtra to be obscured, I have specifically consulted the original Sanskrit manuscripts in the Tripitaka,
verifying them one by one to restore the text to its original form. However, as the various editions of the sūtras, commentaries,

and sub-commentaries were housed in separate cases and volumes, making them inconvenient for study, I have now detached the sub-commentaries and appended them beneath the corresponding sections of the commentaries, integrating the commentaries with their respective annotations.

I have established topical outlines (*ke*) beneath the scriptural text and placed them at the beginning of the commentary (*shu*), valuing above all a single path of thorough penetration so that one may proceed without obstruction;

will this not be convenient for students? Although I have thus divided the sutra, appended the commentary, and linked the outlines with the sub-commentary (*chao*), I do not yet dare to claim this is perfect;
should the wise examine it and find it appropriate, let it be judged by its merits rather than my own conduct.
On the Double Ninth day of the Guiyou year of the Wanli era, Zhenjue, a disciple who received the Bodhisattva precepts at Chuanyi Hermitage on Mount Jing,
respectfully presents this compendium of the *Miaozongchao*,
a commentary on the *Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

Preface to the Lower Volume of the *Miaozongchao* (Exquisite Commentary on the Meaning of the Principal Passages) of the *Sūtra on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shiguan at the Eastern Monastery.
The śramaṇa Zhili of Siming composed this commentary on the meaning of this sutra.

Because people desire pure retribution, there have been many who preach and listen to it. The Master Baoyun, from whom he received his teachings, was the first to compose the sub-commentary (*jiwen*), which has been followed down to the present day;
thus, the writing of commentaries has continued without interruption, all of them taking the Master Zhiyi as their authority. How could this not be so?
Regarding the meaning of the text on the "Marvelous Contemplation for Cultivating the Mind" that evokes the four pure lands:

it is because [the author] deeply pities sentient beings and skillfully adapts to the times through his wisdom that he speaks extensively of phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) while showing little of the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).

His primary concern is that even those at the lowest level of ordinary beings may universally receive the seeds of conditions; thus, in this auspicious era when the Perfect Vehicle (*pūrṇayāna*) is flourishing, those who aspire to study all desire to grasp its essential intent.
Having cultivated and realized [the truth], I have exhausted my humble resolve to transcribe several thousand words to follow the wondrous principle (*miaozong*) and briefly explain this commentary.

This skill in adapting to the times is not within my own power; rather, my wish is that all sentient beings may practice mindfulness of the Buddha through their very minds—this is the reason for the composition of this transcription.
It was begun on the Double Ninth Festival in the year of the Xinyou cycle, the fifth year of the Tianxi era. Thus it is written.
Preface.
[Commentary] *A Commentary on the Sūtra of the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

[Sub-commentary] These eight characters, beginning with "Buddha" (佛), in the title of this commentary fully enumerate the titles of the sūtras; these are all that are being explained, and they pertain exclusively to the commentary (*śāstra*).
The single character is that which provides the explanation; the five chapters now explain the meaning of its eight characters in somewhat detailed fashion, as will be seen within the text itself.
Should one wish to know this in advance, the general outline may be set forth: "Sūtra" is the general designation, while the others are specific names. For now, we clarify the specific [meaning]:

"Buddha-spoken" refers to Śākyamuni, the Lord of Transformation, proclaiming and expounding [the Dharma] through the four analytical eloquences. As for the term "contemplation" (guan), it is used collectively.

To mention the "capable contemplation" refers to the sixteen contemplations; to mention the "object of contemplation," the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, serves as a concise summary that encompasses the fifteen objects.
Setting aside for a moment the "capable speaker," we briefly clarify the "spoken object":

the capable contemplation is entirely the single mind and the three contemplations, while the objects of contemplation are entirely the three truths within a single realm. Vairocana pervades all places and all phenomena.

All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; that which is called the Buddha-nature inherent in sentient beings is neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect—it is the essence of perfect, eternal, and great awakening.
Therefore, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. Regarding all phenomena:
The single characteristic of the *dhātu* (element/realm) is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding *dharmakāya*;

because it is based upon this *dharmakāya* that one speaks of "original enlightenment" (*mūlajñāna*), we know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is the inherent nature-merit (*prakṛtiguna*) possessed by us ordinary beings.
Therefore, among all the practices taught in the various teachings, there are none that do not serve to reveal this essence of enlightenment; thus, the four types of samādhi are given a common name.

The practice of *nienfo* (recollection of the Buddha) is identical, but the gates of its contemplative methods differ. For example, in the *Ekakṣaṇa-samādhi*, one directly contemplates the three paths to manifest the Buddha of the original nature;
in the *Vaipulya-samādhi*, one contemplates the *tánchí* (the open hand gesture) to manifest the Lotus Sūtra;

in the [contemplation of] Avalokiteśvara, one combines the recitation of the sūtra with mindfulness of breath and the awakening of the mind through the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Although these various samādhis differ in their specific applications, they all constitute the recollection of the Buddha.
In both cases, the purpose is to manifest the essence of Great Enlightenment; thus, although both involve mindfulness of the Buddha, they generally reveal the essence of all Buddhas.
However, this specific contemplation gate and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi rely upon the environment and the inhabitants of that Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

By employing subtle and wondrous contemplation, they focus specifically on Amitābha to manifest the true essence of the Buddha. Although they rely upon that realm, one must understand the nature of that reliance.
The True Dwelling is the single mind; the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, such that there is no phenomenon not created by it and no phenomenon not possessed by it.

If even a hair’s breadth of a phenomenon were to arise from outside the mind, it could not be called the Mahāyāna contemplation. The practitioner should know that based upon the nature of the mind, one contemplates those environments and inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *sattva*);
thus the environments and inhabitants can be manifested. Based upon those environments and inhabitants, one contemplates the nature of the mind. The mind... [is the basis].

The nature [of mind] is easily stirred. As for what was said—that the nature of mind possesses all phenomena and creates all phenomena—in reality there is neither a possessor nor that which is possessed, neither a creator nor that which is created.
It is precisely the mind that is the phenomena, and it is precisely the phenomena that are the mind.
The causal conditions that create and the phenomena that are created are, in their very place, entirely the nature of the mind. Therefore, when one now contemplates whether it be the support or...
This is precisely the mind of the Dharma-realm contemplating the objects of the Dharma-realm, giving rise to the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, within the Dharma-realm.
This is what is meant by "only the environment," "only the inhabitants," "only form," "only mind," "only contemplation," and "only objects.

Therefore, the character *guan* (contemplation) is explained through the "three contemplations in one mind," and *Amitāyus* (Immeasurable Life) is explained through the "three bodies in one essence. Thus, the meanings of essence, substance, power, and function are all fully encompassed.

From the perspective of the classification of teachings (*panjiao*), this belongs to the Sudden (*dun*) teaching. The fivefold profound meaning (*wuchong xuanyi*) is essentially the contemplative method (*guanfa*) expounded within this sutra.

The Great Master (Zhiyi) anticipated this in his interpretation of the sutra’s title, intending for practitioners to employ this contemplative method to enter the sixteen gates for the sake of cultivation and realization.
Therefore, in the introductory text, he takes the primary subject to encompass the various elements and the correct principle to subsume the dependent; since the contemplation of the Buddha...

The contemplation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) is none other than the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāḥ*); I address this to the practitioner: although the contemplation is profound and subtle, it is fundamentally intended for those at the initial stage.
If you can advance in your practice, why worry that you will not succeed? Even if you have not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), the causal power is already strong.

Upon reaching that land, you will be admitted to the great assembly; what you perceive of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) is subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable, allowing you to swiftly enter the ranks of the sages.
The salvation of sentient beings is likewise vast and eternally distinct from ordinary matters or the practices of the Lesser Vehicle.

Those who attain rebirth here—such as those from this land whose cultivation was perfected in past lives—perceive signs at the various assemblies that are extraordinary and understand the Dharma with ease.

By analogy, their merit lies in the *Miaozong* (the Wondrous Teaching). However, because their observance of precepts and cultivation of blessings was not refined and they lacked the vow for rebirth, they remain in the defiled realm.
Having heard the Dharma and entered the truth, one must fear that in this Sahā world, Buddhas are not encountered constantly;

even if one meets virtuous friends, if the physical and mental faculties are not superior, it is difficult to arouse the Bodhicitta. Since the sensory realms are coarse and powerful, they are truly a perilous place;

therefore, one must externally apply ritual repentance and internally exert oneself in contemplation of the principle, practicing both the primary and auxiliary methods together. By adding vows and strict self-restraint, one will surely attain swift rebirth in the Jewel Land.
"Realizing non-arising, now I explain the gate of contemplation; its meaning lies herein. Regarding the commentary (*śāstra*): "Commentary" (*shu*) means to loosen (*shu*) and to resolve (*jue*).
It loosens and penetrates the profound meanings and principles above, ensuring they are unobstructed so that practitioners may grasp their intent and cultivate them accordingly.
○ Next is the title of the speaker.
[Commentary] Master Zhizhe of Tiantai said:
[Sub-commentary] This is fully contained in the separate biography (*biezhuan*) and various chapter records (*zhangji*); those who do not yet know it must seek those texts.

○ Second, the explanation of the text. First, the explanation of the preface. Part three: first, stating the intent of the sutra and contemplation; second, first, explicitly clarifying the practice of contemplation; second, first...
The Exposition of the Meaning, Part Two: First, establishing purity in contrast to defilement; Second, the Dharma; First, clarifying the two retributions of suffering and joy.

[Commentary]: Now, the Land of Bliss and the realm of suffering, precious gold and jewels versus silt and sand, the embryonic prison versus the flowery pond, and the thorny forest compared to the jade tree—[these distinctions are manifest].
[Commentary] In wishing to discuss contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one first demonstrates the characteristics of the two retributions of suffering and pleasure.
This passage consists of four phrases, each of which discusses the correspondence between the pure and the defiled. The first phrase contrasts the suffering and pleasure of the lands they produce:

the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) receives only various pleasures and is therefore called a "Land of Bliss" (*sukhāvatī*); the Defiled Land of Endurance (*Sahā*) undergoes much suffering and is thus defined by its meaning [of endurance].

Regarding the second phrase, "the realm of suffering" (*duḥkha-kheda*): it refers to the relative status of noble and base as established by the physical bodies of sentient beings. Since those [in the Pure Lands] consist purely of the seven treasures, they are briefly described as "gold and jewels";

since this [realm of suffering] abounds in various impurities, it is briefly spoken of as "mud and sand. Regarding the next phrase, "at first birth receiving a physical form": it refers to the relative distinction between defilement and purity.
Within the six destinies of this land, all four modes of birth (*yoni*) are present; however, among humans specifically, the majority arise from the womb (*jarāyu-ja*).

When the mother eats cold or hot food, or when she is hungry or full, the child within the womb experiences suffering like that of being in cold or heat, or being suspended upside down and crushed by mountains, as if in hell;
therefore, it is called the "womb-prison. Regarding the nine grades of rebirth in that land, eight arise from within lotuses;

although those of the lowest grade pass through many kalpas, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that those who cultivate goodness with a doubting mind are born in the womb-palace of that realm out of a sense of pleasure.
If even those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are thus, how much more so for those in the eighth or ninth stages who are free from doubt—how could there be suffering for them?
Therefore, taking birth in the Lotus Pond is itself bliss. The subsequent phrase contrasts the coarse and the excellent regarding the dwelling places one visits after rebirth:

whereas this [lower realm] consists of thorny thickets and forests, that [higher realm] consists of golden channels and jade trees. Thus, although each of these four phrases contains both aspects of suffering and bliss, they are distinguished accordingly.

Regarding the mind, it confronts defilement to reveal its pure characteristics; furthermore, one should know that the text concerning the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) appears to manifest only the two lands of the same dwelling (*sahā-loka*).

However, judging by what follows—which clarifies the central thesis by fully discussing the pure and impure characteristics of all four lands—one must conclude that these [four propositions] do not exclusively refer to the land of the same dwelling.
Thus, each of the four propositions applies universally to all four types of pure and impure lands.

The lightness or gravity of one’s afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) results in rebirth in either the joyful realm or the suffering domain of the *sahā-lokadhātu*; the refinement or coarseness of one’s faculties results in rebirth in either the joyful realm or the suffering domain of the *upāya-kuśala* (Skillful Means) land;
the gradual or sudden entry [into the path] results in rebirth in either the joyful realm or the suffering domain of the *bhūta-niṣyanda-rūpa* (True Reward) land;

and the partial realization or ultimate perfection of emptiness results in rebirth in either the joyful realm or the suffering domain of the *prabhāsvara-dharmadhātu* (Nirvana of Tranquil Light). These may be illustrated by the analogies of gold and jewels versus sand and mud, or the womb and prison versus the lotus.
The ponds, thorny groves, and jade trees are likewise so; the main text and the preface are established as a single system and must not contradict one another.
However, while the preface provides a general indication of the central theme (*zong*), the main text explains it in detail; therefore, they appear to differ. Question:

Since the three lower pure lands all possess characteristics, one may discuss matters such as gold and jewels; however, in the Pure Land of *Sambhogakāya* Light (*Jiguang*), these are entirely absent.

Question: How can one speak of the characteristics of the golden jewel lotus ponds and the jade trees? Answer: The sutras and treatises state that the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (Dharmakāya) is "without characteristics" (*animitta*).
This means that the characteristics of defiled obstructions have been utterly exhausted; it is not like empty space where nothing exists at all.

This is because, through the ultimate purification of the three delusions, the physical environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhita*), as well as form and mind, are ultimately and clearly manifest. Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

The *Renwang jing* calls these the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-skandha*). Furthermore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternal," and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is stated that "form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way.
This is what is called the ultimate Land of Bliss, the ultimate gold and jewels, and the ultimate flowers.
Regarding the statement that "the ultimate ponds are made of jade trees," this is because one abandons filth to its very end and pursues purity to its source;

thus, realms of suffering and the like are judged to belong to the three obstacles. Regarding the statement that "the Pure Land uses gold and jewels as the Land of Quiescent Light" (*śāntaprabhāsa*), if one speaks in terms of the equality of the pure and the defiled, then the ultimate mud and sand of the realm of suffering are themselves taken to be the Land of Quiescent Light.
These two explanations— [1] the ultimate ponds are made of jade trees, and [2] the Pure Land uses gold and jewels as the Land of Quiescent Light—are presented.
However, following the *siddhānta*, there is nothing that is not perfectly consummate. When one speaks of the Buddha’s unsurpassed recompense, this is the principle within the phenomenon;
when one speaks of the ultimate quiescent radiance of gold and so forth, this is the phenomenon within the principle. How could there actually be such things as gold?
If both phenomenon and principle were identical and thus intermingled, how could one distinguish between the two lands? The answer is: the Buddha’s unsurpassed recompense is...

Ultimate initial awakening (*atyanta-ādi-bodhi*) is the supreme quiescent light; since ultimate original awakening (*atyanta-mūla-bodhi*) and initial awakening have reached their ultimate limit, how could they be divided into two distinct entities?

One should know that although these two lands are distinguished according to phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), in reality they are neither existent nor non-existent. How could true, excellent, and wondrous existence not be the principle?

For the principle of the secret treasury is certainly not the same as the "small emptiness" (*parīttā śūnyatā*) of the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore, the two names "phenomena" and "principle" refer to one and the same thing.

The substance [of the Buddha-body] is named "unsurpassed retribution" because it returns to the source; it is named "the principle of the supreme tranquil light" (*śānta-prabhā*) because it returns to the source.
Thus, the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states: "The four virtues attained through cultivation and the four virtues existing by nature are equal in their two meanings;

only then is this the characteristic of the body and land of Vairocana. Furthermore, the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) explicitly takes the tranquil light as the Buddha’s *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support).

Thus we know that to insist that the Land of Retribution definitely possesses gold, jewels, and so forth, while the Land of Tranquil Light definitely lacks them, is to be confused by the names and entirely ignorant of their meaning.
○ Second, from "Truly due to... below, it clarifies the two causes of mental activity.

[Commentary: Truly, it is because the mind is divided into defilement and purity that one perceives the rising and sinking of the two lands; because conduct opens into good and evil, one beholds the coarseness and subtlety of the two directions.
[Sub-commentary: "Truly" means in reality; "from" means following. That the purity or impurity of retribution is indeed brought about by the two causes of mental state and conduct.
The mind is deluded regarding the two types of mental activity; activity refers to the two modes of compliance and resistance.

Because the six realms and the three teachings delude the nature of the three virtues and defile them with the three afflictions, it is called a "defiled mind. All karmic actions of body and speech that oppose principle and involve deliberate effort are termed "evil conduct.
This mind and its activities induce rebirth in the four impure lands, which are submerged, coarse, and shallow. Only the Perfect and Sudden Teaching [is exempt].

When the nature of the three virtues is realized and separated from the defilement of the three delusions, it is then called the pure mind; when the various actions of body and speech accord with principle and are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they are termed wholesome conduct.
These mental activities induce rebirth in the four pure lands, which are loftily elevated, profound, and wondrous.

Although the mind is fundamentally one, it must be distinguished as defiled or pure based on whether it is deluded or enlightened; although practices are similar, they differ based on whether they oppose or accord with reality.
One must distinguish between good and evil, for from these two causes, pure and defiled retributions are induced; this should be understood.

For those above the stage of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), the "Dharma-realm of tranquil light" (Jiguang) serves as the essence of contemplation. All stages of cause—whether ordinary beings or sages—are identical with the ultimate;

thus, they differ from those of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), whose mental resolve only reaches the level of the twelve grades [of the Bodhisattva path]. Therefore, the partial realization of the defiled [retribution] belongs specifically to the Separate Teaching. Question: The ultimate principle is subtle and wondrous.
Neither defiled nor pure, without grasping or abandoning—yet now you establish defilement and purity to cause people to grasp and abandon.
Since this deviates from the wondrous principle, it is not the Supreme Vehicle; how can it be called the "Wondrous Contemplation for Cultivating the Mind" that reveals the One True Reality?

Answer: To seek the meaning based on the name, there is not one in ten thousand that succeeds; to determine the name based on the meaning, there is not one in ten thousand that errs. This is because [the meaning] lies outside of mere conceptualization.
The terminology established within the internal schools—both Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, as well as the gradual and the sudden-perfect—is for the most part similar;

one must first determine their orthodoxy or heterodoxy to distinguish between the internal and external, then use emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) to differentiate between the small and the great, and finally employ the gradual and the sudden to divide the distinct and the perfect.
Only when the terminology is rendered free from even the slightest confusion can one rely upon it to establish contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Therefore, our school now evaluates these meanings and employs six propositions to determine their similarities and differences—namely, mutual sublation (*pratighāta*), mutual cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and mutual identity (*tādātmya*), each having two propositions, which constitute the six.
We now employ these six to judge this contradiction, first establishing the identity of their names through distinct meanings;
that is to say, the "annihilation" (*uccheda*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) of the non-Buddhists are not [the same as] "impurity" (*mala*).

The impure view; the emptiness-principle of the Two Vehicles, which is neither defiled nor pure; the realization of the Distinct Teaching’s “Middle Only” (but-madhyama), which is the gate of being neither defiled nor pure;

and the principle of the Secret Treasury of the Perfect Teaching, which is the principle of being neither defiled nor pure. Furthermore, there are four kinds of purity: the view of outsiders who delight in and loathe [existence] while clinging to purity;
the realization of the Two Vehicles’ extinction of delusions as purity; and the gradual purity of the Distinct Teaching’s departure from defilement.

The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is the realization of sudden purity within defilement; once this is understood, one may then discuss the phrases concerning purity and the mutual sublation of the "not-defiled" and "not-pure.
The sudden purity of the Perfect Teaching sublates the two vehicles and external paths of the Separate Teaching;
the "not-defiled and not-pure" of the Perfect Teaching sublates the cultivation of the three types of pure characteristics.
"Phrases" refers to the three kinds of purity cultivated within the secret treasury of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya)—the purity that is neither defiled nor pure.
Cultivating these three kinds of neither-defiled-nor-pure [purity] within the Perfect Teaching is precisely the aspect of purity within defilement;

this "phrase" is the purity within defilement of the Perfect Teaching, which is itself the secret treasury of neither-defilement-nor-purity. That secret treasury of neither-defilement-nor-purity is itself [the phrase].

The purity within defilement is precisely this wondrous contemplation: by contemplating the four pure lands within the defiled mind, one already illuminates the *sāmbhogakāya* (recompense light) and *dharmakāya* (tranquil light).
How could this differ from the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), which is neither defiled nor pure?

If you claim that this present sutra’s rejection of the foul and adoption of the pure differs from the Secret Treasury’s principle of "neither [foul] nor [pure]," then for what reason did Vaidehī, upon hearing the contemplation of the pure lands, realize a partial manifestation of the Secret Treasury?
It should be understood that "purity purifying purity" refers to the principle of the equality between defilement and purity;

this is what is meant by the term "purity" having both a partial and a universal meaning. However, because sentient beings' capacities and conditions involve the forceful abandonment of a defiled mind, it is appropriate to employ the gate of purity to purify all phenomena.
Therefore, the discourse on purity here is not at all contradictory to the state of being neither defiled nor pure.
Furthermore, one should know that taking and rejecting, as well as non-extreme taking and non-rejecting, do not follow different paths. ○ Second, the analogy.
[Commentary]: The analogy is that when the form is upright, the shadow is straight; when the source is turbid, the current is murky.
[Commentary] The upright form is a metaphor for the pure cause—the enlightened nature and pure mind; the straight shadow is a metaphor for the result—the four pure lands.
The turbid source is a metaphor for the defiled cause—the deluded nature and stained mind; the murky flow is a metaphor for the result—the four defiled lands.
If one reverses the above metaphors, the crooked form and the concave shadow can naturally serve as metaphors for practicing in opposition to the Dharma.

Now, within these three, the first clarifies the universality and distinctness of the teaching; first, it correctly elucidates the single transformation.
[Commentary] Generally speaking, the single character "sūtra" (jīng) has seven specific types: it may consist of a single person, a single dharma, or a single analogy;

it may be a compound, or it may be complete. [Sub-commentary] As for the general name, whether teaching is sudden or gradual, provisional or revealing, and excluding the vinaya and śāstras, all are termed "sūtra."
Because it follows the Sūtras, it is called "General" (Sāmānya). As for its specific names, although the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are numerous, we shall follow three types:

namely, the single [categories] of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and parable; the triple combinations of these; and the fully complete one—thus forming seven distinct categories. Regarding the three single categories: a single person is exemplified by the *Amitābha-sūtra* and others;
a single dharma is exemplified by the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others; a single parable is exemplified by the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

The sūtras and so forth are further divided into three types: those concerning the person (pudgala), those concerning the dharma, and those that fully possess both the person, the dharma, and the parable. Those concerning the person are exemplified by the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others;
those concerning the dharma are exemplified by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others; and those concerning the person are exemplified by the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and others.

Those that fully possess the person, the dharma, and the parable are exemplified by the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vai-pulya-sūtra* and others. It is by means of these [three categories] that [the teachings are established].

[The first section] separately and collectively designates the Buddha-dharma of one lifetime. [The second section], "Now, this sutra... and so forth, specifically points to the primary teaching of this specific scripture.
[Commentary]: This present sutra establishes its name based on both the speaker and the subject matter; thus, while the teachings differ, they are collectively designated as "sutras."
This refers to the "Teaching of the Universal" (Jiaotong).
[The *Chao*] states: "In the first fascicle of the *Benlun*, this scripture is referred to as 'one transformation' (*yihua*) in order to clarify the seven distinct types;

it is spoken of in this way because it belongs to the category of the 'single person. Although it belongs to the single person, that person is himself capable of explaining what Śākyamuni taught regarding Amitābha."

These two individuals constitute distinct categories; however, because they share the same transformative teaching (*ekābhisamaya*), they are given a common name. Based on the presence of the character "contemplation" (*guan*), this refers to the convergence of person and dharma.
Since the person is capable of following [the dharma], it is omitted here for the sake of brevity.

Nevertheless, as the detailed explanation distinguishes between the general, the specific, and their differences, it is not yet fully exhaustive. Second, regarding the general and specific aspects of the lower practices (*adhobhūmi-pratipatti*):
[Commentary]: "The practices differ, ranging from one up to the immeasurable; this is the differentiation of practice. They all converge in the eternal and blissful;

this is the universality of practice. [Sub-commentary]: In various sutras, there are instances where a single type of practice is used as a specific name to correspond with a universal name. Thus, the sutra...
If one were to discuss the specific practices within the general course of cultivation, their number is infinite and difficult to exhaustively describe.

Now, for the sake of practitioners, they are presented through increasing numerical categories, which may be readily understood: first, such as the single practice; second, such as the two kinds of wisdom;
third, such as the three contemplations; fourth, such as the four foundations of mindfulness; fifth, such as the five faculties; sixth, such as the six subtle gates; seventh.

As with the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth—eight as the eightfold noble path and so forth, nine as the nine dhyānas and so forth, ten as the ten pāramitās and so forth, up to immeasurable practices numbering in the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions—all such distinct practices lead toward nirvāṇa.

Briefly stated, they consist of the four ultimate virtues; specifically, they are "permanence" and "bliss. Because these distinct practices leading to nirvāṇa are comprehensive, they constitute the *Xingjing* (Sutra of Practice).

In that *Śaṅkara-ṭīkā*, the practices are distinguished as general (*sāmānya*) and specific (*viśeṣa*) by means of cause and fruit; one must understand its underlying intent, for it does not mean that the practice only becomes general upon reaching the fruit.
To know this intent: when each cultivates their own cause, it is termed "specific practice"; when these various [causes] converge toward a single fruit, this very specificity becomes general.

This is precisely what is meant by "the general according to a different time" (*bhinnakāla-sāmānya*) and "the specific according to the same time" (*samānakāla-viśeṣa*). How much less could this apply solely to practice?

The same applies to the principles of your teaching: just as the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teaching are both general and specific, the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.
While each individual understanding implies a distinction in capacity, the single voice represents the universality of the response.

This individual understanding does not depart from the single voice, nor does the single voice obstruct individual understanding. As stated in the *Xuan* (Profound Meaning) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "By means of that which expresses... [the meaning is realized].

Characters serve as the teaching in their general capacity as means of expression (*sūcana*); they constitute the specific teaching in their particular function, which is precisely the four *siddhāntas*.
Each *siddhānta* employs characters, and each character does not depart from the *siddhāntas*. This is like the correspondence between names and reality:
while the general and the specific involve many names, these do not depart from the single reality; yet this single reality does not preclude the existence of many names.
Therefore, the three aspects of penetration (*tong*) and differentiation (*bie*) are entirely simultaneous and of the same category; they are like the melodic resonance of a flute within music.

In terms of sound, they are "penetrating," while in terms of the musical composition, they are "differentiated. The dual functions of penetration and differentiation do not obstruct one another. ○ Third, although the principle is subordinate, the principle encompasses both penetration and differentiation.

[Commentary: Although principle (*li*) is nameless, one uses the names of the gates to designate the principle; thus, the principle conforms to the gates. There are four sets of four, making sixteen, which represent the differentiation of names and principles according to the gates.
Conversely, the gates conform to the principle, which represents the universal application of names and principles.
[Commentary]: Name and reality correspond; the name is itself the gate, whereby four gates manifest a single principle.

This is because while the phenomena are distinct, they correspond to a universal principle. Indeed, many sutras employ a single phenomenon to manifest the principle, thereby attaining distinct names for that principle.
Thus, the title of this sutra uses the name "Amitāyus Buddha" as the specific phenomenon to correspond with the universal principle.

Regarding the title of the sutra, its principles are thus understood: if one seeks to understand the title of a sutra through the distinct meanings of the general and specific teachings within a single dispensation, there is no better way than by means of the four gates as the specific principles.
These four gates are the gate of existence, the gate of emptiness, the gate of both, and the gate of neither.

Although the names of these four gates are common to all, they must be distinguished according to the four teachings: namely, the Tripitaka Teaching, the Shared Teaching, the Distinct Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching.
Each of the four teachings opens four gates—such as existence and so forth—and these four sets of four constitute sixteen gates that expound the distinct principles.
Thus, there are sixteen principles; yet since even a single principle is not one, how could there be sixteen?

Nevertheless, because the principles are unimpeded, they can respond to all gates, just like space: its essence is truly neither square nor round, neither large nor small, for it is unimpeded. Therefore...

It is able to follow objects such as square or round to form immeasurable characteristics; because these are spoken of from the perspective of the immeasurable, they constitute the "distinct principle" (*bieli*).
In essence, they are one emptiness, which is named the "universal principle" (*tongli*). Without the universal there is no distinct, and without the distinct there is no universal;
the union of the universal and the distinct is designated as a single title. Second, "This, concerning the following," is the conclusion.
[Commentary] This explains the general and specific [aspects] based on a single period of transformation.
[Sub-commentary] Within each of the five periods, every sutra title possesses both a general and a specific aspect;

if one does not employ this method of judging through teaching, practice, and principle, then merely distinguishing between the general and the specific is entirely without foundation. Nevertheless, immeasurable practices converge into the one eternal bliss.

The four teachings and four gates equally expound a single principle; if one is exclusively devoted to the Vaipulya [Prajñāpāramitā] and is not yet capable of hearing this, it is because they have already anticipated the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and are speaking by leaping over the stages.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one explains the various sūtras without relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could one ever exhaustively comprehend the Buddha’s entire career?
○ Second, regarding the section "Furthermore, based on the following," this refers to the single title.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the title "The Buddha’s Teaching," it encompasses teaching, contemplation, and practice; "Immeasurable Life Buddha" encompasses principle, teaching, and practice.
Thus, the principles, teachings, and practices are complete, spontaneously possessing both general and specific meanings.

[Commentary: Since the titles of the various translated scriptures involve both general and specific names, and since the three factors of teaching, practice, and principle are extensively interrelated, it may be difficult to contemplate or cultivate them.
Therefore, by clarifying the teaching, practice, and principle within the title of the very scripture currently being explained, these three can be seen clearly.

Each of these three is "specific" (bie) when contrasted with the word "scripture" (jing), yet they are simultaneously "general" (tong) because they pertain to the scripture as a whole; thus, it is said that they naturally possess the sense of both the general and the specific.
I wish to enable the practitioner to, within this very title, explain the teaching and give rise to the contemplative practice that perceives the true principle of the Buddha.
Third, regarding the subsequent section on the single character: although it concerns a single title, it involves three names;

now I shall demonstrate how the three—explanation (*vyākhyā*), practice (*caryā*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*)—are each fully complete within this single character. This is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the character "說" (*shuō*, to speak/explain), which encompasses both.
[Commentary on the Exegesis]:

Regarding the explanation based on a single character, the *Śāstra* states: "That which is practiced is as that which is taught; 'taught' (*yathā-ukta*) refers to the teaching (*śāsana*), 'as' (*yathā*) refers to the principle (*naya*), and 'practiced' (*pratipatti*) refers to the practice (*caryā*)."

[Commentary] The word "as taught" (yathā-ukta) in the title is most capable of manifesting the teaching, the practice, and the principle; therefore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* is cited with the phrase "the practice as it was taught.

This demonstrates that within the "teaching" (ukta), there is contained both "practice" (caryā) and "principle" (nyāya). "As" (yathā) refers to True Suchness (tathatā). "Suchness" means non-differentiation;

the single nature of true awakening is such that subject and object are not distinct and the three periods of time are equal. Only by accords with this principle of Suchness can one [attain realization].

Because what is spoken by mind and mouth does not differ from practice, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* asks: "How should one expound the Dharma for others? It is the Dharma of suchness, which is immovable.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "The emptiness of all dharmas is my seat. Regarding these matters of the characteristics of preaching the Dharma:

the interpretation based on phenomena (*sāmurti*) views them as being non-different because the two things resemble each other; the interpretation based on principle (*paramārtha*) views them as being non-different because the nature of the two things is one and the same.
Because the names do not differ, the interpretation of the sūtras is as follows: these three piṭakas transmit what the Buddha taught;

like water being poured from one vessel to another, they are called "words" (*vyañjana*). It is not so with the Mahāyāna teachings, which generally take the mutual identity of the two truths as "thusness" (*tathatā*);

specifically, only hearing of the Middle Way is taken as "thusness"; and in the Perfect [Teaching], the nature of words being detached is taken as "thusness. Only by means of this can the three teachings be categorized.
It is said: "As for 'text,' when one examines the principle according to the treatise, the principle is attained through speech; as for 'practice,' it is suchness that does not differ from this.
This causes the speaker’s practice to accord with the principle. Second, the passage beginning with "The Buddha" explains the mutual inclusion of the various characters.
[Commentary: The Buddha is the Dharma-body; contemplation is Prajñā; Amitāyus is Vimukti. One should know that these three are one, and through one, the three are realized;
within each of the three, the three are realized. Within the one, the infinite is understood; within the infinite, the one is understood.
[Commentary]: The Buddha’s fundamental source, the ultimate awakened essence (*bodhi*), is neither quiescent nor illuminating; therefore, it belongs to the *dharmakāya*.
The character "contemplation" (*guan*) is pure wisdom, which is eternally illuminating while remaining quiescent; therefore, it belongs to *prajñā*.

"Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*) is sovereign spiritual power, which is eternally quiescent while remaining illuminating; therefore, it belongs to *vimukti*. Here, these characters are individually correlated with the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
There is a profound reason for this; why is that? Previously, we clarified the principle of teaching and practice through a single character (*akṣara*).

Although the explanation was concise, the meaning of the character was complete within the three [natures]. Since it was already established through the perspective of cultivation, it still encompassed the preceding teachings; yet, it had not yet clarified that every single character possesses these three natures.
Therefore, we now specifically employ the three virtues of *Nirvāṇa* in relation to each character, thereby manifesting the nature of all characters.

Each possesses three [aspects], which are beyond the capacity of those taught by previous teachers to conceive or describe; this is because the nature of the three virtues is fundamentally perfect and harmonious, such that each one mutually contains the others.
Thus, the Dharma-body is not merely the Dharma-body, for the Dharma-body necessarily possesses Prajñā and Vimukti;
Prajñā is not merely Prajñā, for Prajñā necessarily possesses Vimukti and the Dharma-body; and Vimukti is not merely Vimukti, for it necessarily possesses the Dharma-body and Prajñā.

Liberation, deliverance, and the Dharma-body necessarily possess the three virtues of Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation; these correspond respectively to the three aspects of Prajñā as teaching, practice, and principle.

Since Prajñā as teaching refers to the wisdom present in the exposition, liberation is the functional application of practice because it arises from conditions, and the Dharma-body belongs to the principle because it is that which is manifested.
Thus, since the character "Buddha" (佛) is the principle of the Dharma-body, it inherently possesses the two virtues [of practice and teaching] as well as the teaching-practice-principle [trinity].
The contemplation of the character [Amitābha] belongs to the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā and likewise possesses both the two virtues and the principles and practices;
the Infinite Life (Amitāyus) is both the practice of liberation and likewise possesses the two virtues as well as the principles and teachings.

If it were not so, how could one attain the three through the one, or attain the one through the three? Now, the question is: since a single character originally possesses the teaching, practice, and principle, why...
Question: How can it be said that the three characters of "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) alone constitute the three [virtues], such that they cannot be called a single character?
Answer: To explain the various characters of the title in relation to the three virtues is indeed an excellent discourse; its value lies in grasping the underlying meaning.
It is intended to let the practitioner know that the nature of the three virtues pervades all places—every single character, every sentence, every verse, and every chapter.

Whether it be a single part, a single sūtra, a single time, or a single transformation—even extending to all phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants, both matter and mind—there are three virtues (triguṇa) in the many, and three virtues in the few.
Even a single speck of dust possesses the three virtues without deficiency, and the ocean of lands possesses the three virtues without excess.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited to say: "In one, understand the immeasurable," and so forth. If one grasps this meaning, then the wondrous contemplation (*miao guan*) of the present [teachings] is present.

In the section on "Cultivation and Practice," a single form of the *rūpa-dhātu* can illuminate the three bodies (*trikāya*) and their dependent retribution; a single speck of dust encompasses the Land of Tranquil Light.
Therefore, all sixteen contemplations illuminate the three truths (*trisatya*). Those who do not believe this would be failing our Patriarch in establishing this Dharma.
2. Second, regarding the "one" below: an analysis of the three [truths] by means of a single character. First, the formal comparison.

[Commentary]: If even a single word can convey immeasurable meanings, how much more so for multiple words? How much more so for a single title? And how much more so for a single sutra, let alone all the sutras! [Sub-commentary]:
Above, we exhausted the subtle purport by proceeding from the broad to the narrow; now, in evaluating the merit, we proceed from the few to the many, beginning with a single word.
Since it elucidates the principle of the Great Nirvana, how could it not be complete and universal as compared to all other sutras? Second, "Therefore, in the sutra...
and so forth, citing the scripture as proof.
[Commentary] Therefore, the sutra says: "If one hears even the name of the title, the merit obtained is immeasurable."
[Commentary]: Works such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and many other Mahāyāna scriptures frequently make this statement. 3.
If not [as explained above], how could one now obtain [these benefits]? [Sub-commentary]: If one does not understand it as explained above, how could one possibly attain boundless merit?

[Commentary]: If one does not understand that a single character is perfectly endowed with the three virtues, then the immeasurable and boundless merit of upholding a single phrase or a single title as taught in the various sutras would become a mere empty fabrication.

Were it not for entering samādhi at the site of enlightenment and manifesting the revolving dhāraṇī, how could one preach so wondrously and with such mastery? ○ Second, first explaining [the general], then proceeding to the specific.
This section extensively clarifies the general explanation and the specific distinctions. The text has four parts; the first explains the character "Buddha" (佛).
Part two [of this section] specifically addresses the name "Buddha" to demonstrate the six levels of realization (*liù jí*).

First, it translates the term and provides an overview. [Commentary]: Regarding the initial explanation of "Buddha," "Buddha" carries the meaning of "awakening" (*jue*), and there are six types of such realization.
[Commentary] In Sanskrit, *buddha* means "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*) in the language of China; this refers specifically to the title of the Teacher.
His common titles are ten in number, and since the ninth is cited here, he is designated as "Buddha. As this is the ultimate fruit, it is the "Ultimate Awakening.
The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* states: "When the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic, being far removed from even the most subtle [distinctions]."
Because of this mindfulness, the mind abides eternally; this is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*). This awakening is perfectly pure and free from all oppositions.

Sentient beings and Buddhas, the environment and its inhabitants, are fused into a single unity, encompassing the ten directions and the three periods of time, penetrating everywhere without exception. The five stages of dwelling and the two types of death are completely purified without remainder.
Immeasurable, profoundly deep, and forever beyond the reach of thought, it is given the provisional name "Sublime Awakening" (*miao-jue*). This is that awakening.
There are six kinds of meaning; "that which is" is precisely this meaning. Now, Śākyamuni is the ultimate, perfectly pure awakening.

Although all ordinary beings and sages are without exception entirely this awakening, because the characteristics of delusion and enlightenment, as well as cause and effect, differ, they are distinguished by these six kinds. This is what is called "principle."
These names, these contemplative practices, these semblances, these partial realizations, and these ultimate realizations are indeed so;
yet, if one does not know that their nature is defiled and evil, then all such defilement and evil must necessarily be severed and destroyed—how then could it be argued that they are "entirely so"?
Because they are entirely so, one is spared from the six types of discouragement and spared from the six types of overweening pride.
Non-separation is precisely non-obstruction; thus, the principle of the six-sixes is established, and the perfected stage may be discerned. Question:

When it is said that the entire being of ordinary beings and sages is identical with the Buddha, does this refer to the Buddha as one's own future fruition, or to Śākyamuni as the Buddha already accomplished?
Answer: The essence of these two Buddhas—the Buddha of one's own future fruition and Śākyamuni the already accomplished—is ultimately no different.

Therefore, because the Buddha of fruition and the Buddha of the nature-of-birth are identical—such that in delusion they are both deluded, and in vision they both see—the Buddha of another and the Buddha of oneself can now be distinguished within the framework of the six stages of identity regarding form and mind.

Furthermore, one should know that the principle of the six stages of identity does not apply exclusively to Buddhas; it extends to all provisional and real beings of the Three Vehicles, down to dung beetles and earthworms.
Regarding the colors and minds of the hells, one must distinguish their initial and final stages through the six identities (*liu ji*).

These range from the "principle *kīṭa* (dung beetle)" and the "name *kīṭa*" up to the "ultimate *kīṭa*. Since the present explanation concerns the teachings of the Master [Zhiyi], he distinguishes them in terms of the Buddha;
for all ten realms are the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and because not a single one is altered, the "name" stage and those following do not merely manifest the nine [realms] as the Buddha.

Likewise, they are equally manifested because upon reaching fruition, all ten [stages] are ultimately perfected; thus, even the dung beetle and other such beings are clearly explained through the six levels of "immediacy" (*ji*).

2. From "Nirvāṇa" onwards, the six levels are extensively elucidated from the perspective of awakening. Initially, the names of the six levels of "immediacy" all signify the non-duality of the essence of principle and phenomena;
yet, while phenomena involve both the adverse and the favorable, the five levels beginning with "name and word" (*mingzi*) represent the favorable practice of phenomena.

Only the principle of reason is one; the purely inverted cultivation of phenomena—these inverted and non-inverted phenomena—are both non-dual with the fundamental awakened essence of reality (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
From what basis are the names "inverted" and "non-inverted" established? One who knows that all phenomena are non-dual and accord with the principle calls them "non-inverted";
one who does not know this finds all phenomena contrary to the principle, and thus they are called "inverted. Regarding the five [aspects] such as name and so forth: if...
Whether shallow or deep, all are known and all are compliant; yet at the initial stage of principle, there is only delusion and only opposition.
However, this matter of delusion and opposition has never for a moment deviated from the awakened principle; therefore, it is called "being Buddha. Why is this so?
It is because the sentient beings' nature inherently possesses defiled evil that cannot be altered. This nature is perfectly luminous, and thus it is named "Buddha-nature," which is defiled.
The entirety of the nature of evil arises as the practice of defilement and the practice of evil; it has no separate substance, for the entire practice is the nature itself.

Thus, one may become deluded regarding phenomena such that there is nothing that is not principle. A Buddha, by means of this very principle, gives rise to delusions and creates karma, cycling through birth and death, yet remains entirely unaware that phenomena are entirely principle.
For kalpas on end they employ the principle, yet for kalpas on end they remain ignorant; this is not due to a lack of [principle].
To know [the Buddha] is contrary to principle; because the Buddha is the totality itself, he is called "principle. Because one does not know him, one is not yet the Buddha.

This applies to the latter five stages as well. "Principle-as-Buddha" (li-ji fo) is the ultimate degree of deficiency, for it entirely lacks understanding, practice, and realization, consisting only of the inherent nature of the principle (xing-li).
Furthermore, Principle-as-Buddha does not mean pointing to the principle as the Buddha apart from phenomena.
This means that the principle of the three obstacles is entirely Buddha.

Furthermore, one should know that while they are not called "obstacles" when they are Buddha, they are called "principle-Buddha" (li-ji fo) because one wishes to manifest that the latter five [stages] possess cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), whereas this single stage consists solely of the rational nature (*tathatā*).
Moreover, although the term "obstacles as Buddha" is still applicable, it refers to the latter five people, for all of them have realized that the three obstacles are [Buddha].
Because this refers to the Buddha, he explains it as threefold; first, he cites various sutras to demonstrate their identity.

[The Commentary] states that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings are themselves the Buddha. It is like the treasures in a poor woman’s house, where all manner of precious objects are fully present, or the radiant pearl on the forehead of a strongman, which is suddenly there.
The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* provides ten metaphors, such as the tattered cloth.
Gold within a clay mold, an image within a dark room, a jar or basin in a well—these seven treasures have existed inherently from the beginning and are not something acquired only now.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that all sentient beings are thusness (*tathatā*).
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* states that the Buddha-realm and the realm of sentient beings are a single realm without distinction.
[Commentary] First, it quotes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the "Kāśyapa-parivarta," which says: "Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha. Why?
Because apart from sentient beings, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In the "Tathāgata-gotra-parivarta," the meaning of "I" (*ātman*) is the Tathāgatagarbha;
that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is the meaning of "I. Such a meaning of "I" has existed from the very beginning.
Having long been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions, sentient beings are unable to see [the Buddha].
It is like a poor woman whose house contains a vast store of genuine gold, yet none of her family members, great or small, know of it.
At that time, there was a stranger well-versed in skillful means who, having arrived at that very house, dug up the hidden treasure of gold. Furthermore...
It is like this: suppose there were a great athlete in a royal household who had a diamond gem between his eyebrows.
While wrestling and contending with other athletes, that opponent struck him with his head;
the gem immediately sank into the skin of his forehead, and he was entirely unaware of its whereabouts. A sore formed at that spot, so he summoned a skilled physician.

Regarding the ten similes of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, from the desire for self-treatment up to the physician holding a mirror to reflect his face and the jewel appearing clearly within that mirror:
of the ten passages in that sūtra, there is one primary teaching and nine similes.

One is the object of comparison (*dṛṣṭāntika*), and nine are the means of comparison (*dṛṣṭānta*). Because the object is derived from the means, they are called the "ten similes. As for the one primary teaching:
The Sūtra says: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajramati:

"With my Buddha-eye, I behold that within the afflictions of all sentient beings—greed, hatred, and delusion—there exists the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s eye, and the Tathāgata’s body, sitting cross-legged, solemn and unmoving.
Good son, although all sentient beings are within the various realms of existence and possess bodies of affliction..."
Within this [tathāgatagarbha], there is the Tathāgata-garbha, which is eternally unstained and fully endowed with virtuous marks, no different from myself.
Following this passage, nine matters are cited as metaphors for this Dharma, each consisting of both prose and verse: (1) the metaphor of the Buddha’s body within a withered flower;
(2) the metaphor of pure honey amidst bees; (3) the metaphor of polished rice within husks and chaff; (4) the metaphor of a precious gem amidst filth...
1. The Parable of Gold; 2. The Parable of the Treasure in a Poor House; 3. The Parable of the Mango Fruit within its Rind; 4. The Parable of the Golden Image in Tattered Garments; 5.
The Parable of the Noble Fetus in a Poor Woman’s Womb; 6. The Parable of Casting an Image from a Scorched Mold. Regarding the "tattered garments," a verse in the sutra says:
"For example, suppose one carries a golden image while traveling to another country, wrapping it in filthy rags and discarding it in the wilderness."
When those with the divine eye see this, they immediately inform the multitude; as the defilements are removed and the true image appears, all rejoice greatly.
My divine eye is likewise: I observe those classes of sentient beings, entangled by evil karma and afflictions, fully equipped with the various sufferings of birth and death.
Furthermore, within the dust and grime of ignorance, I see that the Tathāgata-nature remains unmoving.

Regarding that which can destroy [the mold], the sūtra verses state: "For example, when a great smith casts immeasurable images of pure gold, the foolish observer sees from the outside only scorched black clay.
Once the master has measured that it has cooled, he opens the mold so that the substance may appear;
once all impurities have been removed, the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) suddenly manifest. Thus, with my Buddha-eye, I observe all sentient beings."
It is like this: within the mire of afflictions, the *tathāgatagarbha* exists everywhere. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further states:
"It is as if there were a well and various treasures in a dark room; although people know they are there, because of the darkness they do not see them.
However, when a great bright lamp illuminates them, one is able to see them, yet one never gives rise to the thought [of having found them] at the end."
This water and these jewels did not exist before but exist now; nirvāṇa is likewise: it has existed from the beginning and is not something acquired only now.
The Tathāgata of Great Wisdom, through skillful means, kindles the lamp of wisdom so that all bodhisattvas may perceive nirvāṇa.
The present passage merely cites the dark well containing jewels to illustrate this principle; it does not require that one also know the person [who found them].
It should be understood that all the various metaphors in this passage follow this principle: the underlying logic of these metaphors encompasses both the partial and the complete.
If one were to say that the three obstructions definitively veil the Buddha-nature and that it is only revealed by destroying those obstructions, this would still belong to the partial.

However, if the nature itself constitutes the obstruction, such that the obstruction is itself the Buddha-nature, and the inconceivable virtues cause the obstruction to dissolve, then all the metaphors are complete; only this is the meaning of the present text.

The parable of the "identity with principle" (li-ji) uses the Tathāgatagarbha as an analogy to clarify the distinction between *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; the current text clarifies the Perfect [Teaching].

Next, regarding the Pure Name (*Vimalakīrti*), although all his words involve the Shared [Teaching], one must now have a Perfect understanding. Next, in the lower fascicle of the *Ratnakaraṇḍa*, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati recites a verse to the Buddha:
"One's own realm, the Dharma-realm, and the realm of sentient beings are equal; one's own realm is precisely the mind."

The Dharma and the Dharma-realm are identical to the Buddha-Dharma, for the Buddha takes the Dharma-realm as his essence; when contrasted with the realm of sentient beings, they constitute the three dharmas.
Because the arising of the mind exists in the cause and the Buddha-Dharma exists in the fruit, and these three are without distinction, it is said that "there is one realm and no separate realms.
2. Regarding the phrase "This is," etc.: although various sutras are cited here prior to the section on the clarity of original enlightenment (benjue),...
It was said that the Buddha had not yet definitively revealed the characteristics of awakening, but merely pointed out that the substance of the three obstacles is entirely the principle (*tattva*);

now, by revealing that this principle illuminates itself in its very place, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*), and thus the meaning of "Buddha" is established. This section is divided into two parts;
first is the main doctrine (*samyak-artha*).
[Commentary: This refers to Perfect Wisdom (yuan-zhi), the Perfect Enlightenment (yuan-juo) in which all phenomena pervade every place without exception and are clearly understood. [Sub-commentary:

The phrase "this is" points back to the aforementioned Great Sūtra’s various metaphors for sentient beings being identical to Buddhas, as well as the *Ratnakūṭa* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where all things are like jeweled caskets;
the Dharma-realm and so forth are all the inherently perfect wisdom of the original nature, not merely the fusion of the three types of prajñā.
This subtle and wondrous wisdom is not called "complete knowledge" merely because it individually contains all phenomena;

rather, when the entirety of phenomena is this wisdom and the entirety of wisdom is these phenomena, such that all opposition and duality are severed, it is named Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Since all phenomena—including sentient beings and Buddhas, the environment and its inhabitants, and the three periods of time and the ten directions—are entirely this wisdom, how could they be otherwise?
There may be a place, a thing, or a single atom whose substance is not clearly manifest; yet this clarity is beyond the reach of the mind, intellect, or consciousness.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states regarding the meaning of original enlightenment: "The essence of the mind is free from thought and is all-pervading, equal to the realm of empty space.
Since its fundamental nature is clarity and it is already free from thought, how can one seek it through emotional conceptualization? This is what is meant.

The "inconceivable wisdom" refers to the illumination of equality; do not mistake the tainted mind of the six realms or the realized wisdom of the three vehicles for the characteristic of the clear realization of original enlightenment.
Only the awakening of wondrous enlightenment is the Buddha of Principle (*li-fó*), wherein the entirety of cultivation is present within nature—is this not what is meant?
○ Second, the section beginning with "Although there are five... negates emotional attachments.

[Commentary]: Although the five *ānantarya* [sins] are all characterized by liberation, even though sentient beings are blinded by ignorance and deluded by inverted views, the underlying principle remains.

[Sub-commentary]: Those who cling to emotional attachments say: "Since all beings are bound by karma and obscured by the darkness of ignorance and delusion, how can it be said that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas?
Therefore, to refute this, it is said: "Although karma extends to the *ānantarya* sins, they are all, in their very essence, the three gates of liberation."
Although one may see delusions and afflictions causing confusion and inversion, the principle of original enlightenment has never failed to exist from the beginning;

since delusions and karma are entirely the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) of the *pratyaya-buddhatva* and *hetu-buddhatva*, how could they further destroy the principle? For the sword of the Buddha does not wound itself.

[Commentary: This principle is self-evident: the world is eternally abiding; the presence of a Buddha cannot benefit it, and the absence of a Buddha cannot harm it.
To attain it is not to become exalted, and to lose it is not to become base. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-principle, the Buddha-reality.
[Commentary] That which is eternally abiding in the world refers to each and every one of the ten dharma-realms and thirty worlds, all of which abide in the locus of the *tathatā* (suchness).
Because this locus of reality is eternal, the phenomenal characteristics of the world are likewise eternal.

Although the world is fundamentally characterized by succession and change, it is called "eternal" because all phenomena are identical to true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and this nature does not undergo alteration; therefore, it is termed "eternal. If one were to say...

That which undergoes transmigration cannot be called permanent; this is what is meant by "sentimental views. This is truly because the dharma of birth is itself the nature, and thus it is eternally abiding;
and because the dharma of change and cessation is itself the nature, its permanence is the permanence of the nature. This permanence is neither permanent nor impermanent, and is inconceivable.
Because the words are partial while the meaning is perfect, one may say that arising and ceasing are nothing other than the Middle Way—only arising, only ceasing.

The *迹门* (Trace Gate) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, in its section on the dwelling in the dharmas of "only difference" and "only cessation," reveals what has been realized by stating: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

Although the original and the manifested differ, they are inconceivably one. Because the Buddha can clearly perceive this secret and subtle principle, it is said that it is "vividly manifest.

Now, I, the Wise One (Zhizhe), have accomplished this secret and subtle contemplation; although I possess only the physical eye, it is called the Buddha-eye, for it is able to see the secret treasury.
