[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations of the word "to speak" (shuō): first, the citation and explanation.
[Sūtra Commentary] "To speak" means to express what is cherished in one's heart. [Commentary] "Expressing" (*yuè*) means to give full vent;
"cherished" (*huái*) refers to what is held in the mind. If one considers this in relation to the present sūtra, it refers to that which the Tathāgata has long cultivated.

Having long realized the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and harbored it within my breast, now that the conditions have struck and awakened me, I speak so that what was previously cherished may be fully expressed.

○ Second, "That is, the ten [levels]" and below shows the characteristics; as the present exposition concerns the practice of Buddha-Recitation, the details will be shown in the subsequent text and are not presented here.
Therefore, I shall first provide a general explanation of the characteristics of this teaching. The text has two parts; first, the explanation.
"The characteristics of the teachings spoken.
[Commentary] This refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries, the six perfections, the four immeasurables, and all dharma-gates.
[Sub-commentary] The twelve divisions of the scriptures generally clarify the characteristics of the teaching; that is to say, they are either spoken in prose or in verse.

Regarding the various modes of discourse—such as the *itihāsa* (thus it was), the *adbhutadharma* (marvelous accounts), or the *avyākṛta-svayaṃbhāṣita* (unasked spontaneous utterances)—if one were to fully demonstrate the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries, the various dharma-gates taught therein would total forty thousand; however, this is merely citing a general figure.
One should understand that there are actually many sets of eighty thousand. To illustrate these eighty thousand by way of the Four Noble Truths: if one speaks of the eighty thousand...
The Dharma-treasury (dharmagañja) is the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya); the eighty thousand afflictions (kleśa) are the Truth of Origination (samudayasatya);

the eighty thousand gates of Abhidharma, the eighty thousand gates of samādhi, and the eighty thousand dhāraṇīs are all the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya); and the eighty thousand pāramitās are the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya).

Although only one meaning is shown here, it already encompasses the other three; for the name "Dharma-treasury" carries the sense of a gathered accumulation, which is determined to belong to Suffering.

Furthermore, by the meaning of "aggregates" (*skandha*), the [remaining] three truths are also encompassed; for the four [noble] truths do not exist apart from the aggregates. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The Muni’s collection of Dharma-aggregates (*dharmaskandha*) numbers eighty thousand; their substance is either speech or names, and thus they are subsumed within the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Thus, both the twelve [thousand] and the eighty thousand [aggregates] pertain to both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna. Some say that in the Hīnayāna there are only nine [thousand].

Regarding the categories of the *piṭakas*, there are twelve in the Mahāyāna, or it is said that while the *hīnayāna* has twelve, the Mahāyāna has only nine; alternatively, it is said that both the great and the small have twelve.
Although the six *pāramitās* and four *apramāṇas* belong to the Mahāyāna, they also extend to the three *piṭakas*;

thus, even for a bodhisattva practicing the *vastu-pāramitā*, their names and numbers are identical across the four teachings. One must determine [the specific application] based on the two principles of the *tathatā* (suchness) and the *madhyamā* (middle way) which they respectively expound.

Furthermore, regarding the provisional and the real, there is a discussion of four kinds of skillful means for entering contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), intended to distinguish between the partial and the perfect, so that the jeweled island and the illusory city may not be confused in their direct and circuitous paths.
Second, from "Furthermore, within... onwards, it clarifies the skillfulness of the speaker. This section has two parts;
first, it clarifies the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) within a single teaching and a single gate.

[Commentary: Furthermore, within a single dharma, one performs a fourfold analysis; within each gate, one skillfully employs the four *siddhāntas* to benefit others, causing those who hear it to rejoice, praise its utility, and accept it for practice.
Through faith, precepts, diligence, mindfulness, and wisdom, they attain awakening;
greed, anger, and delusion suddenly melt away like ice, transforming them from ordinary beings into sages as they enter the flow of the Dharma—whether by way of three, two, or [one].
If there were not even a single benefit, it would be better to remain silent.
[Commentary] The eighty thousand dharmas and so forth listed above pertain to all four teachings;

that is, the eighty thousand of the *samskrta* (arising-and-ceasing), the eighty thousand of the *anutpāda* (non-arising), the eighty thousand of the *apramāṇa* (immeasurable), and the eighty thousand of the *anabhisaṃskāra* (unconditioned). As with the eighty thousand of the *samskrta*, they are cited here as representative examples.
A single dharma must be explained through four gates; in these four gates, even the provisional person cannot be found. If one considers its actual nature, the four meanings differ:
according to the gate of existence (*yǒumén*), it is momentary impermanence, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame;

according to the gate of emptiness (*kōngmén*), the three provisional constructs are as insubstantial as clouds and mist; according to the gate of both (*shuāngyìmén*), the two aspects follow one another; and according to the gate of neither (*shuāngfēimén*)...

It is said that by abandoning both characteristics and employing one gate from among the four, the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are applied according to the ripening of the faculties of sentient beings:

for those who have not yet planted the seeds, the *loka-siddhānta* is taught to inspire their desire and lead them to accept the practice; for those who have already planted the seeds, the middle two *siddhāntas* are used;
and for those whose roots of goodness have not yet emerged, the *pudgala-siddhānta* is employed to arouse their past roots of goodness—faith, precepts, diligence, and mindfulness.
For those whose evil has not yet been destroyed, he teaches through the discourse on antidotes so that their three poisons may suddenly melt away like ice;

for those who are already mature, he teaches the discourse on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) so that they may realize the Real, transform from the state of an ordinary person into a sage, and attain the Buddha-wisdom.

By discerning the capacities of beings, his teaching necessarily hits the mark: knowing those who have not entered the principle, it enables them to obtain the three benefits; knowing those who have not yet destroyed their delusions, it enables them to obtain the two benefits.
If it is wholesome to manifest in the world, the Buddha speaks of it merely to give rise to joy; if it were entirely without benefit, the Buddha would not speak of it.
(1) Second, "if one" [instance] below illustrates the four *siddhāntas* for all dharmas and all gates.
[Commentary]: If a single capacity (ji) strikes the Sage and four benefits are bestowed through one gate, it is the same for the other three gates.
Just as it is so when a single dharma is taught for the sake of a single condition (yuan), it is likewise for all conditions and all dharmas.
[Commentary]: It has been explained above that the one gate accommodates sentient beings through the four *siddhāntas*; the same applies to the other three gates.

Since the one among the eighty thousand [teachings] is thus accommodated by the four gates and four *siddhāntas*, it follows that all other dharmas are likewise accommodated by the four gates and four *siddhāntas*.
Since this is the case for all eighty thousand gates within a single teaching, it is likewise so for the three teachings; thus, the entire treasury of the eighty thousand dharmas is encompassed.
For example, regarding the gates of afflictions and their antidotes—such as samādhi, dhāraṇī, and the pāramitās—each of these eighty thousand dharmas contains four teachings;

each teaching contains four gates; and each gate contains four *siddhāntas*. By extension, the twelve divisions of scripture, the six perfections, and the four immeasurables should be understood accordingly.
This briefly clarifies the characteristics of the Buddha’s teaching. 3. Explaining the character "contemplation" (*guan*).
This refers to what has been taught above: are not the twelve divisions and eighty thousand [teachings] of the Dharma what has been taught?

However, those were cited generally to illustrate the "Teacher" (the speaker). Below, the names "Immeasurable Life" and the present term "Contemplation" (*guan*) refer specifically to the meaning taught in this sutra.
The explanation of "Contemplation" is divided into two parts: first, the restatement and explanation with the dual heading.
[Commentary] "Contemplation" (guān) refers to the act of observing. There are three successive contemplations, as well as the three contemplations within a single mind.

[Sub-commentary] The character "contemplation" (guān, level tone) is cited and explained by means of the character "to observe" (guàn, departing tone). This is because one employs the method of contemplation to observe the sublime object;
were it not for the method of contemplation, with what would one observe? This title is established based on the essential meaning expounded in the sutra, which clarifies the ten [stages].

Sixth, regarding the ability to contemplate: the current explanation of the title concerns only the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). While the scriptural text is a specific title, this [explanation] is a general name;

the general encompasses the specific, and the specific relates to the general. If the established title were unable to encompass the entirety of the text, it would fail to conform to the formal requirements of a chapter.
Therefore, we know that the present establishment of the three contemplations as an explanation of "contemplation" is indeed based on the scriptural text.
If one were to demonstrate the characteristics of the three contemplations for each of the sixteen visualizations individually, the text would become overly voluminous;

therefore, they are presented collectively in the explanation of the title. This allows the practitioner, by means of these visualization methods, to enter the sixteen gates such that every object is the three contemplations and every mind is the ultimate subtlety.
Thus, the teachings of the Four Reliances for the sake of sentient beings are expressed with concise words yet encompassing meaning.

Regarding the dual headings for the sequence and the single mind’s three contemplations (*san guan*): this is to manifest the non-sequential through the sequential, and the non-fused through the distinct;

for without distinct contemplation, there is no means to clarify the perfect (*yuan*). This is like how in the *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), the conceivable (*siyi*) is used to manifest the inconceivable (*bushiyi*).

II. From "From the False" (*cong jia*) downward, based on the teachings, the two are explained together: first, the three contemplations in sequence; second, [the three contemplations] in a single mind. I. First, the three contemplations in sequence. 1. First...
The list of names refers to the sutras.

[Commentary: The contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional is also called the contemplation of the two truths; the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness is also called the contemplation of equality and the contemplation of the two emptinesses.
By taking these as skillful means, one attains entry into the contemplation of the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein every moment of mind...
"Quiescence naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge)"—this is cited from the *Vyūha-ratna-sūtra* (*Chūyíngluò jīng*).

The various names listed in the commentary (*Cǎo*) can be seen within their respective explanations. ○ Second, "Now explaining below" refers to the explanation of the characteristics of the fruition and its basis, following the previously listed names to explain the characteristics of the three contemplations (*sanzhànguān*).

[Commentary] Now, I shall explain its meaning: "the provisional" (*jia*) refers to the false and illusory conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while "emptiness" (*kong*) refers to the verified and real ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since one now wishes to leave the conventional and return to the real, it is said that one enters the contemplation of emptiness from the provisional. The provisional is the means for entering emptiness;

first, one must contemplate the provisional and realize its falsity in order to attain union with the real. Therefore, it is said that this contemplation consists of the two truths. This is the contemplation.
If this is accomplished, one immediately realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

[Commentary] Regarding the first, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which has two names: "the provisional" and so forth refers to the fact that the objects grasped by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *tṛṣṇā-kleśa*) do not exist yet are falsely claimed to exist;

this deceptive, mundane state is known as "truth" (*satya*) because it is understood to be empty. The principle of the two kinds of emptiness is the "realized reality" (*paramārtha-satya*), for it is known through the realization of the true Dharma.
The "real" is called the truth (*satya*) because it does not exhaust the conventional; the "conventional" is called empty because its reality is not known.

One must first illuminate the provisional (*prajñapti*) before one can enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*); therefore, this is called "entering emptiness from the provisional. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the provisional is equal [to the real]":

when one is deluded regarding the conventional, one takes what is empty to be real, and thus both are non-truths. If one awakens to the emptiness of the conventional, one will necessarily know the reality; then both are truths.
Therefore, it is further named the "Contemplation of the Two Truths. Regarding this contemplation and so forth: cultivation is termed the cause and realized wisdom is termed the fruit.
In the *Śāstra*, the three types of wisdom are divided and assigned to three types of persons for the sake of easy understanding.

Thus, by correlating the Śrāvaka with the "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), the fruit of the contemplation of emptiness corresponds to the stage of the tenth *vihāra* in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñapti-praveśa-vipaśyanā*): if one dwells in emptiness, how does this differ from the two vehicles?
One would fail to establish the Buddha-dharma and would not benefit sentient beings. Therefore, one contemplates emptiness without dwelling in it, entering into the provisional.

By knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, one administers the medicine according to the illness, enabling them to take and practice it; thus it is called the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness. Thus it is said.
Regarding "equality": looking back from the perspective of equality, the previous stage refuted the provisional by means of emptiness; now, one refutes emptiness by means of the provisional.

Since the refutation of these functions is balanced, it is called "equal contemplation. When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*).
[Commentary] The second, the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), also has two names. First, it refutes dwelling in emptiness and falling into the stage of the Two Vehicles.

Second, it holds that if one cultivates the contemplation of the conventional, one can accomplish the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings. Because one contemplates emptiness as a skillful means for entering the Middle Way, although one realizes the wisdom of emptiness, one does not dwell [therein].
One must sweep away the afflictions and attachments of the triple world so that all phenomena become empty through causes and conditions.
One must thoroughly investigate the root and the branches, as well as the layers of afflictions of view and thought, which are as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand.

To universally observe and universally study with a heart of great compassion is called "knowing the disease. To master every dharma and every gate—breaking through both nature and characteristics and applying each specific antidote—is called "recognizing the medicine.
According to the depth or shallowness of the delusions and the maturity or immaturity of the faculties, one employs supernatural powers to startle and move them through wisdom.
To skillfully expound and propagate the four *siddhāntas* so that each may obtain benefit is like administering medicine only when one is willing to take it;

this is entirely because, having realized emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one is able to enter this conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, this contemplation is called "entering the conventional from emptiness. As for the term "etcetera" (*ādi*):

previously, one removed views and attachments by using emptiness to break through the conventional; now, one removes the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like afflictions) by using the conventional to break through emptiness, [returning] to emptiness.

Regarding the conventional (prajñapti), each has a single function of refutation; because these are equal when viewed in relation to one another from beginning to end, it is further called the "Contemplation of Equality.

As for what is equal in this contemplation, according to the *Śāstra*, if one takes the person of the bodhisattva in relation to the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā), this is the stage of the fruit of the conventional contemplation, located within the Ten Practices (daśaprayoga).
Second, below the two emptinesses, is the third: the Middle Contemplation.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the two emptinesses as the means": first one contemplates the emptiness of saṃsāra, and next one contemplates the emptiness of nirvāṇa;
these two emptinesses serve as the means for simultaneous negation (*dvaya-pratiṣedha*). First one employs emptiness in contemplation, and next one employs the provisional (*upāya*) in contemplation;

these two employments serve as the means for simultaneous illumination (*dvaya-avabhāsa*). Mind after mind returns to and enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), simultaneously illuminating both.
This is the Truth. When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā); this constitutes the third contemplation in sequence.

[Commentary] Regarding the initial dual designation of the first contemplation on the emptiness of birth-and-death: for those of the Separate Teaching (byōdō), at the stage of the initial mind of faith, they now realize that the fundamental nature is the eternally abiding Middle Way Buddha-nature.
Because this proceeds according to the Path of Teaching (kyōdō), it is called "Only-Middle" (tanchū), which is exclusively good and exclusively pure.
Although one is not possessed of defiled evil, even though there is no defiled evil, the nature of spiritual intelligence and awareness suddenly gives rise to a forceful awakening;

thus, objective realms appear. One discriminates these phenomenal characteristics and clings to them as "self" and "person. This unobscured knowing—whereby perverse thoughts and perverse views manifest before one—is defiled evil.

Since this is not inherently possessed by the nature, it exists entirely through the transformation and construction of conditions. Because it is a constructed phenomenon, it is not [inherently real].

Because the nature [of phenomena] is fundamentally thus, the afflictions of view and thought do not coincide with the Middle Way; they must necessarily be destroyed, and therefore the principle of "identity" (i.e., that they are themselves the Middle Way) cannot be established.
Consequently, one cannot say that there is only craving, only views, only form, or only fragrance. Even if one wishes to cultivate the Middle Way, the subject and object will not cease;

thus, cultivating emptiness serves as the primary practice while the Middle Way serves as a secondary support. Why is this? Because the mind has already become attached to existence, it requires a distinct condition [to counteract it].

The emptiness that destroys this emptiness observed through craving and views is the emptiness of the Two Vehicles; it is not inherently endowed (xingju) but must be cultivated separately. This emptiness is not ultimate;
therefore, the contemplation of emptiness merely empties birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Next, one contemplates the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*:

although the existence of birth-and-death has already been demolished, the mind still clings to emptiness. Thus, one must separately take the provisional (*prajñapti*) as an object to demolish this [clinging].

To be attached to emptiness as being merely provisional and established is not the nature-endowed (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) Dharma of a Bodhisattva; it is rather a separate cultivation that can wash away attachment to emptiness.
This so-called "emptiness of *nirvāṇa*" refers to the following: first, by emptying *saṃsāra*, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are forgotten;

next, by emptying *nirvāṇa*, the *pāṃśu-kleśas* (afflictions like fine dust) are exhausted. When both types of afflictions are exhausted, the mind has no partial attachment; therefore, one attains [liberation].

Regarding the statement that the initial contemplation for the skillful means of simultaneous negation (*yugapad-pratiṣedha*) proceeds sequentially to employ both contemplations to contemplate the two truths:

therefore, it constitutes the skillful means of simultaneous illumination (*yugapad-āloka*). Once these skillful means are established, the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*) can be cultivated within the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-praṇidhāna*);

therein, one takes the Middle Way Buddha-nature (*madhyamā-pratipad-buddhatva*) which has been revealed as the contemplating subject, and the contemplation of the Middle Way as the act of contemplating.

Contemplating with clarity that delusion and wisdom are non-dual and identical, and that the three contemplations are perfectly interfused—because this is the practice of non-action—one naturally enters *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
The fruit of this contemplation is named "all-aspect knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*), and its stage is the first bhūmi.

Second, the single mind and the three contemplations: this is to contemplate in accordance with the nature of reality and to illuminate through the transcendence of all dualistic dependencies. Indeed, all dharmas...
The nature consists of the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti, like the three dots of the letter *i*;
these three are not isolated, yet each is perfectly complete. To raise one is to encompass all three; thus, by means of the three virtues, they constitute the three truths.

Prajñā is the true [truth], Vimukti is the conventional, and the Dharmakāya is the middle. Since these virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, the truths transcend thought and transcend discourse.
This is the truth realized by the Buddha; now, taking this truth as the object of contemplation, since the truth is one yet the contemplations are three, how could they be illuminated sequentially?
Therefore, based on the wondrous truth, the gates of contemplation are established; one cultivates the three contemplations within a single mind.
In this contemplation, both subject and object are simultaneously transcended—how much more so for the Original Cultivation of Amitāyus Buddha!
This contemplation accomplishes the three bodies (*trikāya*); the Dharma-body and Reward-body merge, and the True and Responsive bodies are fused as one.

Were it not for this wondrous contemplation, how could the Wondrous Body and the Transformation Lord be revealed? If the retinue is thus, so too is the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*). Since the primary retribution is wondrous, how could the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*) be coarse?

Therefore, all sixteen objects must be contemplated with wondrous insight. This text is divided into three parts; first, the explanation based on the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Second, the first... [text continues].
Explaining the characteristics [of the threefold contemplation] in two parts: first, the explanation according to the Dharma. [Commentary]:
"The single mind and three contemplations" is derived from the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), which states:

"The three wisdoms are actually attained within a single mind; it is but a single contemplation that constitutes the three contemplations. One contemplates a single truth, yet because there are three truths, it is called 'the single mind and three contemplations. Thus, it is named "the single mind and three contemplations."
[Commentary]:

The three wisdoms—namely, the previously explained *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths), and *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects)—are categorized as belonging to three distinct persons for the sake of facilitating understanding;
however, in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), when discussed in its perfected state, these three wisdoms are actually present within a single moment of mind.
Attaining the three wisdoms is the fruit, and the three contemplations are the cause; both cause and fruit reside within a single mind. How could the cause exist prior to or posterior to the fruit?
Only when cause and fruit are non-dual can it be called "perfect cultivation. Therefore, after mentioning wisdom, the three contemplations are immediately clarified.

That which is a single contemplation is itself the three contemplations: to take up one contemplation is to possess all three; to take up one empty contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the provisional and the middle are likewise empty.
Contemplating [emptiness] can thoroughly wash away attachment to marks; therefore, by citing one [contemplation], it is shown that within emptiness, the provisional is also present.

Since all three contemplations possess the principle of establishing phenomena, by citing one [contemplation], it is shown that within the provisional, emptiness is also present, and within emptiness, the provisional is also present.

Because each locus of the three contemplations is entirely free from dependence, if one knows that the three contemplations reside solely within a single mind, then each individual contemplation spontaneously possesses all three. This is contemplation.

Regarding the one truth as three truths: while the names of the truths differ, their essence is not distinct. The complete truth gives rise to contemplation, and that contemplation in turn illuminates the truth.
Since there is no separate essence, for what reason are the truths and the contemplations established?

If one wishes to distinguish them, they are explained in terms of three causes: the nature [of the mind] constitutes the three truths, and cultivation constitutes the three contemplations. Nature is the realization of true nature; conditions are...
This conventional truth is precisely the middle truth; it is not the cause of realization (*vibhāva-hetu*) and is not the great ultimate truth. It is the same within the conventional.

Only these three truths are non-different in essence from the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). To take "stubborn emptiness" as the truth is to have a truth that is distinct in essence from contemplation;

this is likewise the case within the conventional. That the three contemplations are mutually inclusive is because the three natures are fundamentally fused; the nature itself constitutes cultivation.
This is what is meant. ○ The second category is explained by citing examples as follows.
[Commentary] "Category" refers to how within a single mind there are the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; these three characteristics exist within one mind.
[Commentary]: Because conditioned phenomena share the same nature as the unconditioned, the mind perishes at the very moment it first arises; the interval between these two is called "abiding.
Thus, although the three characteristics are not absent, they reside within a single moment of mind.

Since the impermanence of the three characteristics already dwells within this brief thought, the three contemplations—which accord with the nature of reality—being non-active and non-arising, are fully present within a single moment of mind. How could there be any discrepancy in this meaning? 2. This Contemplation.
The lower fruit. [Commentary:
When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the threefold wisdom within the single mind, which is also called the "wisdom of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This refers to knowing all varieties of phenomena, their characteristics, and their appearances within the state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*). This "state of quiescent extinction" is the power of the simultaneous negation of both [subject and object]. It is the seed.
Knowing all such characteristics is the power of dual illumination.

[Commentary] Since it would be unclear regarding the fruit of wisdom and the method of contemplation would have no basis, he demonstrates that when contemplation is perfected, delusions are extinguished and principle is revealed, resulting in a sudden, wondrous realization.

The three kinds of wisdom are actually one in essence within the single mind; they may be discussed as three according to their full attributes, or explained from the perspective of their predominant aspects.
Regarding the statement that "all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā) is merely named as such because it is quiescent," the treatise itself explains this as follows:
All-encompassing wisdom is the simultaneous quiescence of the two extremes and the simultaneous illumination of the two truths.

Regarding the various categories of practices, beginning from the initial resolve, one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations; within the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, moment by moment, both [extremes] are forgotten, yet one remains mindful of both extremes.
The contemplation that illuminates both simultaneously within a single mind through the threefold contemplation is naturally so;

now, entering into partial truth, the manifestation of fundamental wisdom depends entirely upon the power of the initial practices of forgetting and illuminating. ○ Second, citing the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* as proof.

[Commentary: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, themselves the provisional, and themselves the middle. The *Akutobhayā-ṭīkā* explains:
"The three types of wisdom are actually attained within a single moment of mind. This is precisely that meaning.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* states: "Dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I say they are empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

This treatise encompasses all three vehicles; now, as we provide evidence for the Perfect Contemplation (*yuan guan*), what dharma encountered by this contemplation could possibly not be produced from causes and conditions?
Therefore, in practicing the Perfect Contemplation, one must first understand and know both the causes and conditions that produce [dharmas] and the [dharmas] themselves that are produced.
All phenomena that arise are inconceivable; within this realm, one contemplates emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Furthermore, one must understand that both the wondrous truths and the wondrous contemplations are the subjective observers, while the aggregates and other objects produced by causes and conditions are the objective realms of observation.

Previously, it was stated directly that one contemplates a single truth; however, one must know that all three truths are contemplated within the realm of the aggregates and so forth. Thus, one contemplates the one [truth] within these realms.
Regarding the Truths and so forth, do not merely adhere to the abbreviated text; you must seek out and contemplate their meaning.

Furthermore, one cannot claim that because the inconceivable nature of what is contemplated has already been understood, one may not speak of the aggregates (*skandha*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Why? Because it was originally taught that causes and conditions, as well as the phenomena produced thereby, are inconceivable.
If it were not ignorance, how could it be called a "cause and condition"? And if it were not the aggregates and so forth, what would they be?
What is meant by "the person who is produced"? There is one who sees that the mental dharmas are subtle, saying: "Mental dharmas pertain to the cause and are explained in terms of delusion;
the Buddha-dharmas pertain to the fruit and are explained in terms of awakening. He then immediately raises an objection, saying: "If mental dharmas are called subtle, how can they be delusion?

It is precisely because this person does not know that resolving delusion is itself the subtle that he is called a person of the Round Teaching. As it is said: [The text continues with the analogy: "It is like..."

If the Suffering and Origin Truths are called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are called "inconceivable" (*acintya*), can it not be said that inconceivable ignorance is such?
Although people understand that the essence of the wondrous Dharma is delusion, they do not know the principle;

thus, they remain entirely in delusion. Wondrous awakening belongs entirely to understanding. The four intermediate stages consist of a coexistence of both delusion and understanding, which is merely a matter of names.
That is to say, if a person does not contemplate delusion, of what use is the stage of Equal Enlightenment? If one does not shatter delusion, how can one ascend to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment?
Is it not the case that the severing of the lowest-grade afflictions by the highest-grade wisdom is itself the eradication of delusion? The many deviations of humanity are indeed numerous;
the three types of wisdom have already been explained as previously discussed. (0) Third, "This contemplation" and below, [the text] proceeds according to the Subtle [Wisdom].
[Concluding Summary] [Commentary]:
This contemplation is subtle and wondrous; it is three within one, and one within three. One contemplation is all contemplations, and all contemplations are one contemplation.
This contemplation is neither one nor all—it is the contemplation that subsumes all contemplations.
[Commentary] The first phrase is a general praise for its subtle and wondrous nature; the next two phrases praise its wonder by means of the "three-in-one" (san-yi).

"One is not fixed as one, yet one is precisely three"; "three is not fixed as three, yet three is precisely one. The *Shelun* explains this through the non-determinacy of understanding as inconceivable.
The subsequent three phrases praise its wonder by correlating it with the sixteen [aspects]. The above clarifies the fusion and identity of the one and the three.
This is, in total, a single wondrous contemplation (*ekā vipaśyanā*). This very contemplation universally enters all gates; thus it is called "one contemplation as all contemplations.

Although it enters all gates, it remains only this single wondrous contemplation, and is thus called "all contemplations as one contemplation. If the contemplation were fixed as one, it could not enter many gates;
if the contemplation were fixed as many, it could not be one. Truly, it cannot be conceived through the categories of one or many.
Therefore it is said: "Neither one nor all. The latter two phrases conclude by demonstrating that although it is neither one nor many, it can encompass all;

thus, the sixteen [aspects] are none other than the wondrous contemplation. Fourth, the explanation of "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) correctly demonstrates the object of contemplation for the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Previously, the three contemplations were explained using the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and the three causes (*tri-hetu*) as the truths (*satya*).
The objective realm is revealed as the fusion of the observed with its function, thereby manifesting the transcendence of the observing subject;
one must know that the three virtues within the nature are the very substance of the Buddhas' three bodies. These three virtues and three bodies are my own single mind and the three contemplations.
If it were otherwise, then the Buddha-realm would exist externally to the contemplation and not be identical to the mind; how then could it be called the Perfect Teaching’s absolute non-relation?
In this contemplation, one may also take the three bodies of Amitābha as the Dharmakāya and one’s own three contemplations as the Prajñā.

When the contemplation is perfected and the Buddha is seen, this is itself liberation. Just as the letter "I" (i) is complete with all three strokes when one is raised, so it is with the contemplation of the Buddha;

and since the contemplation of all environments and inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) follows the same principle, there is no different path. This meaning is not clear [in other texts], and thus this is explained here through the contemplation of the Buddha.
Regarding the first [section], the names are cited from the Sanskrit:
[Commentary] "Immeasurable Life" (Wúliàngshòu) is called Amitābha in the language of India (Tiānzhū).
[Sub-commentary] "Immeasurable Life" is already the Chinese translation; in the Indian Sanskrit language, it is called Amitābha. 2.
The Buddha originally descended from the True [Dharma] to emerge into the mundane world. First, regarding the original state, there are three points:

first, it is designated as "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*), taking "immeasurability" itself as its measure; thus, the title already speaks of the "measure of life. Since this measure of life is established in dependence upon the body, there are two meanings.
Therefore, one discusses existence and non-existence by means of these three meanings.
[Commentary] The Buddha fundamentally has no body, no lifespan, and no measure.
[Sub-commentary] That which is called "Buddha" is ultimate awakening. Since both principle and wisdom have reached their limit, the beginning and the source are both forgotten;
being without marks and without name, it cannot be demonstrated or shown. How, then, could one establish its body or its measure of lifespan? 2. Following... below.
In accordance with worldly convention, two [categories] are established for each; first, the three bodies are listed, each with three [aspects].
[Commentary]: In accordance with worldly convention, the three bodies are discussed; likewise, in accordance with worldly convention, the three lifespans are discussed;
and likewise, in accordance with worldly convention, the three measures are discussed.

[Commentary]: According to the ultimate awakening of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), it cannot be said that there are bodies or lifespans for the sake of saving sentient beings; rather, because names and characteristics are established in accordance with worldly convention, the three bodies and three lifespans are taught. Thus, while the true Buddha has no three [bodies] as he transcends the world, they exist in accordance with the world. However, one must understand the intended meaning regarding their existence and non-existence. That which is fundamentally without body and without lifespan merely lacks the three non-existences that follow from conceptual signs;

it is not that its nature lacks the subtle and wondrous body and so forth. Therefore, the true Buddha ultimately encompasses all dharmas of purity and defilement. If [these dharmas] were entirely non-existent, how would this differ from the ultimate truth expounded by the Hīnayāna?
Thus, [the claim that] the real is non-existent while the conventional is existent, or that the real is existent while the conventional is non-existent, [is untenable].

This *siddhānta* (established tenet) must not be adhered to in a partial or biased manner. The intent of the present text is to establish the three bodies (*trikāya*) as an explanation of Amitāyus, fearing that one might cling to the idea that he definitively exists [in a fixed way].
Therefore, it first states that the Buddha fundamentally has no three bodies, yet speaks of their existence in accordance with the world.

Having grasped this meaning, one may then differentiate the three bodies, the three lives, and the three measures without any obstruction. 2. Explanation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), etc. below.
Regarding the three bodies and their three meanings, there are two parts: first, a classification according to their meanings; second, a synthesis based on principle.
Since the subsequent text exhaustively treats the synthesis based on principle, for now we shall provisionally classify them according to the cultivation of the two natures.
This first section is further divided into three parts, beginning with the Dharma-body, which is again divided into three sub-sections for individual explanation.
[Commentary]: As for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it takes the dharma-nature (dharmatā) as its teacher and model, and further takes that very dharma-nature as its body.

This body is neither material substance nor mental consciousness; it is not comprised within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), or sense bases (āyatana). It is merely a designation whereby the dharma-nature is pointed to as the "Dharma-body."

[Commentary] Regarding the first [meaning], the "Dharma-body as the teacher's model": the term "dharma" (law/principle) applies both generally and specifically. Generally, it refers to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which serves as the model for both sentient beings and Buddhas.
However, while the nine realms [of sentient beings] take this as their model, they act in opposition to it—just as a person may rely on a teacher yet refuse to follow the teacher’s instructions.

Only the Buddhas, from their initial aspiration, model themselves upon the Dharma and practice accordingly; thus, they are now able to reach ultimate realization in profound accord with the nature of reality.
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.

Because they accord with the nature of the Dharma, the Dharma is called their teacher. In reality, it is not that the object of veneration (the teacher) and the subject (the Buddha's body) are separate entities;

rather, the very Dharma that is the object of veneration constitutes their body. Although it is called a "body," it has already transcended the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus it is not a material substance of form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, that which is neither mind nor consciousness is matter (*rūpa*), which constitutes the first aggregate (*skandha*); that which is mind or consciousness constitutes the [remaining] four aggregates.

Since these are neither aggregates nor bases (*āyatana*) or elements (*dhātu*), they are not included within the three categories (*triskandha*). Thus, by being maintained and subsumed under these [categories], one has already excluded the *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vedanīya* (transformational) types of birth and death, as both are subsumed within the aggregates and so forth.

Alternatively, "matter" (*rūpa*) may be used to exclude the substantial (*dravya*), while "mind" (*citta*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) may be used to exclude the retributive (*vipāka*); thus, the three categories are distinguished.
Since the causes are not of this nature, why are they designated as "dharmas" and "faculties"? Therefore, one forcibly points to the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) and names it the *dharmakāya*.
Second, [the section on] the longevity of the *dharmatā*.
[Commentary: The lifespan of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is not a life-faculty obtained as karmic retribution (*vipākaja*), nor does it possess the continuity that maintains existence;
yet, by way of metaphorical designation, its non-transmigration and non-alteration are termed "lifespan.

[Sub-commentary: Lifespan as the maintenance of continuity directly depends upon the life-faculty; however, this lifespan of the *dharmatā* is not obtained as a retribution of consciousness, breath, or warmth.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also not the lifespan that sustains the continuity of the three things; rather, it is designated as the virtue manifested by the substance, which is the *dharmatā*.
It does not undergo transition through the eight phases, nor does it change through the nine periods; it is only provisionally termed "lifespan. ○ Third, regarding the measure of this lifespan:

[Commentary] This lifespan is neither of long measure nor of short measure; it is without extension and without contraction, being forcefully pointed out as identical to the Dharma-realm and having the measure of empty space.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the measure of lifespan, one might discuss its length and shortness, as well as its extension and contraction; however, the lifespan of the Dharma-nature is in reality non-existent.
These characteristics regarding measure are explained in general terms; if distinguished specifically, "long" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense Buddha) and "short" refers to sentient beings.
That which can extend or contract is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

Since these measures do not exist [in the ultimate sense], for the purpose of establishing contemplation, one forcibly points to the Dharma-life-span as being equal in measure to empty space. ○ Second, from "This is" onwards, is the general demonstration.
[Commentary] This refers to the body that is not a body, the life-span that is not a life-span, and the measure that is not a measure.

[Sub-commentary] The three meanings of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) are not a body as an aggregate of the aggregates (skandhas), nor is it a life-span obtained through karmic retribution, nor is it a measure of length;

yet, because they are forcefully described as "body," "life-span," and "measure" within the context of the dharma-nature, [these terms are applied]. ○ Second, the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya). Part One: Corresponding to the Dharma.

Regarding the first part of the second [section] on the retribution body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the commentary cites a scripture: "The *Lotus Sūtra* says that what is attained through long-cultivated practice is *nirvāṇa*;
it is called 'Great Parinirvāṇa' because it is obtained by practicing the path."
[Commentary] "Recompense" (hō) means to repay. Practice is the cause, and the elicitation of the wondrous recompense is the repayment for that cause.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The light of wisdom shines immeasurably; this is what is obtained through long-cultivated practice. This refers to the realization of the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* refers to the realization of the merit of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). These two fruits of merit are the responses to the causes of cultivation; therefore, they are called "recompense. (2) Second.
As explained below regarding the characteristics:
[Commentary] "The wisdom of suchness illuminates the object of suchness; the wisdom of bodhi corresponds with the dharma-nature.
Regarding "correspondence" (*xiang ying*), it is like the correspondence between a box and its lid. Regarding "mysterious correspondence" (*xiang ming*), it is like the blending of water and milk.
[Commentary]: As for what the characteristics of the time of receiving retribution are like, they are revealed by means of one dharma and two metaphors.

"As names do not differ from that which is observed" means that if there were differences in what is observed, it would not be called "as. "As objects do not exist externally to cognition" means that if objects existed outside of cognition, it would not be called "as.
"Cognition is as object, and object is as cognition"—because this cognition and object are thus, they attain resonance with the ultimate reality (yǐngmíng).
Because "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is a general term, it is distinguished by the "fruition-awakening of enlightenment" (*bodhi*);
this refers to the wisdom of unsurpassed *bodhi* which accords with and merges into the realm of *dharmatā*. First, the metaphor of the box and its lid is employed to illustrate their correspondence;

however, fearing that one might think the box and lid, though their edges meet, still maintain two distinct forms, the metaphor of water and milk is further used to illustrate their state of mutual integration.
The profound command is that one should know that the beginning and the root are identical in being the nature of awakening; their substance is utterly merged, exactly like water and milk.

Thus it is revealed that outside the realm there is no wisdom, and outside wisdom there is no realm—this is as visible as water and milk. Second, regarding the Dharma-body and below, the three [aspects] are established based on the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);
these are the three aspects of the lifespan of the very body itself. Within each of these three, the term "Dharma-body" is used because it is that which the Reward-body’s wisdom merges with.
Because there is no retribution apart from the Dharma, it is the first body [the Dharma-body].

[Commentary: Since the Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body, and wisdom likewise corresponds to this state of being neither body nor non-body, we conventionally designate this wisdom as the "retribution body" (saṃbhogakāya).

[Commentary] To say it is "not a body" means that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) Buddha does not have a body with limited dimensions; to say it is "not not a body" means that the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward-body) Buddha does not lack a body with unlimited dimensions.
Furthermore, "not a body" means it is not existent, and "not not a body" means it is not non-existent.

This is the Middle Way Dharma-body, which is the essence of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). When awakening is thus merged with its object, even this capacity for merging is forgotten. For the sake of establishing contemplation, it is given this provisional name.
The Wisdom of Retribution. ○ Second, from "Dharma-life" (*dharmāyuṣ*) downward, the life-span is clarified.
[Commentary]: Since the wisdom that the Dharma-life is neither life nor non-life should correspond to the profound mystery, it is also neither life nor non-life;
yet, for the sake of designation, that which is not life is forcibly named "life."

[Commentary]: To say it is "not a life-span" means it is not the same as the life-span that maintains continuity; to say it is "not not a life-span" means it is not the retributive wisdom that does not maintain continuity.
This intention of provisionally naming the essence of the Dharma within the dark middle that transcends both extremes is the same as in the previous section.
○ Second, from "Dharma-measure" (*dharmapramāṇa*) onwards, the measures are clarified.

[Commentary]: Since the wisdom that is neither of the measure of phenomena (*dharmamāna*) nor of non-measure (*amāna*) is already in accordance with the profound mystery (*míng*), it is neither of measure nor of non-measure;
yet, by force of convention, that which is non-measure is designated as "measure. [Sub-commentary]:

It is not that there is a measure corresponding to the response, nor is it a non-measure resulting from retribution; the meaning of being free from these two extremes is identical to that of the body and lifespan. 3. Third.
The first of the three [aspects of] the *nirmāṇakāya* clarifies that there are three types of bodies corresponding to sentient beings.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *nirmāṇakāya*, it means manifesting a body in accordance with the myriad things.

[Sub-commentary]: It is like a valley responding to an echo, where the magnitude follows the sound; or like a mirror manifesting forms, where the beauty or ugliness depends on the object. Thus, it responds to the myriad [beings].
Sentient beings perceive [the Buddha] manifesting superior or inferior bodies. Second, his lifespan should be equal to that of those below. [Commentary (Sū):
His lifespan should be identical to theirs as the continuity of existence. [Sub-commentary (Chǎo):
Since the body is already the same as that of sentient beings, how could the lifespan differ according to their capacities? Third, his physical dimensions should be equal to those below.
[Commentary] It should be measured according to its length and breadth.

[Sub-commentary] Depending on what is appropriate, one demonstrates the measure as either finite or infinite. ○ Second, regarding wisdom and below, it clarifies that based on the two types of existence there should be three initial dharmas.
[Commentary: Wisdom merges with the essence and is thus able to give rise to great function. [Sub-commentary:
Wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), and the essence is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). When these two merge in mystery, their application is boundless and unimpeded.
2. This is like the metaphor of water below.
[Commentary] It is like quicksilver mixed with pure gold, which can be used to coat various images.
[Sub-commentary] Pure gold of the highest quality must be mixed with quicksilver before it can be applied (the tone is *qù*) to objects;
lacking this one condition, the gold has no application for coating. Third, the section on "merits" below corresponds [to this].
[Commentary] The merit of the Reward Body (saṃbhoga-kāya) accords with the Dharma Body (dharma-kāya) and manifests its presence everywhere.
[Sub-commentary] The merit of the wisdom of the Reward Body accords with the Dharma Body; wherever there are sentient beings with the capacity for response, it manifests without exception.

○ Third, "Able to act as... and below clarifies that the Responsive Body (nirmāṇa-kāya) pervades the three lands. Part one: A dual clarification of the Reward and Responsive Bodies. Part two: "Having a limited... and below clarifies the Responsive Body alone.
This indicates the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
[Commentary: It can manifest as a body or as a non-body; it can manifest as eternal life or as impermanent life;
it can manifest as immeasurable or as measurable.
[Commentary] Regarding the first meaning: what was explained above concerns retribution as the subtle dharma, which refers specifically to self-enjoyment.

Now, we clarify the manifestation of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), wherein the eternal response of other-enjoyment is contrasted with the impermanent response of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).

Thus, both traces of activity are revealed. Therefore, both bodies are clarified; the "body" here refers to the birth-body, which possesses the characteristics of limitation and finitude. Hence, it is so named.
Because it is a body that is not a body, being the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) which has no limits or boundaries, it is called "not a body. The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* states:
"What the Buddha calls 'not a body' is named the 'Great Body' (*mahākāya*). This Great Body is the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Because this body without limits has an eternal lifespan, it is immeasurable; whereas a body with limits has an impermanent lifespan, and thus it is finite.

Regarding "measure" (*pramāṇa*), these two applications abide according to the two principles of the True [Dharmadhātu] and the Middle; they are perceived by means of the two consciousnesses of the "basis" (*āśraya*) and "activity" (*karma*).

Their abiding in principle is explained at length in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-ṭīkā*. As for the details of the two consciousnesses, they are clarified in the *Aśvabhāva-śāstra* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith). The essential meaning of that treatise is as follows:

when perceived by the consciousness of activity (*karma-vijñāna*), one perceives the Buddha of Response (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), because it grasps the delimitations of form and characteristics. When perceived by the consciousness of activity (*karma-vijñāna*), one perceives the Buddha of Activity (*karma-buddha*).
Because it is free from the marks of spatial limitation, this is the *saṃbhogakāya*. This meaning will be explained later in the *Guānfóguān chāo* (Notes on Contemplating the Buddha).

Practitioners must know that the eternal body is immeasurable and universally responds to beings in the three lands, whereas the non-eternal body is limited and responds only to those in the Land of Common Residence (*sahāloka*).
Why is this so? It is because the capacity for the true recompense (*sambhoga*) is discussed in terms of partial realization, whereby one perceives the *parasaṃbhogakāya*.
In the lands of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*), those who receive only the *bié* (separate) or *yuán* (perfect) teachings may perceive the physical marks of the Buddha as being small or superior;

yet these are not the *shēngshēn* (birth-body), but are all *bàofó* (recompense Buddhas). In the *tóngjù* (co-resident) land, where the capacities for all four teachings are present, those who receive the *bié* or *yuán* teachings are able to behold the *bàofó*.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that [the Buddha] eternally dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that he preaches the Dharma throughout the end of the future.

Since all Mahāyāna teachings manifest this Dharma-nature body of sublime distinction (*viśiṣṭa-kāya*) through appropriate responses, one knows that the eternal body universally responds within the three lands. If it were merely an impermanent body, it would respond only to the *Sāṃbhogakāya* (Shared Land) to accommodate the capacities of those for whom the *Tripiṭaka* and *Vaipulya* vehicles are intended, thereby generating the wholesome roots of ordinary beings. The second section, the analysis of meaning, is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the sense of having limits; second, [clarifying the sense of being limitless].
