This proceeds from the general toward the particular, and from the broad toward the narrow; it moves from the superior to encompass the inferior.

When the Buddha dwells in the royal city, he necessarily encompasses those in the desire and form realms as well as the three vehicles. Since the Buddha’s dwelling is itself supreme, there is no dharma that does not abide therein;
yet, because he does not dwell in evil for the sake of attracting sentient beings, he speaks here of the wholesome, and within the wholesome, specifically of worldly wholesomeness.

Because it briefly designates and gathers all wholesome qualities, it is called "Heavenly" (*deva*) and "Brahma. Within the supramundane, because it briefly designates and encompasses both the small and the great, it is called "Noble" (*ārya*) and "Buddha.
Others do not understand this; they merely say that one who is able to abide in the dharmas of the mind dwells in the city of Rājagṛha and so forth.
This suppresses the ultimate Sage by equating him with the dwelling of an ordinary person, let alone the distinction between ordinary and noble beings.

Each has its own corresponding state of abiding. For instance, when a bhikṣu cultivates morality, concentration, and wisdom, he dwells in his quarters through the celestial, Brahma-like, and noble abodes;
whereas one who violates the precepts dwells in his quarters through the hells.
If there is one who can cultivate the three contemplations with a single mind, then the very place where they dwell is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—how could this not be so?
The *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi] is the Dharma in which one abides; if even those at the initial stage of the mind are thus, how much more so for the Buddha of fruition, who dwells solely in his body.

II. Regarding the section on Rājagṛha, the explanation of the location has two parts: first, the individual explanations of the city and the mountain; second, the explanation of the city. First, the translation of the Sanskrit name.
[Commentary] "Rājagṛha" is called Rājagṛha in India [Sanskrit].
[Sub-commentary] It is also named Magadha, which means "Non-Harming. This refers to the fact that the laws of this country do not employ corporal punishment;
those who commit crimes punishable by death are sent to be placed in the Śītavana (Cold Forest). 2. Explanation of the Treatise, Part 3: Initial Analysis... [text continues]
"Various kings ruled and transformed the Śākya [clan].
[Commentary]: The *Śāstra* explains that the King of Magadha had a woman who gave birth to a son with one head, two faces, and four arms;
people deemed him an ill omen, so the king immediately tore his body and head apart and cast them into the wilderness, where they were seized by a rākṣasī demoness.
He was named Śūra; he reunited his body and was subsequently raised on milk. Later, when he had grown to full maturity, his strength was such that he could overpower kings and rule over the world.
He took eighteen thousand kings and established them upon these five mountains.
By virtue of his great power, he governed Jambudvīpa; because of this, the people of Jambudvīpa call it the City of the King’s Abode (Rājagṛha).
[Commentary] Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore, previously" explains [the situation] by way of relocating to escape the fire.
[Sub-commentary] Furthermore, when a fire broke out in the city where they had previously resided, burning it down seven times in succession, the people became exhausted by the labor.
They gathered wise men who determined that it was appropriate to move to another location; thus, they searched for land and discovered these five mountains.
It is surrounded like a city and contains palaces; because the King dwells therein, it is called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
[Commentary] Thirdly, the following explains the name based on the place obtained through fear of punishment.
[Commentary: Furthermore, in ancient times there was a king named Vasu who grew weary of the world and studied the arts of the immortals.
He falsely claimed that one must kill living beings within the celestial sacrifices and consume their flesh; consequently, he fell into hell. His son, Viśvakarman, succeeded him as king.
He thought to himself, "My father entered hell while still alive; now I wish to leave the household life, yet I fear hell, and if I wish to govern the world, I am again afraid."
When he was thinking, "Where should one who has committed a transgression place themselves? a voice spoke from the air:
"If you see a place that is difficult to encounter and rare, you should make it your dwelling. Then, while the king was out hunting, he saw a deer running as swiftly as the wind;
the king pursued it until he reached this mountain, which was surrounded by steep and solid crags, with level ground where fine, soft grass grew.
Excellent flowers covered the ground, and the lush forests, blossoming fruits, hot springs, and bathing pools were all completely pure.
Heavenly fragrances rained down, and celestial music was performed; as soon as the Gandharvas and others saw the King arrive, they each departed.
Because he beheld this spiritual wonder and established a residence therein, it is named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
[Commentary] Second, regarding "Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak), there are two parts: first, the translation of the name; second, the explanation of the meaning.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain," the translated name is "Lingjiong" (Spiritual Vulture).
[Commentary] Second, regarding "all sages," there are three parts; first, the explanation based on the reliance upon the spiritual sages.
[Commentary] Various sages and immortals dwell in reliance upon it.
[Sub-commentary] Second, the name is explained below in terms of the mountain’s shape resembling a vulture.
[Commentary] It is also called Vulture Peak because its form resembles a vulture.
[Commentary]: Third, the name of the mountain is explained in terms of its being a place where vultures dwell and hide.
[Sub-commentary]: Furthermore, to the south of the mountain is the Śītavana (Cold Forest) cemetery; after the vultures have finished feeding on corpses, they rest upon that mountain.
[Commentary]: Second, from "However, as for the Dharma [Body]" onwards, it provides a general demonstration of the application of the Dharma.

[Sub-commentary]: However, the Dharma Body is formless and truly does not depend on a physical ground for its abode; yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it manifests according to the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) to clarify the dwelling place of the Transformation Lord.

[Commentary] It is not said that "retribution" (報) is excluded; for retribution can both harmonize with the Dharma and manifest responsive transformations. Since it is already stated that "Dharma" and "response" (應), retribution is included therein.

The three bodies (trikāya) are fused and subtle; while they are provisionally distinguished, their essence is eternally identical. Six: Regarding the phrase "together with Mahā... and so forth, there are two parts:
first, the heading and the analysis; second, the explanation.
[Commentary: The section beginning with "Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" lists those who heard the teaching together.

First the śrāvakas and then the bodhisattvas are presented to show that, within the teachings, the external manifestations of the two vehicles appear superior; however, although the bodhisattva's mind is indeed superior, its external manifestations are not fixed, and for this reason they are mentioned later.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second section, "The Śrāvakas," the following is an explanatory interpretation in sequence. First, the assembly of Śrāvakas; second, first, the division of the outline and the brief indication. [Sub-commentary]:

Why does the *Śū* (the *Śāstra*) first indicate their ranks and list their numbers, yet not praise their virtues? It is not that they lack virtue; it is because the translators of the scriptures [chose not to include it].
The person is omitted.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
[Commentary] Second, the word-by-word explanation of the text, beginning from "with" (yú). First, the designation of the positions. Fourth, first, the explanation of "with" (yú).

[Commentary]: "With" (yǔ) carries the meaning of "together. Because they share one place, one time, one mind, one precept, one path, one view, one liberation, and so forth—all being identical—they are called "together.
In this sutra, because [the Buddha] hears together with Ānanda and the great assembly, it says "with."
[Commentary]: "With" (*saha*) has the meaning of "together. By explaining the seven types through the principle of "seven and one," the meaning of "together" is established.

If judged according to time, they already belong to the stage of "milk and butter" (the early disciples); however, we shall follow the primary explanation here. These seven share: 1) the same time of encountering the Buddha; 2) the same location at the Deer Park;
3) the same Prātimokṣa precepts; 4) the same mind of omniscience; 5) the same untainted right view; and 6) [the same] three [trainings].
The seventeen paths are equally characterized by remaining liberation; what was previously shared as seven is now equally heard.
However, regarding this gate of contemplation, the Buddha brought Ānanda and Maudgalyāyana into the inner palace of Vaidehī to proclaim it for the great assembly, which had not yet heard it.
Only upon returning to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa did Ānanda recount it in full, whereby they were finally able to hear it together. (Section Two: Explanation of the Great Meaning.)
"Great. [Commentary]: There are three meanings of "great": it is great because it is vast, supreme, and honored by heavenly kings and great beings; thus it is called "great.

It is called "extensive" because it provides a thorough understanding of both internal and external scriptures. It is called "supreme" because it excels over the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths. These are as follows:
Because these are the ultimate among the vehicles of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they are called "Great.
[Commentary] The Chinese word "Great" (dà) is *mahā* in Sanskrit, which contains three meanings: great, many, and superior.

Therefore, one must explain it according to these three original meanings. It is that to which Great Beings return; its magnitude of virtue is vast. Thus, the Brahman King [Brahmā] was the teacher of Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

Because Śakra, the Teacher Kāśyapa, and others were well-versed in both internal and external scriptures and possessed extensive understanding, they excelled in the ninety-five types of views and knowledge;
because they were free from doubt and liberated, they were the most supreme among the "lesser" [vehicles]. Although the primary meaning is indicated as one, it must necessarily possess three.
○ Third, the explanation of the *bhikṣu* has two parts: first, the enumeration of the six meanings.

[Commentary] Regarding the term *bhikṣu* (monk), there are six meanings consisting of three causes and three fruits. The names for the causes are "mendicant" (*yācanaka*), "frightener of Māra," and "destroyer of evil.
The names for the fruits are "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*), "slayer of thieves" (*vadhaka*), and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).
[Sub-commentary] There are three causes and three fruits, each paired with its primary counterpart. First, following the essential points of the *Śāstra*, the three causes are explained.
Third, if one has attained the fruit, one should self-restrain and, wishing to practice again, emulate those who cultivate the causes; thus the causes are explained.
Among these three, the first concerns the *bhikṣu* (mendicant).
[Commentary: In the *Śāstra*, Viśuddhanetra asked Śāriputra: "There are four kinds of food for a *bhikṣu*, which are like medicinal ingredients."
Eating from what is planted in one's own garden is called "mouth-food from below. Gazing at the stars and constellations for sustenance is called "mouth-food from above.
Using clever speech in the four directions is called "mouth-food from the sides. Relying on incantations and divination is called "mouth-food from the intermediate points.
A bhikṣu who does not engage in these four types of livelihood is a pure mendicant.
[Commentary]: Now, the meaning of Śāriputra’s response to that mendicant Viśuddhanetra is presented: one must abandon food from above, below, and the four cardinal directions;

by constantly practicing alms-gathering to sustain one's life with purity, one is called a "mendicant" (bhikṣu). Upon reaching the fruition, this becomes the virtue of being a "worthy of offerings" (arhat).
○ Second, "frightening the māras."

[Commentary: Regarding "frightening Māra": when one resolves to leave the household life, the *yakṣas* who roam the earth cry out, and their voices are transmitted through the air until they reach the sixth heaven;
upon hearing this, the King of Māras becomes terrified, fearing he will lose his followers.
[Commentary]: The Lord of Māras increases birth-and-death through the enjoyment of desires at home; he who leaves the home life abandons defilement and proceeds toward the unarisen (anutpāda).
Therefore, when the King of Māras hears this, fear arises within him; yet for one who breaks the precepts out of defiled desire, Māra returns to joy.
By diligently cultivating the three trainings, one realizes the fruit of the unarisen. 3. Destroying Evil.
[Commentary] "Destroying Evil" (Pò è): One who can destroy the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of affliction, severing them all completely, is thus called one who "destroys evil.

[Sub-commentary] The ninety-eight latent tendencies, consisting of the two categories of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*), are termed "evil" and "thieves"; the cultivation of contemplation to investigate and exhaust them is termed...

To destroy evil and realize wisdom so as to bring it to total cessation is called "slaying the thief. Regarding the fourth section, the fourfold assembly (*catvāri parṣad*), the following explains the three aspects of the assembly:
first, the explanation of the general name.
[Commentary]: "Assembly" (*parṣad*) refers to four or more persons, up to hundreds, thousands, or immeasurable numbers gathered in one place for the performance of *karmavācanā* rituals.

When the procedures for the *śalākā* (counting sticks) and the *poṣadha* are consistent in both principle and practice, and there is no conflict or dispute, this is called a "harmonious assembly" (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*).
[Commentary] Section 2.1: Explanation of the distinct characteristics.

[Sūtra] First, monks who possess a sense of shame uphold the precepts without transgression; second, monks who lack a sense of shame do not uphold the precepts and do not distinguish between what is good and what is not.
The three types of "evil" Saṃghas are as follows: first, those who have not broken the precepts yet fail to distinguish between what is light and what is grave;

second, those who engage in mutual dispute but are unable to reach a verdict, remaining silent and speechless; fourth, the "true" Saṃgha, which refers to those who are both learners (śaikṣa) and those beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
[Commentary] 3. From "Now, in this... below, the taking and rejecting are clarified.

[Sub-commentary] Now, regarding these two types of *saṃgha*, they may perform a communal *karmavācanā* and share in the hearing and verification of the testimony; however, only those who are *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training) are accepted.

[Commentary: Since *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) apply to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), those who possess a sense of shame (*hrīmattva*) are selected; these two types of Saṃgha are precisely the "those possessing shame" in the true sense.
The *Śāstra* states: "Among these, the two kinds of Saṃgha may jointly perform the one hundred and one *karmas*, hearing and attesting to them with faith;
they are even more restricted than the learners (*śaikṣa*), for the former three [categories] are entirely excluded."
Together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

[Commentary] Regarding the enumeration "two thousand two hundred" and below, there are two parts: first, the heading indicating the number of people; second, the detailed enumeration. First, the combination of one thousand.
[Sub-commentary] "One thousand two hundred and fifty people" refers to the enumeration. As for the three Kāśyapa brothers, they had one thousand younger brothers.
*Uruvilvā* is translated here as "Pawpaw Grove" (*mōgū-rin*); *Gayā* is translated as "City"; *Nadī* is translated as "River.
In the past they together raised a single banner, and now their branches are joined. [Commentary]:
From the second mention of the *śarīra* (relics) downward, they total two hundred and fifty.
[Commentary: The name Śāriputra is translated as "Pearl" (Zhūzi) and also as "Son of the Body" (Shenzi). His clan name is Kauṣṭhila.
Maudgalyāyana’s clan name is Maudgalya; it is translated as "Praise" (Zànsòng), or "Radish," or "Horse-bean.
These two together had two hundred and fifty disciples.
[Commentary]: Regarding "The two Kāśyapas," this explains the reason for their constant attendance. [Sub-commentary]:

Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, and others previously all served fire and practiced heterodox paths; it was only after many years of arduous effort that they entered the True Path, yet they had gained nothing at all.
Upon encountering the Buddha but once, they immediately attained the supreme fruits. Moved by the profound kindness of the Buddha, they constantly attended upon him as his attendants.
The Buddha [taught] for the assembly of those who heard together, with thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, of whom Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince was the foremost. [Commentary]:
Regarding the second section, the assembly of bodhisattvas, there are four textual divisions in the initial analysis.
[Commentary]: Within the section on the Bodhisattvas, there are four parts: first, the general clarification of their status; second, the enumeration of the thirty-two thousand people;
third, the naming of Mañjuśrī; and fourth, the conclusion identifying him as the leader.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, "The Two [Meanings] of India," there are two parts: first, the explanation of the title.
[Sub-commentary] In India, it is called *mahābodhicittotpādaka-sattva*; this is translated here as "One who Accomplishes Sentient Beings through the Great Bodhicitta."
[Commentary] The second section, "Mañjuśrī," concerns the translation of the name.
[Sub-commentary] Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). One who transforms others through the Dharma is called a "Dharma Prince" (Dharmaputra).
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the Introduction, there are two sections: first, a comparative discussion of differences; second, a general enumeration of distinctions.

[Commentary: Second, regarding the introductory section on the occasion of the teaching (*nidāna*), various sūtras differ: some involve the emission of light, the shaking of the earth, a smile, entering meditative absorption, or the Buddha personally announcing his title and rank to exhort others to inquire.
[Commentary]: "Emitting light" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where light from between the eyebrows illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction.
"Shaking the earth" refers to the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, causes the great trichiliocosm to quake in six ways.

"Smiling" refers to the *Kṣāranadī-parivarta* (or *Bao'en jing*), where it says: "At that time, the Tathāgata smiled with a serene countenance. "Entering dhyāna" refers to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
In the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, at that time, the Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable and profound *dharmatā*, personally proclaiming his own title, as in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*:
"I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus throne. He exhorts others to inquire, as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where he universally addresses all sentient beings:
"The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is about to enter *nirvāṇa*; if there is anything [you wish to ask]..."
I now inquire about all these doubts as my final questions. However, the introductory events of various sutras may include several factors combined;

for now, I shall cite one aspect from each to clarify the characteristics of their introductions. II. Now, regarding this present sutra, the second section [of the introduction] correctly reveals the present sutra.
This has two parts: first, the correct revelation.
[Commentary] Now, this sutra specifically takes the murder of one’s father as its introductory motif.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," it explains away potential doubts.
[Commentary] Why is this act of transgression cited as the introductory motif? It is to manifest the extreme evil of this realm and to cause people to...
If one who has even cast aside their own biological child can still harbor thoughts of harm toward them, how much more so would they desire others to share in the joy of the Pure Land?
Therefore, Vaidehī, I pray that you will speak of the place free from sorrow and affliction; she finds no delight in this turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa.
[Commentary] Second, a general outline and brief explanation of the middle and lower sections. First, the division of the sections.

[Sub-commentary] Within this, there are two parts: first, from "At that time" onwards, the actual explanation of the killing of the father; second, from "Questioning the gatekeeper" onwards, the explanation of the intent to harm the mother.
[Commentary] Regarding the second question, there are three parts to the explanation: first, the question and answer resolving doubts; second, the initial question.
[Sub-commentary] Question: For what reason did Bimbisāra dispatch someone to preach the Dharma, while for what reason did the Tathāgata go in person to Vaidehī?
[Commentary]: Both Bimbisāra and Vaidehī invited their disciples to attend the banquet of Bimbisāra;
for what reason did [the Buddha] send only Maudgalyāyana and Rāhula to attend the banquet of Vaidehī? For what reason did the Tathāgata go there in person? 2. The Answer.
[Commentary]: The answer is that the father’s vow was to hear the Dharma, so he sent [his son] to transmit and bestow it for the sake of transforming others;
the mother’s desire was to be reborn in the Pure Land, which cannot be opened by anyone other than a Buddha, therefore she had to go herself.
[Commentary]: King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Videha wished to hear the Dharma of the precepts and dispatched a messenger to bestow them upon Queen Vaidehī of the kingdom of Magadha;
her spiritual capacity lay in wondrous contemplation, which required the Buddha’s personal instruction. The titles "father" and "mother" were obtained from King Ajātaśatru.
(1) From "King Bimbisāra" onwards, the names are translated in advance.
[Commentary]: Bimbisāra means "Molded Fruit" (móshí) and is also called "Shadow-Firm" (yǐngjiān). Vaidehī means "Reflection" (sīwéi).
Ajātaśatru means "Unborn Enemy" (wèishēngyuàn), or alternatively Vālaruci, meaning "Broken Finger.
He was given the name "Good Vision" (Shànjiàn) by his inner attendants out of protective consideration.
[Commentary] Regarding the first section of the third part, following the topical outline (*ko*), the initial portion of the sutra correctly explains the killing of the father.

This is divided into two parts. [Sūtra Commentary]: The first section consists of four parts: 1) Bimbisāra becomes his son and is imprisoned in seclusion; 2) the State Grand Lady secretly serves the king food to sustain his life;
3) after he has finished rinsing his mouth, the Sage preaches the Dharma for him to moisten the king’s heart.
Fourth, at this time, it is explained that due to food and also because of hearing the Dharma,
he did not die for many days. At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a crown prince named Ajātaśatru who,
following the evil teachings of his friend Devadatta, seized his father, King Bimbisāra, and confined him within seven layers of chambers, restricting all [contact].

[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "At that time" refers to when the Buddha was not far from the city at Vulture Peak Mountain.

Previously, Ajātaśatru was translated as "Unborn Enemy" (*Mishengyuan*); now the meaning is explained: on the day he was in the womb, there were signs of harm from an enemy, and a diviner predicted this in advance, and thus he was named accordingly.
○ Second, "In accordance with... and below clarifies the fifth [point]: complying with a friend to commit a transgression.
First, the explanation of the name and clan of the evil friend.
[Commentary]: "One who follows the teachings of the evil friend Devadatta"—Devadatta is here translated as "Heavenly Heat" (Tianre) and also as "Bestowed by Heaven" (Tianshou).
He was the son of King Droṇodana and the paternal cousin of the Buddha; he was the elder brother of Ānanda. Ānanda is translated here as "Joy" (Huanxi).
He is also called "The Undefiled" or "The Joyful. Devadatta had thirty characteristics of one who has left the household life;
he recited sixty thousand dharma-aggregates and mastered the twelve Vedas.
[Commentary]: The second section, "For the sake of profit," explains the schemes and arts of evil friends. First, he learns the arts from people.
[Commentary]: For the sake of gain and offerings, he went to the Buddha’s presence to seek instruction in supernatural powers (ṛddhi).

The Buddha did not teach him, but instead directed him to contemplate impermanence (*anitya*), saying that by this he could attain the Way himself. He then went to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and even to the five hundred disciples, but none of them taught him the method for attaining supernatural powers.
Ānanda, however, being his own younger brother, bestowed it upon him before he had attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Devadatta mastered the methods for attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and entered the mountains to train until he had acquired the five *abhijñās*.

[Commentary]: Ānanda’s own younger brother knew how to take up these methods; however, because Devadatta himself had not yet attained the *abhijñās*, he did not understand his [Ānanda’s] mind, and thus Ānanda bestowed them upon him.
○ Second, from "He thought in his heart" onwards, it describes how he lured others to join in a conspiracy.
[Commentary: He thought to himself, "Who is acting as the donor? Prince Ajātaśatru possesses the marks of a great king;
perhaps he has transformed himself into an elephant or a horse treasure to embrace and kiss the prince before him, and has further gone up to heaven to fetch celestial flowers and celestial food.

[Commentary] He fashioned elephant and horse treasures to deceive King Ajātaśatru with the affairs of a wheel-turning monarch, and by acts such as embracing him, he sought to engender affection in him.
○ Third, from "He spoke to the king" onwards, it clarifies the verbal instructions of the evil friend.
[Commentary] He said to the prince: "I shall become a new Buddha and you shall become a new king; would this not be joyful?
[Sub-commentary] This means that while I, following the True Teaching, commit the act of rebellion, you shall kill the Muni to become a new Buddha. You shall kill Bimbisāra to become a new king.
That a new king and a new Buddha together transform the world—would this not be most joyful? 4. Following... below.
[The Prince] Mingtai (Jiaye) commits a rebellion.
[Commentary (Shu): Following an evil friend, he seizes his father, the King. [Sub-commentary (Chao):
Jiaye, having received these instructions, proceeds to commit the act of parricide. ○ Fifth, [the section on] Tiabao (Devadatta) below clarifies how an evil friend commits a rebellion.
[Commentary]: Devadatta split the Saṃgha; Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana converted him and brought the community back together.
When he pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha, Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi brandished his vajra-staff at it, causing the rock to shatter and fly toward the Buddha, wounding the Buddha’s toe.
The Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā rebuked him and struck him with her fist, causing his eyes to pop out. Having committed these three ānantarya sins, he was born alive into hell.
[Commentary] Devadatta personally committed three of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) and further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father;

thus, having both personally performed and incited others to commit the preparatory acts for the remaining two—hearing his mother and killing an Arhat—he fell into hell due to these five heinous crimes. ○ Second, the prior causes of the father and son, beginning with "Bimbisāra... and so forth.
[Commentary]: In the past, when Bimbisāra was wandering about Mount Vipula hunting deer, he found none at all.
He encountered a rishi sitting in meditation and ordered his men to drive him away; they then proceeded to kill him. At the moment of death, the rishi harbored a malevolent thought, vowing:
"In my next life, may I still harm you with mind and speech, just as you have done today."
[Commentary]: Because the slain seer gave rise to an evil thought, he immediately came [as his son]; thus, even while still in the womb, there was the resentment of one who had harmed his father.
○ Second, from "In this way" onwards, the provisional transformation is summarized.
[Commentary: Such matters as these are all the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) manifested by the Great Being (Bodhisattva) as he practices upon what is not the Path to penetrate the Buddha-path.
Because the root-natures (*indriya-gotra*) of sentient beings differ, their entry into the Path varies—some through opposition and some through compliance.

To propagate the Way and benefit all things, he manifests conduct that appears uninterrupted, yet remains free from affliction or anger. King Ajātaśatru manifested opposition in order to cause evil people to cease [their wickedness] and not...
They manifest as rebels.
[The Commentary] states: Devadatta, Ajātaśatru, Bimbisāra, and Vaidehī were all great manifestations of expedient power; they manifested rebellion or compliance to benefit sentient beings.
Second, the two queens present food.
[Commentary: Second, it explains how the Queen presented the food.
The Queen Mother, named Vaidehī, respectfully bathed the Great King to ensure he was pure;
she then mixed parched grain flour with ghee and honey to smear upon his body. She placed grape juice within various necklaces and secretly offered them to the King. At that time, the Great...
The King ate parched grain flour (*piṣṭaka*), drank thin gruel (*mantha*), and sought water to rinse his mouth.

[Commentary: The King ate the flour, drank the gruel, and seeking water to rinse his mouth, joined his palms and paid homage from afar, requesting to receive the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) and bathe himself until pure.
△ Third, the two sages preached the Dharma for him.
Having finished rinsing his mouth, he joined his palms in reverence and, facing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, prostrated from afar to the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you are my dear friend; I pray that you will arouse compassion and bestow upon me the eight precepts.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana flew like a hawk or a falcon and arrived swiftly at the king's location. He bestowed the eight precepts upon the king every day in this manner, and the World-Honored One did so as well.
He dispatched the Venerable Pūrṇa to preach the Dharma for the king.

[Commentary] Regarding the three sages preaching the Dharma for him, there are two parts. First, the explanation of Maudgalyāyana bestowing the precepts; second, the explanation of his swift arrival. First, the explanation of his swift arrival.

[Commentary]: Maudgalyāyana was a disciple on the Buddha’s right side. In a past life, he was a pratyekabuddha who shaved his head and made a kaṣāya for him, vowing to attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
[Sub-commentary]: Because he had served a pratyekabuddha in a previous existence, he now attained supernatural powers and arrived swiftly at the king's location. (2)
The explanation of the precepts for the eightfold fast is conferred below.

[Commentary] To confer the eight precepts means: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, not drinking intoxicants, not wearing flowers or perfumes, not attending performances of music or dance, and not using high or luxurious beds—these eight constitute the precepts; one must not eat past midday.
In this *Abhidharma*, the wearing of perfumed garments and sitting upon high beds are not [prohibited]; since these are both places of adornment, they are combined into one.
[Commentary]:

First, the wearing of perfumed garments and sitting upon high beds were established as two separate items among the eight precepts of the Eightfold Fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), but subsequently they were merged.
Using perfumes, fine clothing, and high beds as the seventh, and abstaining from eating at improper times as the eighth—thus the fast (upavāsa) is contained within these eight;
in the Dharma there is no increase or decrease, though the enumeration may be expanded or condensed, it is all called the Eightfold Precept Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).
Second, the section below "Pūrṇa" explains how Pūrṇa preached the Dharma.
[Commentary: Pūrṇa is here translated as "Son of Full-Vow" (Mǎnyuàn zǐ) or "Son of Full-Love" (Mǎncí zǐ), named after his parents.
Because he was foremost in preaching the Dharma and skillfully opened the minds of others, he is specifically singled out and dispatched.
After this period of twenty-one days had passed, because the King had eaten parched grain and honey and been able to hear the Dharma, his complexion became harmonious and joyful.
[Commentary]: From "four bimbas" onwards, it describes how the Dharma-food prolongs his life.
[Commentary] Fourth, Piṇḍola, because he heard the Dharma while eating food, was able to remain alive for many days.
[Sub-commentary] Second, "Next, harming" and below clarify the two instances of intending to harm his mother; first, the division of the sections.
[Commentary] Next, regarding the section on harming his mother, it is divided into four parts: 1) the son’s confinement; 2) the invitation to the Buddha due to his imprisonment;

3) the Buddha and his disciples’ arrival in response to the invitation; 4) the sight of the Buddha, the expression of grief and admiration, and the request for the Dharma. Within the first part, there are again three sub-sections: 1) the desire to harm the mother;
2) the two ministers’ remonstrance and the refusal to listen to their plea against the harm; 3) the command to the palace officials to confine her.

[Commentary] Regarding the second [section], the first part consists of four sub-sections explaining the text in sequence. First, the prince was confined in secret; this has three parts. First, the desire to harm his mother; this has three parts.
First, the King asks whether he is there or not.
[Sub-commentary] First, King Jaśodharman asks the gatekeeper whether the King is present or not.
At that time, Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper, "Does the Father King still exist?
[Commentary] Under the second section on the gatekeepers, he answers according to the facts.
[Sub-commentary] The two gatekeepers answer according to the facts.

Then the gatekeeper addressed the Great King, saying: "The Queen Mother has anointed her body with parched rice flour and honey, and carrying a jeweled necklace filled with wine, she went to offer it to the King.
The śramaṇa Maudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa have come through the air and are preaching the Dharma for the King;
they cannot be restrained."
[Commentary: When the three kings heard this, they were filled with wrath.
Upon hearing these words, Ajātaśatru became enraged at his mother and said: "My mother is a thief and associates with thieves!

Thus we know that the Buddha’s power assists those who wish to see, enabling their contemplation to result in vision.
The subsequent text states: "All sentient beings contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss through the power of the Buddha."
Because one shall attain the vision of that pure land, one sees the Buddha through *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, which is discussed in terms of three powers:

first, the power of the Buddha; second, the power of samādhi; and third, the power of the practitioner’s own fundamental merit. Furthermore, "the mind" refers to the manifestation of the land within the light, which is seen with one's own eyes.
These two types of vision both arise from the resonance between cause and response (*ganying*); thus, though distant, it is near.

However, if the nature of the mind did not inherently contain the dust-motes and lands [of the universe], there would be no principle for the Buddhas to manifest in response, nor would sentient beings possess the capacity to perceive them through their own resonance;
therefore, when this sutra speaks of "this mind is Buddha," to contemplate this meaning while remaining deluded is not the wondrous essence of the teaching.

Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three kinds of merit: first, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, practicing compassion and refraining from killing, and cultivating the ten virtuous actions;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct;
third, generating the bodhicitta, deeply believing in cause and effect, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna sutras, and encouraging others to practice them. As it is said:
These three matters are called the pure karma. The Buddha said to Vaidehī: "Do you now understand?
These three kinds of karma are the direct causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the three periods of time."
[Commentary] Part Three: First, the Correct Demonstration of the Causes for Rebirth, in Two Sections. First, the Correct Demonstration, in Three Parts. First, karma shared with ordinary beings.

[Sub-commentary] The first [part] concerns the practice of filial piety toward one's parents, serving teachers and elders, respecting those above and assisting those below, and acting with a compassionate heart.

Cultivating the ten wholesome karmas constitutes the practice of cessation (*śamatha*): removing the three perversions of the body, abandoning the four transgressions of speech, and severing the three evils of the mind.

[Commentary]: Although this sutra is primarily intended for those of sudden-capacity practitioners, even when cultivating the conduct of a Buddha, how could one not [respect] one's parents and teachers?
If one serves the Wheel-Turning King with filial piety, how could the ten precepts not be practiced?

It is simply that when one cultivates them so that each thought accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), what harm is there in sharing the wholesome deeds of compassion and filial piety cultivated therein with ordinary beings? Second, the lower [level] shares in the karma of the Two Vehicles.
[Commentary] Second, regarding the Three Refuges, these are the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. "The lay precepts" refers to the ten precepts;

"fully possessing the multitude of precepts" means that both monastics and laity receive them all, observing even the most minute details without violation. "Maintaining dignified deportment" means that none of the three thousand rules of conduct are deficient.
[Commentary]: How could a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle contravene the monastic forms of the Hinayana, such as the three refuges, the various precepts, and the rules of decorum?
It is only that their mind of upholding [the precepts] accords with the One Body and relies upon the ultimate;
yet the dharmas they practice are common to those of the Two Vehicles. ○ Third, the non-common karma of the Mahayana.
[Commentary] Third, the arousal of the bodhicitta refers to the aspiration and mental orientation toward awakening; this is called "arousing the mind.
Bodhi is the Way and the fruition of Buddhahood, which is described as "perfect penetration" (pūrṇa-prativedha).
Because it can transport one across [to the goal], it is called a "vehicle" (yāna). Since the other two [vehicles] cannot compare to it, it is termed "Great" (mahā).
[Commentary] Relying on the realm of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), to give rise to a vow without an object of reference is called the "arising of the bodhicitta.

Its true nature is non-dual, yet it is established as dual through the distinction between cause and effect; though dual, it is non-dual, for the principle remains one from beginning to end. Only by believing in this causality can it be called "profound.

One who studies and recites the Mahāyāna, cultivates the understanding of the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*), and practices the conduct of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*)—teaching through such understanding and practice—is [the true practitioner].
The practitioner of these [practices] is called one who "exhorts and advances" these three types of karma.

Because those who attain the former do not necessarily attain the latter, while those who attain the latter must necessarily have attained the former, the practitioner today is able to cultivate the first two;
however, as the first two cannot cultivate the Mahāyāna, it is said that "the other two do not equal this," referring to the Mahāyāna. ○ Second, the Buddha said:
The following section concludes with an exaltation.
[Commentary]: The Buddha told Vaidehī, "These three types of karma are the fundamental causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time"—this is the language of exaltation.

[Commentary]: Since these are the deeds of the Buddha, it is verified that they are the result of perfect cultivation. Therefore, in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there is another "single practice" called the "Tathāgata Practice.
Although it is called a single practice, it actually encompasses five practices; likewise here, although these are the deeds of the Buddha, they encompass three types.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!
The Tathāgata now, for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages who are harmed by the thieves of affliction, shall expound the karma of purity.
Excellent, Vaidehī, that you have asked about this matter so joyfully!”
[Commentary] "Listen attentively" and so forth praise the question asked.

[Sub-commentary] "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. "Listen attentively" is intended to produce the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "reflect well" is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

and "retain it in mind" is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). As for "the thieves of affliction," these are so called because they can damage the life-force of wisdom and wound the Dharma-body.
They are thieves.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Listen attentively" and so forth: in all sutras, these words of admonition for listening are invariably intended to cause beings to give rise to the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).

One must examine the teachings to clarify whether the wisdom is partial or complete, as well as the relationship between that which listens and that which is heard, and that which contemplates and that which is contemplated.

If one contemplates what is to be contemplated with an understanding of arising and ceasing, this refers to the three wisdoms of the Tripiṭaka; if one has an understanding of non-arising, it refers to the three wisdoms of the Shared Teaching;

the immeasurable and the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings can be understood accordingly. Now, I cause Vaidehī and the others to give rise to the three wisdoms of the Perfect and Sudden teachings;
were it otherwise, how could they realize the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) in this very seat?
Ānanda, you should receive and uphold these words of the Buddha and proclaim them extensively for the sake of the great multitude.
The Tathāgata now instructs Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
By the power of the Buddha, they shall behold that pure land as clearly as seeing one’s own facial reflection when holding up a bright mirror. Thus shall they see it.

Because his mind was filled with joy due to the supreme and wondrous bliss of the land, he immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at that very moment.
[Commentary]: From "immediately attained" onwards, the entrustment to Ānanda is briefly mentioned.

[Commentary: One immediately attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Regarding this, the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) speaks of five patiences: first, subduing; second, faith;
third, conformity; fourth, non-arising; and fifth, extinction. This [attainment] corresponds to the first stage of the first dwelling.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "the sutra is like holding a bright mirror," etc.: one contemplates the Dharma as a mirror and cultivates it as if holding it;

when the contemplation is perfected, the land appears just as a facial reflection appears in a mirror. This indicates that by possessing three kinds of pure karma externally and being fully equipped with the sixteen subtle contemplations internally, one attains such vision.
Although this briefly addresses the intent of pure karma, it is actually explaining the subtle contemplations for those at the initial stage (Prathama-bhūmi) and the first ground (Prathamā bhūmi).

To abide perfectly in the distinct stages while simultaneously shattering ignorance is the stage of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), the wondrous and profound position of the single reality. The *Miaoxuan* states:
"If one enters the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*), one is precisely shattering ignorance; this is the stage of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* in the Perfect Teaching.

My present intention in citing the five types of patience from the *Ratnarāśi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) is to demonstrate that the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* resides above the three [lower] patiences. If one relies on...

In the Separate Teaching (*prātibhedika-yāna*), there are the Ten Faiths as the Patience of Subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), the Ten Abidings as the Patience of Faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the Ten Practices as the Patience of Accordance (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the Ten Grounds as the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and Wondrous Enlightenment as the Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). If categorized according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) stages: the Five Ranks are the Patience of Subduing;

the Purity of the Six Sense Organs comprises both the Patience of Faith and the Patience of Accordance; from the First Abiding up to Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*) is termed the Patience of Non-arising; and Wondrous Enlightenment is termed the Patience of Quiescent Extinction. However...
Since the first stage (*bhūmi*) is identical to the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching, one should cite the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) to verify this present position.

Practitioners should know that when the Tathāgata was about to expound the sixteen contemplative methods, he prefigured what he was to say by declaring that these were the perfect and subtle contemplations; thus he said:

"If all sentient beings contemplate the Ultimate Bliss and their contemplation is perfected, they shall immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, Vaidehī...
Regarding the statement that "hearing the teaching on the sixteen contemplations following speech" constitutes the realization of this wondrous stage:

the sutra demonstrates that these contemplations are the direct and swift gateway for attaining the first dwelling (bhūmi). Therefore, one must not say they are merely conceptualizations of phenomena.
II. First, clarifying the [sixteen] below; second, clarifying the sixteen wondrous contemplations as the answer to "correct reception. A. First, the division of sections.

[Commentary] First, it clarifies the reason why Vaidehī beheld the land; next, through one question and answer, it clarifies the method for requesting to see the land for the sake of future sentient beings.
The Buddha told Vaidehī: "You are an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
your mental conceptions are weak and inferior, and you have not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), so you cannot see from afar."
"Observe that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess diverse skillful means (upāya) which enable you to see [this land].
[Commentary] Second, "You are... and below follows the sequential explanation in two parts; first, it clarifies the reason why Vaidehī was able to see the land.
[Commentary]: You are an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); this clarifies your status, as you are unable to observe from afar.

Vaidehī is, in fact, a great Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in this very assembly. However, she manifests as being among ordinary people because her mental faculties are weak and inferior, and she has not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to perceive from afar.
To enable you to see that land, there is a distinct skillful means (*upāya*) for seeing that realm from another direction.

"Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers here to the sixteen contemplations; it is not merely that the name "contemplation" signifies expedient means. Because one sees that land through the power of the Buddha, this too is an expedient means.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "not yet having attained the divine eye," etc.: A questioner asks, "Aniruddha’s divine eye is the most supreme, yet he only sees [a limited distance]."
Question: Is it possible for one who has attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to see the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) across hundreds of thousands of billions of lands? Answer:

This statement cannot yet be definitively established, because the divine eye of a Bodhisattva who has attained true realization is not that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Therefore, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fascicle 22, states:
"The pure divine eye obtained by a Bodhisattva is different from that obtained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; it is by virtue of this difference [that he can see it]."
Therefore, it is said that at one time they see all the Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions; the *Mahā-śāstra* explains this in the same way.

That Vaidehī was indeed a great Bodhisattva reveals that Vaidehī originally dwells in the Dharma-body, yet she manifested in the manner of an ordinary person in order to inspire the practice of the visualization of the Pure Land.
As for the phrase "those in this assembly who immediately attained the realization of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), "immediately" (*jì*) refers to the present moment.

It is because at this assembly, [Vimalakīrti] heard that [Vaidhaya] was about to realize the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); it does not mean that the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) mentioned in the preceding text was realized by Vaidhaya.
That preceding passage is a general statement regarding future sentient beings who, by practicing the sixteen contemplations, can attain non-arising.
When [the Buddha] showed that human vision is the same as that of ordinary beings, one must not immediately conclude that the preceding text refers to what was realized by Vaidhaya.
To know [this] is to have attained it, yet it is not as if it were already attained. Since they are called "actual great bodhisattvas," they are those who have long realized non-arising;
yet, according to their manifested traces, they are said to be ordinary beings. Their mental conceptions are weak and inferior, and they manifest as inferior ordinary beings.

By practicing this, they attain patience (*kṣānti*), thereby revealing this wondrous contemplation. It can transform base ordinary beings and suddenly bring about the perfection of a sage. This differs from other skillful means in sixteen ways.
Contemplating the phenomena is a marvelous skillful means; thus, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"The sūtras teach a superior skillful means of binding the mindfulness to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to cause rebirth in that land. This does not mean that merely contemplating the name is the skillful means.

This refers to two skillful means regarding the primary and secondary [recompenses] (*adhiṣṭhāna-adhibhoga*), by which ordinary beings of this land can attain vision: first, the cultivation of contemplation and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Through skillful means, he causes the mind’s eye to see the two Buddhas; through the skillful means of manifesting supernatural power, he enables one to witness them with the physical eyes.
Since there are two ways by which this vision is attained, it is said that it is not merely direct observation (the departing tone for *guàn*) that constitutes the skillful means.
That the Buddha’s power causes one to see is itself a skillful means, whereby Vaidehī attains these two kinds of vision: the first is that which is about to arise in accordance with...
The commentary explains that by contemplating this, one sees both [the pure land and the impure world], which is a vision manifested through the Buddha’s power;
thus it is called "the reason why Vaidehī saw the land.
At that time, Vaidehī said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as I do now, by the power of the Buddha, I see that land."
"World-Honored One, if after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings are oppressed by the five sufferings of the turbid, evil, and unwholesome age,
how shall they be able to see Amitābha Buddha and the world of Ultimate Bliss?"
[Commentary]: The section beginning with "The two Vaidehīs" constitutes the second part, which requests the method for seeing the land for the sake of future generations;

this is divided into two, the first being the request itself. [Sub-commentary]: When Vaidehī said to the Buddha, "As I am now," and so forth, she was requesting on behalf of sentient beings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

"Turbidity" refers to the five turbidities; "unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome actions; and "five sufferings" refers to the five realms of existence, which are not true happiness—thus they are called the "five."
Suffering consists of the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings. The five evils are killing, excessive lust, false speech, and drinking intoxicants, as manifested in the Great Sūtras.
The five pains refer to encountering calamities and hardships, or being subjected to the punishments of the king’s law.

The five burnings refer to the bitter poisons of falling into the three miserable realms in the future; these are called the five burnings. How can one come to behold the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha?
The Earth Deity (Pṛthivī) formally makes the request.
[Commentary]: Vimalakīrti first had her manifest skillful means to make the request; for this reason, the Sūtra says:
"Just as I now, by the power of the Buddha, see that land. Nevertheless, she formally requests the skillful means for contemplating the Dharma.
Because sentient beings serve as the condition for this request, the Sūtra states:

"If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings are oppressed by the five sufferings of turbid, evil, and unwholesome [deeds], how shall they behold the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Regarding these "five sufferings," the Commentary provides two interpretations:
first, interpreting them as the lack of bliss in the five destinies; second, interpreting them as the retributions summoned by the five transgressions. This is the first interpretation.
The suffering of burning in hell; the suffering of hunger and thirst among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); the suffering of being slaughtered and dismembered among animals (*tiryagyoni*);
the eight kinds of suffering in the human realm; and the suffering of the five signs of decline in the heavenly realms. Next, regarding the explanation: the Sage’s intention is manifold.
To further clarify how the five evils invite these two names, it is stated in the *Mūla-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, which is here referred to as the *Mahāsūtra*. This is the commentary text.

First, the names of the three and five are listed; next, from the "five evils" downward, the text explains the "three and five killings," which constitute the causes for the fifth evil, drinking alcohol.
As explained in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (Da jing), the subsequent section on the "five pains" refers to the retributive results in this life (*huabao*).

The following section on the "five burnings" explains the five burnings as the karmic fruition (*guobao*). However, although these two types of retribution are both devoid of fixed numerical characteristics, each is designated as "five" based on their respective [causal] origins.
Because they are established based on five kinds of evil causes, the five passages that follow all conclude by stating:
"This constitutes one great evil, one pain, and one burning," and so on, up to the general statement: "Thus there are five great evils, five pains, and five burnings.

Therefore, we know that both sets of five are established according to their causes. II. The Response. Part One: Listing the Contemplations and Dividing the Sections. Part Two: Listing the Contemplations.

[Commentary] Among the answers, there are sixteen contemplations: 1. Contemplation of the Sun; 2. Contemplation of Water; 3. Contemplation of the Ground; 4. Contemplation of the Trees; 5. Contemplation of the Ponds; 6.
General Contemplation of all towers, grounds, ponds, and so forth; 7. Contemplation of the Flowered Seat; 8. Contemplation of the Images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
9. Contemplation of the Buddha’s Body; 10. Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara; 11. Contemplation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta; 12. [The twelfth...]
13. Universal Rebirth Contemplation; 14. Miscellaneous Clarifications on the Contemplation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; 15. Superior Grade Rebirth Contemplation;
16. Middle Grade Rebirth Contemplation; 17. Inferior Grade Rebirth Contemplation.

[Commentary] The *Yili* (Examples of Meaning) states: "As for the three contemplations (*sanguan*), their meaning consists of only three types: First, 'following practice' (*cong xing*): this involves contemplating the single mind within the myriad objects.
Although the myriad objects differ, the principle of the wondrous contemplation is equal; the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth is precisely its intended meaning.
Second, 'concerning the characteristics of phenomena' (*yue faxiang*): as in the passage concerning the Four Truths and the Five Practices, one enters them into a single moment of mind."

The third type, "Perfect Contemplation by Relying on Phenomena" (*yuan guan san tuo shi*), refers to names such as Rājagṛha or Gṛdhrakūṭa, which are established based on phenomena; one borrows these phenomena as objects of contemplation to guide the deluded mind. Examples from the Vaipulya scriptures, such as those concerning Samantabhadra, can be recognized as following this pattern. Question: Among these three types, to which category do the sixteen contemplations of the present [scripture] belong? Answer: Since they do not merely summarize the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to enter the mind and form contemplation, it is clear that they do not belong to the first two categories. Furthermore, because they are not yet fully integrated with the ultimate principle, they cannot be classified as the third either. Therefore, they must be understood as a distinct category. This is because the sixteen contemplations are established by taking the physical features of the Buddha’s land as their basis, thereby inducing the practitioner to visualize the Buddha’s land through the medium of these phenomena. Consequently, they are neither identical to nor different from the aforementioned three types. This is why the *Sutra* states: "If there is anyone who wishes to see the Buddha of Infinite Life, they should contemplate the Buddha’s land. This is because the land is the dwelling place of the Buddha; thus, by contemplating the land, one naturally comes to see the Buddha. It is for this reason that the *Sutra* says: "If one contemplates the Buddha’s land, one will see the Buddha. This is the meaning of the phrase "contemplating the Buddha’s land" in the *Sutra*. It is not that one first contemplates the land and only afterwards sees the Buddha. Rather, it means that by contemplating the land, one simultaneously sees the Buddha. This is because the land is the Buddha’s abode; therefore, when the land is contemplated, the Buddha is necessarily seen. For example, when one enters a king’s palace, one necessarily sees the king. Thus, the contemplation of the land is the contemplation of the Buddha. This is why the *Sutra* says: "If one contemplates the Buddha’s land, one will see the Buddha. This is the meaning of the phrase "cont

Furthermore, the "attached dharmas" (*fufa*) do not establish the object or the contemplation by borrowing from the meaning of those external phenomena; thus, it is clear that they do not rely on phenomena for their clarification.
The Tathāgata’s direct discourse on the sixteen gates of contemplative practice and realization is precisely concerned with following the practice itself. [The interlocutor] asks:

"The three types of 'Meaning Examples' (*yili*) are all contemplations of principle (*li guan*); how then are the sixteen [contemplations] of today—which rely sequentially upon the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants—related to these three types?"

Answer: Regarding the two types of the three contemplations—those based on phenomena (*dharmas*) and those based on events (*vastus*)—and their respective aspects of event and principle (*tattva*), let us set them aside for now.

As for the three contemplations practiced according to conduct (*caryā*), for what reason can they not proceed sequentially through each event? Since it is said that they follow conduct, there must be four modes of conduct;

even in the single practice of constant sitting (*ekāsanika*), one directly contemplates the principle. How could the other three samādhis not also involve events, as in the case of the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Banzhou sanmei)?

The *Guan li nianfo shi* (Contemplation on Successive Acts of Mindfulness of the Buddha) corresponds to the three contemplations of the Vaipulya [sūtras]; the *Li chizhou shi* (Successive Practice of Holding Mantras) corresponds to the three contemplations of the *Lotus Sūtra*;

the *Li songjing shi* (Successive Practice of Reciting Sūtras) corresponds to the three contemplations of the *Qing Guanyin* (Invoking Avalokiteśvara); the *Li shuxi shi* (Successive Practice of Counting the Breath) corresponds to the three contemplations of the *Jueyi* (Awakening the Mind);

and the *Li sanxing shi* (Successive Practice of the Three Natures) [corresponds to the same]. If these successive practices were not subsumed under the category of "practice" (*xing*), to what would they belong? They are fully encompassed by the initial contemplation of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*.

From the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel at the soles downward, one contemplates in reverse order up to the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*. When contemplating those marks, one employs the three contemplations;
since that is based on practice, why now alone is it not so? Furthermore, as for the principle of analogy, it says: "One contemplates the single mind within ten thousand objects.
How could it be that the primary and secondary [marks] here are not all of one mind? For the *Sūtra* itself lists the characteristics of sixteen objects in detail.
The Master merely indicates the three perfect contemplations (*yuan san guan*) in the title of the work, intending for one to employ these contemplations to observe the sixteen objects;

this shows that although the ten thousand objects differ, their principle is equal within the wondrous contemplation. Furthermore, if the present three contemplations and the various sequential three contemplations were not "from practice" (*cong xing*) and so forth, why would it say that the meaning of the three contemplations consists of only three types?
Question: In the present sutra, regarding only the Semblance Dharma (*xiangfa*)...

The *Guanshi* (Contemplation and Instruction) states: "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Since none of these passages contain the phrase "contemplating the principle," one knows that everything other than the Buddha consists of phenomenal contemplation (*shiguan*).
Even if one were to apply this principle as an analogy for contemplating the fifteen [aspects], this would be the practitioner’s intent to employ the contemplation of principle (*liguan*).
However, based on the explicit text of the sutra, it is merely phenomenal contemplation. [Question: If one were to practice according to the sutra itself...

Regarding the contemplation of the entry into realization (*praveśa-sākṣātkriyā*), why is it necessary to rely on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) to explain the intent of the sūtras and establish the methods of contemplation?

Because the Great Master profoundly grasped the Buddha’s intent, he explained the contemplating subject (*sākṣātkartṛ*) in the title as the "wondrous three contemplations" (*myō san-gen*) and the contemplated object (*sākṣātkarman*) as the "wondrous three bodies" (*myō san-shin*).
He stated: "Although 'contemplation' (*kan*) consists of sixteen [aspects], when one speaks of the Buddha, it is already complete. Now, we shall follow the Great Master and employ these three.
When the *Miaoguan* (Sublime Contemplation) contemplates the sixteen objects, how could this be merely the practitioner’s own subjective application of contemplative intent?
One should know that among the four kinds of samādhi, there is none that does not contemplate the principle of the three truths within phenomena.

However, in cases such as the *Banzhou sanmei* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi), because the mental faculty relies upon meditative concentration and allows the wholesome or unwholesome phenomena of daily activities to proceed freely, it specifically receives the name "contemplating phenomena" (*lishi*). This is not the case with practices such as constant sitting (*changzuo*).
One directly contemplates the Three Truths within the affairs of the three realms, rather than concurrently practicing good or indulging in evil;
thus, it receives the name "receiving instruction. How could the contemplative method of this present sutra differ from the four samādhis?

Therefore, we know that these sixteen [contemplations] are precisely the practice of traversing phenomena to contemplate principle. One should understand that all sixteen employ the three contemplations as their mental objects.
Because the three contemplations of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are subtle, one first contemplates the setting sun and clear water;

as these three contemplations gradually become manifest, one then contemplates the earth, trees, the seat, and the body of the Buddha. For all objects below these, one must likewise employ the three contemplations.
○ Second, the classification of the ten lower sections.

[Commentary]: Regarding the sixteen contemplations, the text is divided into three parts: first, six contemplations observe the "retributive environment" (*āśraya-phala*); second, seven contemplations observe the "primary retribution" (*mukhya-vipāka*);
and third, three contemplations clarify the rebirths of the three grades and nine levels.

[Commentary] Dividing the sixteen contemplations into three categories, six belong to the environment (niśraya-vipāka). The sun indicates the direction for sending one's thoughts, and the ice represents the ground of lapis lazuli;
although these are objects of this land, they are intended to manifest the realm of that [Pure Land]. Therefore, the six contemplations all pertain to the environment of that land.
Seven belong to the primary retribution (sattva-vipāka): the seat is the direct support for the Three Sages, and its appearance resembles the Three Sages themselves.
Because their true essence is identical, the seven contemplations are all termed the "correct retribution" for the persons of the three grades.
From this world to that world, the cultivation of causes and the entrustment of substance differ in their phenomenal characteristics; therefore, these three constitute a single category. II.

Following the topical outline, the explanation of the first [section] below has three parts. First, the six contemplations observe the "dependent retribution. The first is the contemplation of the sun, which has two initial sections. First, the establishment [of the practice].
Sectioning the Text by Topic.

[Commentary] The first part, "The Contemplation of the Sun," shows how to fix the mind. From "The Buddha said" below, it briefly explains fixing the mindfulness and provides a general exhortation to practice the contemplation.
From "How" below, it correctly explains the performance of the contemplation of the sun. From "All those with eyes see the sun set" below, it provides an illustration.
Regarding the object of contemplation, one should give rise to the visualization; the subsequent instruction on observation constitutes the conclusion of this section.

[Commentary] First, perform the visualization of the sun with the intention of binding the mind. Since the ordinary mind is dark and distracted, how could it clearly perceive the wondrous realm of the Pure Land?

Therefore, one is instructed to focus exclusively on the form of the setting sun; by binding the mind upon this single object and contemplating it without ceasing, its image will gradually become clear.
The mind shall be concentrated; if the mind is calm and subtle, one may cultivate various methods of contemplation.

Regarding the method for binding the mind, it must be directed toward the setting sun, so that the thought of concentration may incline toward the west, as that is the direction where Amitābha resides.
○ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the general exhortation to practice the visualization.
The Buddha told Vaidehī: "You and all sentient beings should single-mindedly fix your attention on one place and visualize the West.
[Commentary]:
In the sutra, the phrase "Vaidehī and all sentient beings" refers to Vaidehī and others who are the present recipients of the teaching.
Since all sentient beings are the potential recipients (*bhājana*) for the future, it is known that the cultivation of contemplation does not depend exclusively upon the Buddha’s own era;

how much more so since Vaidehī was the initiator [of this teaching], and the primary purpose is for people of the present to request the correct method of practice. For this reason, our Buddha exhorted sentient beings to cultivate the Dharma.
How could such cultivation be restricted to a single location, namely the Western [Pure Land]? Second, regarding the section beginning with "How," it is the actual [explanation].
Tomorrow, regarding the three initial stages, first we shall set forth the object of contemplation.
How does one form mental images? Generally speaking, when forming mental images, all sentient beings—unless they are born blind—are among those with eyes who see the sun set.
[Commentary] The meaning of the sutra passage is as follows: those who have previously seen the sun, or see it currently setting, take that appearance as the object of contemplation.
This meditation is universally applicable to all, with the sole exception of those born blind or those whose both eyes are blind;
since they do not recognize the sun, they are unable to form a mental image of it. However, even those who were once sighted but are now blind may still practice this meditation.

To illustrate this with a present example: when one clearly sees the sun with one's own eyes, it is easy to cultivate [the visualization] by taking that very sun as the object and imagining it so that the sun within the meditative observation arises.
Second, one should proceed to the actual instruction for observation.

One should give rise to the thought of sitting upright facing west and contemplate intently the place where the sun is about to set, causing the mind to remain firmly fixed and the visualization to be unwavering.
Seeing the sun about to set, its appearance is like a suspended drum; once the sun has been seen, whether with eyes closed or open, one must ensure it remains clearly manifest.
