According to the topical outline, the sutra is divided into three parts: First, the initial section on the power of light subduing and naming the sons; second, the detailed exposition of all the lights. 1. The initial section on the power of light subduing and naming the sons is divided into two parts:
first, the universal manifestation of all the lights.
Next, one contemplates Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The dimensions of this bodhisattva’s body are likewise like those of Avalokiteśvara;
his halo and face each measure one hundred and twenty-five yojanas, illuminating two hundred and fifty yojanas.
The light from his entire body shines upon the lands of the ten directions, appearing the color of purple gold, such that all sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection are able to see him.
[Commentary] Second, "But seeing... and below correctly establishes two names.

Because one sees the light from a single pore of this bodhisattva and thereby sees the pure and wondrous radiance of the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, this bodhisattva is named Boundless Light (*Anantaprabha*).
By means of the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all things.
Because he leaves behind the three miserable realms and attains supreme power, this Bodhisattva is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. [Commentary]:
Because his light illuminates the ten directions, he is given the name Amitābha (Boundless Light).

Because he enables those in the three miserable realms to attain the ten powers of a Buddha, he is given the name Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Great Power Attained). A practitioner should know that the light of his entire body is raised up as wisdom.
Hui-guang [argues] that because these are adjacent to the ultimate, matter and mind are non-dual; were it otherwise, how could the marks of matter be called the Dharma-body?
II. Clarifying the similarities and differences with Avalokiteśvara, divided into three sub-sections: First, "This Bodhi... and below, correctly clarifying the similarities and differences.
This Bodhisattva’s celestial crown has five hundred jewel-flowers;
each jewel-flower has five hundred jewel-terraces, and within each terrace, the vast and expansive characteristics of the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear.
His usnīṣa on the crown of his head is like an udumbara flower, and atop this usnīṣa is a single jewel-vase filled with various radiances.
He universally manifests Buddha-activities, and his other physical characteristics are no different from those of Avalokiteśvara and others.
[Commentary]: Second, "This Bodhisattva... and below further demonstrate his walking and sitting.
When this Bodhisattva walks, all the worlds of the ten directions tremble; at the places where the earth shakes, there are five hundred...
Each of the billions of jewel lotuses was magnificently adorned and exalted, like those in the world of Sukhāvatī.
When these bodhisattvas sat upon them, the lands of the seven jewels shook all at once;
from the Buddha-field of Golden Light below to the Buddha-field of King of Radiance above, throughout this interval, there appeared immeasurable dust-motes of emanations of the Buddha Amitāyus.
The Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta all gathered like clouds in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, filling the void;
seated upon lotus thrones, they expounded the wondrous Dharma to deliver sentient beings from suffering.

[Commentary]: Does the walking or sitting of Avalokiteśvara not likewise cause the earth to tremble and assemble the Buddhas? It is simply that these are described within the visualization of Śrī-Ālokita.
If this were not the case, how could it be said that, "except for the jeweled vase upon his head, he is otherwise no different from Avalokiteśvara"?
Third, from "performing this" onwards, the characteristics of the visualization are established.
One who performs this visualization is said to be visualizing and beholding the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
this is called the eleventh visualization, the visualization of the physical marks of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "The characteristics of form. The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states that if the Dharma-body were not entirely form, it would be mind;

since form is created by mind, how can the characteristics of form be called the Dharma-body? This refers to the Dharma-body of the single realm of the Three Truths, which gives rise to the prajñā-phase of the three contemplations within one mind.
When the characteristics are seen in their profound correspondence, the three liberations are perfectly manifested; therefore, it is called "Buddha."
The *Commentary* states: "The Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance involves entering into correspondence with the mind;
without this correspondence, the sublime signs will not arise. (0) Third, the section beginning with "Eliminating [sins]" below encourages practice by means of the destruction of offenses.
One who performs this contemplation eliminates the sins of birth and death throughout countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;

such a person does not dwell within a womb but constantly wanders through the pure and wondrous lands of all Buddhas. Once this contemplation is perfected, one is said to be fully endowed with the contemplations of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

[Commentary]: Regarding the title "The Contemplation Fully Possessing Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta," it is because these two Bodhisattvas differ only in two respects—the transformation Buddha atop their heads and the jeweled flask—while all other characteristics are identical. Because the similarities and differences are clearly distinguished, it is called the "Contemplation of Full Vision.
Sixth: The Twelfth, the Universal Rebirth Contemplation. Part One: The Structural Outline. Part Two: The First [Section]. Part One: The Correspondence.

[The section on] Distinguishing the Differences between the Universal Contemplation and the Universal Mixture. [Commentary: Why are the twelfth [section], the Universal Contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*), and the Universal Mixture (*sāmānyasaṃkīrṇa*) established as two distinct categories?

The Universal Contemplation involves forming the thought of going to oneself [to the Buddha-land] and contemplating each object of that realm in detail. The Universal Mixture clarifies the spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [whereby they manifest themselves] spontaneously.
Because they transform such that their size is not constant and is indeterminate, or because they manifest according to objects, they are called "mixed" (*miśra*);
this serves as the distinction [from the preceding]. [Commentary]: Second, regarding the "Universal" (*sāmānya*), the section is divided based on the categories of "middling" and "inferior."

[Commentary: Within the section on "Universal [Visualization]," there are two parts. First, from the passage "When one sees this matter, one should give rise to one's own mind" onwards, it describes the mental visualization of oneself going there.
Second, from the passage "The transformation bodies of Amitāyus Buddha" onwards, it describes the manifestation of the transformation bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to appear.
[Commentary] Regarding the two scriptural passages, first is the clarification of the visualization of one’s own body going [to the Pure Land].

When seeing this scene, one should give rise to the thought from within oneself that one has been born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) and is sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower.
One should form the visualization of the lotus flower closing and the visualization of the lotus flower opening. When the lotus flower opens, there are five [aspects].
Visualize that light of a hundred colors comes to illuminate your body and your eyes open, seeing Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the void of space.
Imagine that the sounds produced by water, birds, trees, and forests, as well as those of all the Buddhas, all expound the wondrous Dharma in accordance with the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
When emerging from meditative absorption, remember and maintain this without loss. Having seen these things, it is called "seeing Amitāyus Buddha."
The twelfth contemplation is the Universal Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Commentary]:

Although the various contemplations discussed above—whether following the sequence of the primary and secondary, or the sequence of the principal and subordinate—have all been successfully accomplished through visualization, they were not yet universal or comprehensive;

furthermore, one had not yet visualized one's own body being born there and seeing it directly. Therefore, this contemplation now requires one to visualize that one’s own body will ultimately be reborn there.

At that time, Universal Vision (Samantadarśin) is not merely the realm of individual observation; rather, it is the sudden fulfillment and rebirth through the accomplishment of mental visualization, which may be compared to the preceding text’s contemplation of the "recompensed environment" (*niṣyanda-bhājanaloka*).

While the initial stage involves specific observations of trees, ponds, and so forth, and the subsequent stage involves the comprehensive vision of the four matters once the tower-observation is perfected—thereby termed "universal observation" (*sāmānyālambana*)—here one is only able to universally visualize the four matters of the recompensed environment as they arise through mental conception.

Because he universally sees and universally hears all aspects of both the primary and secondary realms, he is called "Universal Contemplation" (Puguān). [Question: Now, those of the highest grade of the highest birth ride the diamond platform;
those of the highest grade of the middle birth ride the purple-gold platform; and those of the highest grade of the lower birth enter the golden lotus flower.

Since the contemplations of the Three Sages have now been accomplished, one should then practice Universal Contemplation. Why, then, is this [Universal Contemplation] assigned to those of the highest grade of the highest birth?
Is this the same as being born in the lower grade of the highest level? Answer: Regarding the sixteen contemplations in relation to the nine grades of practice, there are many interpretations.
For now, let us proceed generally: those accomplished through the three holy contemplations and the universal contemplation constitute the "corresponding" upper-middle grade;

those accomplished through the four contemplations of the three ranks constitute the "actual" upper-upper grade. Therefore, although one sees [the Buddha] seated at the conclusion of the upper-middle grade, [it does not yet correspond to the actual upper-upper grade].
The "Purple-Golden Terrace" refers to this terrace reaching that [Pure Land] to become a great jewel-flower, which opens after having spent one night there.
This text also states that one is born in the realm of Ultimate Bliss seated upon a lotus flower; one should form the visualization of the flower opening and closing.

When the lotus flower opens, one sees Buddhas filling the void as they preach the wondrous Dharma—this precisely accords with the characteristics of being born in the highest grade of the middle class. As for the flower of the highest grade of the lower class...

After seven days had passed, he was finally able to see the Buddha; yet, because his mind was not yet clear regarding the various marks [of the Buddha], one knows that this passage corresponds precisely to the stage of "birth" (jāti-lakṣaṇa) in the Middle Grade.
If one were to correlate these grades with the distinct and perfect stages [of the Tiantai system], it would be possible to discuss them in detail only upon reaching the third grade of contemplation.
Second, from "immeasurable" onwards, it clarifies the manifestation of the three sages.

The Buddha of Immeasurable Life manifests countless transformation bodies, which, together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, constantly come to the place where this practitioner resides. [Commentary]:

In the previous visualization, one contemplates being born in that land after death and seeing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; now, while the visualization has not yet concluded, one contemplates the Three Holy Ones.
That they constantly come to enter my thoughts is fundamentally because the present moment of mindfulness is itself the limit of the future; thus, one is able to anticipate events yet to arise.
Furthermore, because the essence of the Buddhas and sentient beings is not distinct, this causes the Three Sages to come without coming.
This is achieved by the simultaneous operation of the three contemplations within a single mind, whereby the mind and the Buddhas travel there and come here.
Know that the essence of contemplation is beyond words and thought. (7) Thirteenth: Miscellaneous Clarification of the Contemplations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Now, in evaluating this contemplation, there are briefly two intentions: first, for those who have not succeeded in the superior marks of the previously contemplated Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it causes them to abandon the [vast] great forms and contemplate the sixteen-foot [image]; second, for those who have already perfected the contemplation of the aforementioned superior marks.
This causes them to further contemplate the superior and inferior modes of transformative activity throughout the worlds of the ten directions, thereby causing their stages and ranks to advance.
If one were to say this is not so, what benefit would there be in practicing the subsequent contemplations once the preceding ones have already been accomplished?

The Commentary (Sūtra-śāstra) follows the former intention and thus provides a clarification to dispel doubts and generate a deeper understanding; for those who have accomplished these contemplations know for themselves the meaning of the Sūtra. Therefore, the Great Master [Huiyuan]...
The initial intent is shown by explaining this in two parts: first, the division of sections.
[Commentary] The thirteenth section, "Miscellaneous Contemplations," has two parts: first, contemplating the sixteen-foot image;
second, the boundless body-measure of Amitāyus Buddha. Below, it clarifies the sovereign transformation of Amitābha, so that the practitioner may always remain steadfast.
Practice the contemplation with tireless cultivation.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the sequential explanation, there are two parts. First, from "The Buddha addressed... onwards, it concerns the contemplation of the sixteen-foot image.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "If you wish to give rise to a sincere mind to reach the Western Land, you should first contemplate..."
The image one *zhang* and six *chi* tall appears upon the surface of the pond water.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "If one desires... and so forth: although the practitioner has not practiced for long the various meditations on the primary and secondary marks before them, their intent to seek rebirth there becomes increasingly earnest and focused;
this is called "sincere mind" (*zhìxīn*). Because of this, it causes such a person to abandon the superior and take up the inferior.
Because one has not yet contemplated the two attendants but first contemplates Amitābha, it is said that one should first contemplate the image one zhang and six chi tall.
Since the practitioner wishes to entrust themselves to the lotus pond of that land, they are instructed to contemplate the image upon the waters of the pond.

One should know that since this superior body is produced by the mind, and the mind is [ultimately] empty, how could this present image of one zhang and six chi not also be a mental construction? For the person of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), both "creation" and "action" are fully understood as such.

The mind alone is entirely possessed and transforms; that which is entirely transformed is itself the possession. Since possession and transformation are non-dual, this applies equally to the observation of whether the marks of the Buddha are superior or inferior.
○ Second, clarifying the sub-section on Amitābha’s manifestations, part two: first, showing how the transforming subject accords with sentient beings;
second, beginning with "As previously [stated]," exhorting constant cultivation of the visualization.
As previously stated, the physical dimensions of Amitāyus Buddha are boundless and beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings;
nevertheless, by virtue of that Tathāgata’s power of past vows, anyone who brings him to mind will surely achieve success.
Merely contemplating the Buddha’s image yields immeasurable merit, let alone visualizing the Buddha’s body endowed with all its perfect marks.
[Commentary]: The second section, "Amitā," clears away the doubts of the multitude.
Amitābha Buddha’s spiritual powers are as he wishes; he manifests with sovereign ease throughout the lands of the ten directions.
He may manifest a great body that fills the void of space, or he may manifest a small body of one zhang and six chi or eight chi. Whatever forms he manifests are all of a true golden color.
The halo, the emanated Buddhas, and the precious lotus flowers are as described above.
[Commentary] In the first part of the second section of the *Śū*, from "the object of contemplation" onwards, the characteristics are shown and doubts are addressed.
[Śū] Whether large or small, all that is contemplated is the body of the Buddha; this sweeps away the various doubts and gives rise to profound reverence in people.
"How can the assembly have doubts?
[Commentary] 2. "Previously heard... and below indicates the doubt and clarifies its resolution.

[Sub-commentary] Previously, one heard of the vast and immeasurable; now, hearing that the contemplation is small, one suspects it is not the Buddha’s body and thus fails to show respect for the small.
Therefore, it is necessary to sweep away [this doubt] and clarify that these are all the Buddha generating this profound intention.
[Commentary]: Although one may not achieve success in the practice of the visualization of the Victorious Body (Sambhava-kāya), one can still realize its vastness and immeasurability.

Now, hearing of the visualization of the Small [Pure Land], one suddenly finds it to contradict what was previously taught; how could one avoid a slight suspicion? To sweep away this doubt, the divine power of Amitābha is explained.
The supernatural power of mastery over the mind can make one large or small, fully encompassing the entire Dharma-realm;

simply contemplate with a sincere heart to bring this to accomplishment, and do not doubt that when the body perishes, you will not fail to be born in the Western Land. II. Clarifying Birth Together with Those in the Position of Successor.
A. First, from "Observing the World" onwards, clarifying birth together with those in the form of inferior response.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta manifest bodies identical to sentient beings in all places. [Commentary]:
Since the Buddha’s response conforms to the myriad things, those who occupy the position of succession likewise manifest in the same manner as sentient beings. II.
From "But observe" below, the method of contemplation is discussed by emulating the superior body.
By merely observing the head [of Amitābha], one knows this is Avalokiteśvara;
by knowing this is Mahāsthāmaprāpta—these two bodhisattvas assisting Amitābha Buddha to universally transform all beings—this is called the Thirteenth Meditation on Mixed Visualizations.

[Commentary]: The preceding section clarified the method for contemplating the superior body of Avalokiteśvara, wherein first visualizing the crown and topknot causes all other marks to become clear in succession.
In the contemplation of Bhaisajyarāja (Śrī-vidyut-dhara), there is a jeweled vase within the topknot; the rest of the bodily marks do not differ from those of Avalokiteśvara.
Because these two features are the distinctive characteristics of the bodies of these two Great Beings, the practitioner is instructed to contemplate only these distinctive marks.
If the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are manifested, then the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) become clear.
[Commentary: Regarding those who interpret the observation of the hand-marks as being performed by the Head (the Leader):

the previous statement says that within the celestial crown on the head of Avalokiteśvara there is a standing emanation Buddha, and on the head of Śrī-vidyut-dhara (Śrīkūṭa) there is a precious vase; taking these as the distinct characteristics.

Regarding the "hand interpretation," the preceding passage states that his hand is soft and supple and possesses eighty-four thousand lines; it uses this precious hand to guide and receive sentient beings.
This is all based on the scriptural text, and its application is not limited to a single context.

[Commentary]: Although the commentary’s explanation of the "foremost mark" (śīrṣa-lakṣaṇa) admits of two interpretations, it should be understood that while the "head" of the head and the "hand" of the hand are both specific marks (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), they can all manifest the general [characteristic].
Regarding the visualization of the Buddha’s sixteen-foot body, one first visualizes the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) before the various other marks become manifest;
this is explained in detail as previously set forth in the commentary based on the case of Śākyamuni. ○ Third, the subsequent [section].
The Three Contemplations Clarify the Rebirth of the Three Grades. First, the reason for establishing these contemplations. [Commentary]:
The fourteenth section is the contemplation of rebirth in the upper grade. Regarding these three subsequent contemplations that observe those who attain rebirth, there are two purposes:
first, to cause them to recognize the three grades of rebirth so that they may abandon the middle and lower grades and cultivate the upper grade; second, to...
The superior, middling, and inferior levels of the stage of consciousness correspond precisely to the three grades within the *Moheben* (Great Root).
[Commentary] Within this, there are two meanings. The first concerns the "mixed contemplation" (*zaguān*), wherein one contemplates the Inferior Response-body;

its level is middling or inferior, yet through the cultivation of superior contemplation, one ascends to the superior grade. The second meaning refers to the aforementioned contemplation of the Superior Response-body and...

Cultivating the contemplation of diversity (*miśra-saṃjñā*) according to the capacities of beings at the stages of the eighth and ninth levels of faith, one now causes this person to use the sublime three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*) to distinguish the nine grades—namely, the matters of the three ranks in the *Maha-sukhāvati-vyūha Sūtra*.

When the principle and phenomena reach their ultimate depth and one ascends to the tenth level of faith, it is stated that "below this, the three contemplations involve two meanings regarding those who contemplate rebirth. This refers to practitioners who have cultivated the aforementioned contemplative methods.
Observing the signs of rebirth in the nine grades is not for those of ordinary or small capacity who merely seek birth;

even if one were to alter their practices based on the current scriptural text of the three grades, this interpretation would still be incidental and secondary, rather than the intended meaning for advancing one's contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Second, explaining and reconciling the sutras and treatises, which has two parts: first, reconciling the treatises, specifically the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The treatise now states that this is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* (Wǎngshēng lùn) composed by Vasubandhu. It contains seventeen sections of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
In the sixteenth section, "Accomplishment of the Great Meaning Gates," a verse says: "In the realm of Mahāyāna roots of goodness, there are no names of reproach;
women, those with impaired faculties, and the seeds of the two vehicles do not grow therein. The commentary explains: "Therefore, [this is] the fruit of the Pure Land."
The retribution for avoiding the two kinds of reproachful faults consists of: first, the substance (*tattva*), and second, the name (*nāman*).

There are three kinds of substance: first, those of the Two Vehicles; second, women; and third, those with incomplete faculties. Because one lacks these three kinds of substance, it is called "avoiding reproach. The names are likewise of three kinds;
not only is one free from the three substances, but one does not even hear the term "Two Vehicles."
Because women lack three of the faculties, these seventeen [attributes] are established as being fully present;

since these clearly manifest the retributive fruits of that land, there are no followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) there. This is all in reference to that land and does not mean that followers of the Two Vehicles cannot be born here in this world.
Fearing that those who are confused might not understand, I shall provide a harmonious explanation in two parts: first, the reconciliation; second, the two [sections].
"Riding upon the two [vehicles], one is not born in the first assembly.

[Commentary] To explain this according to the sutras and treatises: A questioner asks why, based on the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), those of the Two Vehicles cannot be reborn, whereas in this sūtra, those of the Lesser Vehicle in the Middle Grade can be reborn.
The answer is that while those who practice the Lesser Vehicle do not attain birth in its true sense, it is essential that they resolve toward the Mahāyāna at the end of their lives.
Only when the seeds exist can they be produced; the Sūtra speaks of the present state, while the Śāstra cites the original and the initial.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, according to that Śāstra’s statement that the seeds of the Two Vehicles are not produced, both [types of seeds] are said here in this Sūtra to be produced through the minor precepts, because the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and the śrāmaṇera precepts, etc., constitute the seeds of the Lesser Vehicle. Thus, these two explanations appear to be contradictory.
To answer this objection, I shall now interpret it by means of the "turning of the mind" (*cittavivarta*) while remaining in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Because one remains firmly fixed in the path of the Lesser Vehicle with no further aspiration, seeking nothing other than that, it is said that one is "correctly situated.

However, if one turns from the Lesser toward the Great, transforming the karma of the *Hīnayāna* into the cause for the Pure Land, it is said that this "must depend on the sutra. This is taught in reference to the present time when one is turning toward the Great; therefore, [the attainment] is obtained.
The *Jushelun* (Treatise on the Production of Sentient Beings) explains that because [beings] abide in their original and initial states during the period of infancy, they are thus "unborn.
However, the *Lun* (Treatise) states that in that land there are no followers of the Two Vehicles, because [the causes for such states] have been transformed within this very body.

[Commentary]: Why is it further proven that those who have attained the small fruits [of the Śrāvaka path] will eventually enter the Great Vehicle? Although they may have generated the great resolve (*mahācitta*) near the end of their lives, they previously studied the Small Vehicle extensively.
Upon hearing of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence there, their original understanding is awakened, and they first realize the small fruit.
Having attained the small fruit, they do not abide in the small; they must necessarily return to the Great Vehicle.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the passage below that explains the realization of the fruit: "Why is it that those who, at the end of their lives, turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, are born in that land?
Furthermore, why is it that those of the three grades of the Middle Class are born there and yet realize the fruits of the Small Vehicle?

The intent of this explanation is as follows: because they have turned their minds [toward the Great], they attain birth; because of their habitual tendencies, they realize the Small. Although they realize the Great, they realize the Small; they do not cling to the partial truth.
And thus they shall ultimately and before long realize the Great [Enlightenment]. ○ Second, the question regarding women in the lower assembly.

[Commentary]: The question concerns the statement in the treatise that women and those with deficient faculties are not born here [in this world], yet Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants all attained rebirth together.
The treatise’s explanation that women and those with deficient faculties are not born refers specifically to them.
Those born in that land possess pure faculties and are free from desire; therefore, there are no women and no sexual organs. Because the essence is supreme, there are no physical defects.
As stated in the sutras, because they first proceed with a virtuous mind, all are able to go there.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, the passage from the treatise’s verse stating that "women and those with impaired faculties are not born [there]" is juxtaposed with the account in this sutra regarding the birth of Queen Vaidehī’s attendants, thereby posing a challenge to these two statements.
Now, by reconciling these two accounts, the treatise explains that they concern the transformation of karmic retribution;
therefore, in that land, there are no women nor those with impaired faculties, whether in name or in fact.

Because the *Tǐjīng* (Body Sūtra) states that those who cultivate the practice of purity in this land possess a virtuous mind and can all go [to the Pure Land], and because the *Dàmítuó jīng* (Great Amitābha Sūtra) states that even the *pṛtīdaka*—all wriggling and crawling insects—can attain rebirth, one knows that there is not the slightest contradiction between the sūtras and the śāstras. **2.
Questioning the Great [Sūtra] below to reconcile the scriptures.** This section has two parts: first, posing dual questions in response to the sūtras.

[Commentary] Question: In the *Mūla-sūtra*, it is stated that those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or slander the Dharma cannot be reborn here; yet in this sūtra, it is said that even those with the sins of such transgressions can attain rebirth.

[Sub-commentary] That "the sins of transgression can lead to rebirth" refers to the passage concerning the lowest grade of the lowest birth (*adhamādhamotpatti*). II. Explaining the existence of the lower grades and establishing the doctrine through a dual explanation.
1. First, regarding the repentance, there are degrees of lightness and gravity.
[Commentary: There are two meanings to this explanation regarding the commission of offenses by persons, categorized as superior and inferior.

Those of superior faculties are like King Ajātaśatru, who committed a parricidal offense but necessarily felt profound remorse, which caused the offense to be attenuated and permitted him to be reborn there.
Those of inferior faculties commit parricide and generally lack such profound remorse; therefore, they cannot be reborn there.

[Commentary]: "Superior" refers to those of sharp faculties; "inferior" refers to those of dull faculties. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The offenses committed by the foolish and the wise differ in gravity.
A small sin committed by a fool causes him to fall into evil realms, whereas a great sin committed by a wise person allows him to escape suffering.

It is like a lump of iron: though small, it sinks in water; yet a large quantity of iron fashioned into a bowl can float. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are two kinds of wise persons: the first is...
There are two ways not to commit various evils, and two ways to repent after having committed them. The fool also has two [faults]: first, committing sins; second, concealing them.
For example, King Ajātaśatru killed his father and harmed his mother, yet at the assembly for the *Nirvāṇa*, his body became swollen with sores and fever.
He gave rise to profound shame and remorse, reproaching himself for his transgressions. Jīvaka encouraged him to go to the Buddha’s presence, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him.

The attainment of rootless faith is recorded in the "Brahmacarya" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. This scripture clarifies that those who have committed heinous crimes can still be reborn in the Pure Land;

this is equivalent to King Ajātaśatru’s repentance with superior faculties, sharp intelligence, and a profound mind. Conversely, those mentioned in that same scripture as not being reborn are inferior-faculty fools who, by the time of their death, are unable to repent with such intensity.
II. Second. (Note: The character "二" at the end of the second sentence appears to be a section marker or a scribal error for "下" [inferior], which is repeated in the prompt.)
Regarding practice, there are the categories of concentrated and dispersed.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding the distinction between concentrated and dispersed practice: the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha is called "concentrated cultivation," while performing other wholesome deeds is termed "dispersed.
Because the power of dispersed wholesome deeds is subtle, they cannot eliminate the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and thus one cannot attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
It is with reference to this that it is said they do not arise; yet this sutra clarifies that through meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), their arising is attained.

[Commentary] "With reference to this in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*" refers to the aforementioned fact that the power of scattered wholesome roots is slight. "This sutra clarifies contemplation" refers specifically to the Buddha-contemplation samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
Question: If one attains the lower-of-the-lower grade through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*), why is it said that such a person is oppressed by suffering?
"How can one possibly recollect the Buddha? A virtuous friend said to him, "If you cannot recollect him, you should instead invoke the name of Amitāyus Buddha.

In this way, with a sincere mind, let the sound not cease for ten moments; these ten recitations should, in principle, be no different from those performed with a distracted mind according to the *Mahāyāna* [Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra].
[The opponent] replied: "Although he had committed evil, because he had previously practiced contemplation, it enabled his virtuous friend to appear at the moment of death."
If one is encouraged to recite the ten recitations with a settled mind, it will likewise be accomplished; this refers to a person whose vehicle is urgent but whose precepts are lax.
Because they cultivate contemplation, their vehicle is urgent; because they commit evil, their precepts are lax. Due to the urgency of their vehicle, they encounter virtuous friends.
Even if they do not practice samādhi in the present life, because their past seeds have now matured, they attain rebirth; thus, the lotus blossoms.
Seeing that these two Great Beings expound the Dharma of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), who else but those with established goodness (*niyata-kuśala*) could reach such a state?

Thus, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states: "Those who encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the moment of death and achieve the ten recitations (*daśanāman*) do so because their past wholesome karma is powerful;
it is only then that they encounter a spiritual friend. One should know that only by providing this kind of explanation does one accord with the meaning of "established goodness" in this context.

If one has not originally cultivated samādhi, it belongs to the category of prior regret and carries the sense of being slight. ○ Third, the classification of the nine grades based on the stages of practice (san-i-pin ting-wei):
Part One, a general demonstration of the nine grades; Part Two, first, showing the three grades based on the three lower levels; second, within these, the nine grades are fully contained.
[Commentary] Within the three grades, there are further nine.
[Sub-commentary] The scriptural text reveals that each of the three classes contains three subdivisions. Second, the determination of the nine grades as belonging to the three [classes]:
first, the lower grade of the superior class is determined according to its stage.
[Commentary: Those of superior capacity range from the stage of the "seed of practice" (*śikṣā-bīja*) up to the Bodhisattva of "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Those of middling capacity begin from the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) among the external ordinary beings (*bāhya-prthagjana*). Those of inferior capacity are the common people of the present day who remain in a state of worldly indolence.

[Commentary] Although nine grades are distinguished, when defined by their meaning, they do not exceed three positions: namely, the inner ordinary beings (ābhyantara-pṛthagjana), the outer ordinary beings (bāhya-pṛthagjana), and those who are merely indolent.

However, the names "habitual seeds" (*vāsanā-bīja*), "practice and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*), and the "ten stages of faith" (*daśa-śraddhā*) refer to the stage of ordinary beings prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
Regarding why these are taken as the stages for rebirth in this sutra, there are briefly three reasons: first, to correspond to the sequential order of the distinct stages;...

The first distinction is that this [text] clarifies the stages (pin), whereas the other [text] distinguishes the two types of practitioners; the second is that this [text] fully encompasses the four contemplations (guan) to accommodate a broad range of capacities, whereas the other [text] primarily judges the nine grades based on the persons being contemplated.

If one were to judge the current stage of the perfect contemplation (yuan guan) by means of the nine grades, then the three levels of the "Worthy" (san xian) would correspond to the current ten levels of faith (shi xin);
those ten levels of faith correspond to the current five grades (wu pin), and the latter's state of "leisurely drifting" corresponds to the person at the level of "name-only" (ming zi).

Because the stage of "name" (nāman) encompasses both those who have practiced and those who have not yet practiced, one should know that the *Śāstra* employs these three stages to distinguish the nine grades of persons;
its intent is profound and subtle, and cannot be grasped with a coarse mind. Now, I shall attempt a brief explanation:

generally, if all wholesome roots can be dedicated toward enlightenment, they are causes for the Pure Land; likewise, if all evil deeds can be repented and vowed against, they too are causes for the Pure Land.

Therefore, the varying depths of various well-cultivated virtues are none other than the nine grades; likewise, each instance of evil, when considered in terms of the power of its repentance, also consists of nine grades.
Thus, the highest-of-the-high grade of virtue may correspond to the lowest-of-the-low grade of evil, and the lowest-of-the-low grade of evil may correspond to the highest-of-the-high grade of virtue.
As for the three minds and the six recollections, if one has merely heard of them or practiced them but is unable yet to subdue the afflictions, they belong to the lower three grades.
By means of this, one subdues delusions and enters the three middle grades; only when one is able to destroy two types of delusions does one then participate in the three upper grades.
For example, the merit of ten recitations at the moment of death for those who have committed the five heinous crimes belongs to the lowest of the lower grades.

King Ajātaśatru, through his profound repentance, attained rootless faith (*amūla-śraddhā*), which is precisely what is encompassed by the three upper grades. Is it not the case that the five heinous crimes themselves are transformed according to the power of repentance?

The nine grades are divided into seven intermediate categories: whether virtuous or non-virtuous, whether cultivated or repented, each must be clearly understood according to the depth of its merit within these nine grades.
According to the scriptural text, the three lower grades consist solely of non-virtue; the middle-lower and middle-middle grades consist of worldly virtue;

the middle-middle and middle-upper grades correspond to the practices of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); and the three upper grades consist solely of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). According to the *Shu* (Commentary), it employs exclusively the Mahāyāna perspective.

Regarding the classification of the three grades into nine levels: because the middle three grades dedicate their merit toward the Mahāyāna, those of the lower three grades rely on the Great [Vehicle] to extinguish their offenses;
thus, each of the nine grades becomes a single grade of the Great [Vehicle]. If one reaches the stage of the Three Worthies (triyāna-kṣānti), one belongs entirely to the upper three grades;
if one reaches the stage of the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā), one belongs entirely to the middle three grades. As for those who have not yet subdued their afflictions (kleśa):
Regarding the lower three grades, one should know that the Sūtra establishes them in order to exhaustively encompass all capacities;

thus, it distinguishes nine grades by means of the Great and Small Vehicles and good and evil, as these are mutually manifest according to their relative superiority and inferiority. When the Great Master grasped the intended meaning, he judged the nine grades according to three stages;
thus, what capacity would not be included, and what practice would not be profound? This is because his wondrous understanding of the Great and Small Vehicles was so sublime.

When one contemplates that the karmic actions of good and evil cultivated through practice are entirely identical to their nature (*dharmatā*), each and every act is fully present within the four kinds of Pure Lands.

It is simply by means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) that the four types of blissful realms manifest according to the capacity of the function. Those who speak thus mostly do so with reference to a single practice;

according to the depth or shallowness of its power, one passes through the nine grades. Furthermore, there are those who change their practice at every stage and likewise pass through the nine grades.
Regarding the classification of the nine grades (*navavidha-pudgala*) to determine their relative status—whether they are subject to change or not—all such distinctions remain without confusion.

Now, as for these sixteen contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*), since they are cultivated as a complete whole (*pariniṣpanna*), do each individual contemplation apply to all nine grades, or must one modify the contemplation at each stage to enter the respective grade?

Answer: Although both are complete contemplations, the objects upon which they rely are modified according to what is appropriate and according to the practitioner’s inclination. Thus, there is modification.
Regarding the two paths concerning whether or not to alter [the visualization], if we follow the extant text, it mostly adopts the view of alteration.

Throughout the nine grades, although a beginner understands that both sense organs and objects are the Dharma-realm, their mental conceptions are weak and inferior, making it difficult to contemplate such a sublime realm.
Therefore, the Tathāgata established a distinct expedient means: first contemplating the setting sun in the west to stabilize the mind. As the *Sū* (Commentary) states:

Excluding those who have committed the five heinous crimes, this is discussed from the perspective of the lower grade; thus we know that through the wondrous contemplation of visualizing the setting sun, one attains the lowest of the lower grades.
Next, by means of the three contemplations, one visualizes water freezing into ice, which corresponds to the middle of the lower grades.

Then, by further transforming the visualization to perceive lapis lazuli, one has a coarse vision of that ground, which corresponds to the upper of the lower grades. If one attains samādhi, one will see that jeweled ground, as well as the jeweled trees and jeweled ponds.
Although the five grades (pañca-vidhā) begin at this point, they are collectively termed "perfectly subduing" (*paripūrṇa-vinodana*) and are called the attainment of samādhi.

Within these five grades, the middle and lower levels constitute the general perception of the environment and its inhabitants (*pratyaya-bhoga*). The mind during the middle grade corresponds to the central lotus throne visualization; once the five grades are completed, the final mind corresponds to the middle-upper grade.
Although these three grades constitute the attainment of samādhi and are able to subdue the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the five stages, they have not yet been severed.

Because the phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) still persists, one cannot yet immediately perceive the marks of the sublime and wondrous body; therefore, one cultivates the three contemplations to observe a jeweled image.

When the perception of the image manifests before one, both afflictions of view and thought are exhausted. The reason they are exhausted is that the power of concentration on the phenomenal object is profound enough to suppress the afflictions of view and thought;
one thus immediately ascends to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Once the lower and upper grades of phenomenal consciousness are entirely exhausted...
Based on the karmic consciousness, one may contemplate the true Dharma-body of the Three Sages and universally observe its perfection within the eighth and ninth stages of faith;
because this constitutes the upper-middle grade, the inconceivable marks, the radiance of the Dharma-realm, and the Buddha-activities of the ten directions can all be clearly perceived.
Subsequently, through the cultivation of miscellaneous contemplations and the contemplations of the three grades, one shall achieve the tenth stage of faith, which is the uppermost grade.

Because external dust-like afflictions are spontaneously eliminated and exhausted, one responds to capacities, manifests signs, and clearly observes and proclaims various karmic activities without end;

this refers to the practitioner who, from the subtle to the manifest, completes the contemplations of the three sages and subsequently practices the mixed contemplations and the contemplations of the three ranks—therefore it should be understood thus. If, however, the contemplation of the superior marks is not accomplished:
Initially relying on miscellaneous meditations and the sixteen-foot body, such a person may belong to one of the lower three grades or have attained the middle grade;
now, by contemplating the nine grades, they will certainly be able to advance their practice, moving from the inferior toward the superior and seeking inclusion among the higher ranks.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "It causes one to recognize the three grades of rebirth, so that one may abandon the middle and lower grades and cultivate the superior grade. This follows the thematic divisions.
It is said that one may enter the stages through the sequence of transforming the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). There are also those who, by transforming the contemplation, transcend the stages;
these cannot be definitively determined. All of the above refers to those who transform their objects and cultivate contemplation according to the sequence.

As for those who do not transform [the object], they should select whichever of the sixteen objects they prefer and cultivate it with sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), never abandoning it. Thus it proceeds.

Cultivating the practice through names and entering the stage of semblance involves traversing the nine grades; however, among these sixteen [aspects], the Buddha-realm is most suitable for contemplating the superior from the inferior to achieve the nine grades.
Therefore, the Commentary instructs that one should contemplate the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) of Śākyamuni as the gradual entry point for the beginner’s mind.
While the Sūtra does not explicitly state that one should contemplate the image of the Buddha at one *zhang* and six *chi*, it permits such contemplation.
It is said that proceeding from the single mark (ekalakṣaṇa) into [the higher stages] accords with principle;

yet, according to the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, one observes sequentially upward from the thousand-spoked wheel mark (*sahasrāra-cakra*) on the soles of the feet up to the fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on the crown of the head.

Thus, we know that one merely understands the present abiding and the preceding three stages to judge the nine grades. Whether there is change or no change regarding the object and the practice follows naturally through successive comparison; it is not otherwise.
Only now, in the ninth grade of this sutra, as with the five grades of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the meaning is likewise the same; thus one thousand [beings] have attained deliverance.

[Commentary]: How is it known that those of the superior grade who see the Buddha and hear the Dharma immediately awaken to non-arising are thus people of the "Dharma-Seed" stage?
It is because even those of the inferior grade who have committed the four grave offenses can attain rebirth; by analogy, the case here is similar.

[Commentary]: Since the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is located in the first ground (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*vyavasthāna-yāna*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*aṇḍa-yāna*), how could those in the ten stages of dedication of the Separate Teaching or the tenth faith of the Perfect Teaching see the Buddha and immediately ascend to this stage?
If it is so for the highest levels, one should know by analogy that the same applies to all other grades.

Furthermore, one may verify the lower three grades by the fact that those in the internal and external ordinary stages (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) of the Separate and Perfect Teachings do not commit various evils.

Since this is explained in terms of offenses, we know that such a person has not yet entered the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). By analogy with those who are similar in this regard, and because the sūtras do not provide explicit clarification, one must infer and verify this through cases such as attaining awakening or committing transgressions.
This is because the Great Master [Nāgārjuna], while honoring the sūtras and being humble toward others, often provides interpretations that appear unconventional.

The noble lineage (āryagotra) is fivefold; the nature of awakening (bodhitva) is sixfold; and the nature of wondrous awakening is likewise. Question: Since this superior grade belongs to the stage of emerging into the conventional (niryāṇa-avasthā), it should reside in a defiled land (saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra) to benefit sentient beings. Why, then, does one seek birth in a pure land (śuddha-kṣetra)? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 43, explicitly states this. It asks: "According to the Dharma of a Bodhisattva, one ought to deliver sentient beings. Why then do they seek birth in a pure land? Once their faculties are perfected, they can then return to the defiled lands to deliver sentient beings. This is why they seek birth in a pure land. Furthermore, the pure land is the place where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell; by seeking birth there, one will be able to hear the profound Dharma and quickly attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In response to the question of how one reaches the land of the Pure and Immeasurable Life Buddha, it is said that there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:

first, those who possess a heart of compassion and act extensively for the sake of sentient beings; second, those who extensively accumulate the merits of all Buddhas and delight in such accumulation.

Those who delight in accumulating merit reach the land of the One Vehicle, the Pure Land of Immeasurable Life, while those who prefer to act extensively for the sake of sentient beings [reach the Land of Utmost Bliss].

Regarding those who have been born [into this state], because they hear the sound of praise for the Triple Gem where there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, we know that although Bodhisattvas who sever delusions are equal in one respect, there are two distinctions due to their differing inclinations. Furthermore, the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states:
"There are two types of Bodhisattvas: those who first accomplish merit for themselves and subsequently deliver sentient beings, and those who first [accomplish...]"

Since sentient beings must first achieve merit for themselves before they can do so, we know that a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Dedications who seeks rebirth in a Pure Land is one who has already achieved merit for themselves.

Thus, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* clarifies that as long as one has not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one must always remain inseparable from the Buddha; therefore, one must seek rebirth. II. Once Attained.
The following seeks [the meaning] according to two principles.
[Commentary]: First, there is the difference in the speed of attaining the Way; second, there is the difference in the vehicle mounted.
Regarding the first, these are the golden lotus flowers beneath the purple-golden platform within the diamond terrace.

[Commentary]: Having attained the highest grade of birth, one immediately awakens to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In the middle grade, after seven days have passed, one attains non-retrogression.

In the lowest grade, after three minor kalpas have passed, one dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, and realizes "non-retrogression through mindfulness";
this is precisely the Stage of Joy. ○ Fourth, the word-by-word explanation of the text, which consists of the final three contemplations among the sixteen.
The preface of the *Yi shu* states: "The following three contemplations concern the person who attains rebirth. If one merely reads the text, it cannot be called 'contemplation.

One must examine the characteristics elucidated in the sutras and integrate them into a single moment of mind, employing the subtle contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way to illuminate the nature of the mind.
Thus, the pure land, its causes and conditions, its retributions, and the Buddhas and sentient beings are all inherently present."
The causes and effects of the pure lands of all Buddhas, which are without distinction, are already perfected;

they are able to respond to sentient beings, and because sentient beings possess the causes and effects of the pure lands, they are able to evoke the Buddhas. This principle of responsive origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is neither identical nor different;

each aspect is harmoniously subtle, and every characteristic is distinct yet complete. According to their respective capacities and merits, they evoke the Buddhas and evoke the pure lands. If one contemplates this without ceasing—

The causes and conditions for the inconceivable conventional truth of the Pure Land are naturally and clearly understood. Regarding the stages of such clear understanding, there are three general classifications:
if the clarity is similar [to the ultimate], it belongs to the three superior grades; if it pertains to the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it belongs to the three middle grades;

and if it consists of the conceptual understanding of names and words, it belongs to the three inferior grades. Although there are distinctions of high and low regarding the severance and subduing of afflictions, all are equally characterized by this clear understanding.
All good and evil deeds, dedications, and repentances universally encompass the nine grades;
whether shared or unshared, transcendent or non-transcendent, altered or unaltered, progressing or not—these varieties are ten thousandfold and difficult to describe in full.
If it were otherwise, how could one be called an observer of those who attain rebirth through the three grades? First, the fourteen [sections] concern birth in the superior grade.
Contemplating the Three [Stages], Part One: Superior Birth in the Highest Grade.

Section One: Dividing the Text. [Commentary]: Regarding the first section, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land," which is the formal explanation;
third, "From this name downward," which is the concluding explanation. Within the explanation, there are four further parts, the first of which clarifies the cultivation of causes.
The second section, from "When one is born in that land," clarifies encountering the conditions; the third, from "When the practitioner has seen [it]," correctly clarifies attaining birth there;
and the fourth, from "Being born in that land," clarifies the benefits after birth.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has three parts. First, the heading:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Regarding those who attain the highest birth in the highest grade...
[Commentary] Second, the explanation has four parts. First, clarifying the causes for birth.
If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, they shall attain rebirth there simply by giving rise to three kinds of mind.
What are these three? First, the sincere mind; second, the profound mind; and third, the mind of dedication and aspiration.
Those who possess these three minds will certainly be born in that land. Furthermore, there are three types of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth there. What are these three? One...
First, one who possesses a mind of loving-kindness, refrains from killing, and fulfills all the precepts; second, one who reads and recites the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;

third, one who practices the six remembrances (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), dedicates their merit, and makes the vow to be born in that land—possessing these merits for even one day up to seven days, one shall immediately attain rebirth there.
[Commentary]: "The mind of utmost sincerity" refers to the words of those sentient beings who practice according to reality;
it is the expression of single-minded sincerity. "Deep" means that the fruit of Buddhahood is profound and sublime; because one seeks it with the mind, it is called the "deep mind.
It arises from profound principle and also arises from the thick roots of goodness and joy. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* speaks of "entering the deep and vast mind," and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

Because its roots are deep and difficult to uproot, it is called the "deep mind. Regarding the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*)—the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, giving, precepts, and devas—to settle the mind immovably upon these six matters is termed "recollection" (*anusmṛti*).
[Commentary] The sutra consists of two sections; since the first section states that one will attain birth in the Pure Land immediately upon generating the three types of mind, this is known.
The three minds refer to a single person’s initial aspiration; the subsequent section states, "Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth.
Based on this, it appears that these are three distinct individuals, each practicing and perfecting three types of conduct.

However, as for those who practice, they may cultivate one specific path alone, combine several paths, or practice them all in full; provided they can reach the stage of the *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of the paths) within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), they will attain rebirth.
The tenth stage of faith is perfected and may thus be called "the highest birth in the superior grade. Regarding the three minds beginning with "sincerity" (zhìchéng):

these correspond in meaning to the three minds described in the *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* (*Qǐxìn lùn*). That treatise states: first, the direct mind (*zhíxīn*), because it correctly contemplates True Suchness (*tathatā*);
second, the profound mind (*shēnxīn*), because it delights in accumulating all virtuous practices; and third, the mind of great compassion (*dàbēixīn*).
Because he wishes to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings, he now first explains "sincere" (*zhéngchí*) through the terms "exclusive" (*zhuān*) and "substantial" (*shí*);
for how could one be called sincere if one does not contemplate *tathatā*? Regarding the "profound mind" (*shēnxīn*), although the commentary provides three meanings, they do not exclude one another:
to seek the lofty and profound fruit, one must accord with and realize the profound principle; to realize the profound principle, one must possess thick and joyful roots of goodness. This is...
Establishing practice by relying on principle to seek the fruit; the two sūtras establish and verify three kinds of profound meanings that do not exceed those discussed in that treatise:

the joyful accumulation of all virtuous practices, the dedication and aspiration of the mind as explained in the *Sūtra Commentary*, and although the meaning is not fully understood here, it corresponds to the meaning in that treatise of using great compassion to uproot suffering—namely, the virtuous mind that proceeds toward the fruit through the true recollection of *tathatā*.

The two mental qualities are skillful dedication and the vow to be born in a pure land, to swiftly realize the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and to extensively uproot the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings.
These three mental states accord with three dharmas: the first thought accords with the single nature of the equality of *tathatā* (suchness);
the subsequent two correspond to the two types of practice—cultivation for oneself and cultivation for others. Since these are indeed practices, [they are so designated].
Regarding the two natures, the first arises from the aspiration for the three dharmas in their perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). Now, these three minds are cultivated within a single thought-moment;

as the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (those to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (those to be abandoned by cultivation), as well as those of the *rajas-rajas* (dust-like) category, are spontaneously eliminated, one enters the tenth stage of faith (*śraddhā*). Therefore, this corresponds to the present chapter.

If these three minds can merely suppress [the afflictions] in a perfectly integrated manner, they correspond to the middle three grades; if they have not yet suppressed them at all, they correspond to the lower three grades.
The text herein encompasses the meaning of the following eight scriptures: practicing the precepts with a compassionate mind and refraining from killing;
knowing that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature through non-referential compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) and not harming the lives of sentient beings;

reciting the Vaipulya sutras while forming contemplations according to the text; and practicing the six mindfulnesses. Regarding the latter, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "The first three [mindfulnesses] concern others."
The latter three recollections are: self-restraint as the cause for birth in heaven, the precepts as the cause itself, and giving as the practice that leads to the fruit of heaven.
Regarding the "near" and "far" fruits of heaven—the far being the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*)—the commentary below clarifies the meaning of "recollection":
it means that the Three Jewels of the same essence, the single mind of precepts and giving, and the principle of Ultimate Meaning are all non-dual.
Because they are moved by the two extremes, the general designation "sūtra on mindfulness" includes dedication, making vows, and so forth; this is discussed collectively.

Practices such as non-killing must all involve skillful dedication and the vow to be born in a pure land, and after realizing non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must extensively deliver all sentient beings.
If a sūtra possesses these merits—whether in their entirety or in part—it may be said to possess them for even a single day, and so on.

Regarding those who attain rebirth in seven days: for those who practice each of the aforementioned stages and achieve them up to the level of the "Path of Cultivating the Seeds" (*dharmākara-mārga*), it is most excellent to do so over a long period;
however, even down to seven days or a single day, they shall all be included among those born in the highest of the superior grades (*uttarottara-agra*).
All of these cases must be distinguished according to whether the lower eight grades [of afflictions] have been abandoned, suppressed, or not yet suppressed at all.
If it were not so, how could those who have only recently begun practicing the six mindfulnesses—whose three delusions are still raging—be expected to ascend immediately to the highest grade?
One must understand that while the nine grades are difficult to establish through fixed rules, they can only be determined according to one's merit;
this point is clearly explained in the commentaries on the sutras and treatises, though it is not explicitly marked in the *Chao*.
When one is born in that land, because this person has been diligent and courageous, Amitābha Tathāgata, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, the great assembly of śrāvakas, and immeasurable devas,
will arrive at their place of practice within a palace made of the seven treasures; Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, holding a vajra platform, will come together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Then Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body and extends his hands to welcome them;
Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and countless bodhisattvas praise the practitioner and encourage their mind.

Having seen this, the practitioner rejoices and leaps for joy; seeing himself mounted upon a vajra pedestal, he follows behind the Buddha and, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, is reborn in that land.
Having been born in that land, he beholds the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all its marks, and beholds the bodhisattvas, their forms and features likewise complete.
Having heard the sublime Dharma expounded in the Forest of Radiant Jewels, they immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In the brief interval of a moment, they served various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions; before each of those Buddhas, they received their successive predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), and upon returning to their own lands, they attained immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharani-doors.

[Commentary: The term "patience in non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) refers to ascending to the first stage (bhūmi). As for *dhāraṇī*, it is a "total retention" (*saṃdhāraṇa*) because it is first able to maintain what is wholesome and second able to obstruct what is unwholesome.
This is called "the highest grade of the highest rebirth."
[Commentary]: Regarding those of the highest grade who are born in the middle [level], there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, the cause for rebirth; second, "From this point on" and below, clarifying the meeting with conditions;
third, "The practitioner sees for himself" and below, attaining birth; and fourth, "The practitioner’s body becomes the color of purple-polished gold" and below, the benefits of rebirth.
Those of the highest grade who are born in the middle class do not necessarily uphold, recite, or read the Vaipulya sutras, yet they well understand their meaning and intent;

their minds are not shaken by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they have deep faith in cause and effect, and they do not slander the Mahāyāna. By means of these merits, they dedicate them toward the vow to seek birth in the Ultimate [Pure Land].
[The Land of Bliss.

[Commentary: Regarding the superior grade of middle birth, the cause for rebirth is clarified as follows: "It is not necessary to uphold the Vaipulya sūtras, nor to be well-versed in their meanings and purports," and so forth.
This refers to a person who maintains the meaning (an artha-dhāraka), who does not delight in reading or reciting, but merely takes up a single phrase from within the sūtras.
The verse states: "Profoundly exhausting the ultimate intent beyond the reach of words and thought, the mind is not startled by this deep and vast principle;
furthermore, the mind abides securely in the Middle Way, unshaken by the two extremes. Thoroughly realizing that cause and effect are both the true nature (*dharmatā*), this is called 'deep faith.
Although one may not have practiced universally, upon hearing the Great Teaching or encountering diverse explanations suited to different capacities,"
Knowing that this reveals the single principle, one does not give rise to doubt or slander; this single cause also extends through all nine grades.
However, because this stage of contemplation reaches the eighth and ninth stages of faith within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it corresponds to these grades.

If the understanding of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) has not yet fully subdued the afflictions, it is subsumed under only the three lower grades. This is like the case of Constantly-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta), who did not specialize in recitation.

However, because one deeply understands the meaning by bestowing even a single phrase of prostration upon others and does not slacken for many years, this constitutes the first stage of the practice of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Starting from the stage of names (*nāma-mātra*), one passes through the five stages of the five ranks until reaching the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).
Thus, one knows that the four practices—recitation and so forth—can all be cultivated starting from the stage of names, up to the attainment of the purity of the six sense faculties.
This is for those who have realized the true [nature] and do not practice with partiality.

When the life of one who practices this comes to its end, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a vast assembly of followers including Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, will arrive before the practitioner holding a purple-golden platform and praise them, saying: "O Son of the Dharma!..."

Because you practice the Mahāyāna and understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), I have now come to welcome you; together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, we extend our hands to you at once.
The practitioner sees himself seated upon a purple-golden platform, joining his palms and praising the Buddhas for the duration of a single thought-moment.
Immediately upon being born in that land within the ponds of the seven treasures, this purple-golden platform—like a great precious lotus flower—opens after one night.
The practitioner’s body becomes the color of polished purple-gold, and beneath their feet there are likewise lotuses of the seven treasures.

The Buddha and the bodhisattvas simultaneously emit light that illuminates the practitioner’s body, and their eyes immediately open and become clear. Due to their prior habitual practice, they universally hear all manner of sounds.

He spoke exclusively of the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Immediately, he descended from the golden platform, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined, praised the World-Honored One for seven days.
At that very moment, he attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that very moment, he was able to fly through the air, traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to serve all Buddhas, and at the abodes of those Buddhas, he practiced.

Through various samādhis, one attains the realization of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) within a small kalpa and receives a manifest prediction [of enlightenment].
[Commentary: "The profound ultimate truth" refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is beyond the path of language and where the movements of the mind cease;
it is called "profound, subtle, and exquisite. "Vigorous effort that is foremost" refers to the path of *anuttara-avaivartika* (unsurpassed non-retrogression).

The planting of the seeds of bodhi also pertains to the stage of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā-bhūmi*), the stage of non-retrogression, and the stage of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in the presence [of the Buddha].
Regarding the four types of predictions, the first is the "prediction in the presence.

[From the *Chao* (Commentary): Regarding the phrase "the profound, wondrous, and sublime diligence" within the section on benefits after birth, the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states that it refers to the assembly of those who have heard [the Dharma].
The teaching on the ultimate truth (paramārtha) can accomplish the principle of entering the inconceivable contemplation;

since emotional defilements and subtle obstructions are suddenly and utterly extinguished, one’s progress is as swift as the wind. Compared to other modes of practice, which are mixed and sluggish, this diligence is preeminent and is thus called the foremost.
The commentary cites "Anuttara-avaivartika" and explains it as the "Bodhi of the Path-species" (mārgākāra-bodhi).
The term *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
This is the fruit sought by those on the path, which is the fundamental nature of the practitioner's mind. Regarding non-retrogression from this state, there are three levels:

first, "non-retrogression in position," which means that upon severing the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), one never again loses the supramundane status of the stage of the "nature of cultivated seeds" (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*).
Furthermore, to subdue and sever the dust-like afflictions is called "non-retrogression in practice," whereby one never loses the bodhisattva practices;

this refers to the *gotrabhūmi* (nature-lineage stage) and the *mārgajñatā-bhūmi* (path-lineage stage). If one breaks through ignorance, it is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness," whereby one never loses the right mindfulness of the Middle Way;
this is the *āryagotra* (noble lineage stage). Regarding those born among the superior [beings], these are those who have already attained the *gotrabhūmi* bodhisattva in this land.

Regarding the statement that one attains the noble lineage of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the beginning of a single eon and now, within seven days, attains the non-retrogressive state of bodhi:
this meaning refers to the non-retrogression of the "seed-bodhi" (*mārga-bīja-bodhi*).

It is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) in general because it is the basis upon which both ordinary beings and sages rely. As for the four types of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), those that manifest immediately are as described by Vimalakīrti.

The Great Commentary (Daishu) sets forth four types of predictions (vyākaraṇa): the prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds, the secret prediction, the prediction in the presence [of the Buddha], and the prediction of non-arising.
Regarding the statement "in the first instance, the prediction in the presence," this is because the prediction in the presence applies to both ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and sages (ārya);
here, in the stage of non-arising, the Buddha provisionally designates it as "prediction in the presence" by way of general application.
This is called "one of the highest grade who is born in the middle.

[Commentary] Regarding those of the highest grade who are born in the lower level, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "Furthermore, they believe in cause and effect";
and third, the conclusion of the explanation beginning with "This is called... Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, clarifying the causes for rebirth; second, the practice...
When such a person’s life is about to end, they encounter the conditions for the third vision; upon seeing this, they attain rebirth in the fourth [heaven] for one day and night.
Regarding those of superior grade who are reborn below: [The text continues:
...Regarding those of superior grade who are reborn below.
Furthermore, they believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahāyāna, and simply give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment;
by dedicating these merits, they vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary] Those of the lower grade of the superior class also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna; because this is the same as the middle grade, it is so named.

While the former practices a distinct path by means of comprehending the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this one practices a distinct path by merely generating the mind set on supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhicitta*).

Although they differ in their initial aspiration—whether for the investigation of principle or for the gathering of sentient beings—they are no different in their progression through the stages from the state of an ordinary person to sainthood.
That is to say, based upon the wondrous realm of the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one generates the four great vows; this is called the "True" [Vehicle].
Having correctly resolved upon the bodhicitta, I vow to enable those who have not yet crossed over suffering to cross over, because the aggregates and sense bases remain as they are;
I vow to enable those who have not yet attained liberation to attain liberation, because afflictions are fundamentally pure;

I vow to enable those who have not yet found peace on the Path to find peace, because delusions are transformed into wisdom; I vow to enable those who have not yet realized cessation to realize it, because birth itself is cessation.
The arousal of this bodhicitta also encompasses the nine grades within the names [of the stages]. Its arising from stillness or distraction corresponds to the lower three grades;

its progression through the five stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) corresponds to the middle three grades; and once the three types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are distinguished, it corresponds to the upper three grades.
