Since the *śikṣamāṇā-gotra* (the grade of practicing the seeds) is now being aroused, it belongs to this [middle] grade. As this mind functions profoundly, one may ascend to the stage of partial realization (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*). How could this not be so?
Is it not possible to reach the highest of the high grades? Judging by their respective stages, there is no dharma that is not included within these nine.

When a practitioner’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and their retinues, holding golden lotus flowers, manifest as five hundred transformation Buddhas to welcome this person. These five hundred transformation Buddhas appear simultaneously.
Extending his hand, he praised him, saying: "O son of the Dharma, you have now purely resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; I have come to welcome you.

When he saw this, he immediately saw himself sitting upon a golden lotus flower; once seated, the flower closed, and following behind the World-Honored One, he attained rebirth within a pond of the seven treasures.

After one day and one night, the lotus flower finally opened; within seven days, he was able to see the Buddha. Although he beheld the Buddha’s body, his mind was not yet clearly enlightened regarding its various marks and signs.
Only after twenty-one days did he see with perfect clarity and hear all the various sounds, all of which expounded the wondrous Dharma.
He traveled throughout the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he heard the most profound [teachings].
Through the Dharma-sūtra, during three minor kalpas, one attains the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the "attainment of the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it is because one enters the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas to increase wisdom and contemplate the meanings of various dharma-gates.
Regarding the "Stage of Joy," it is the first realization of the state of a sage (*ārya*), so great joy arises frequently.
This is "Joy. [Commentary]:
Regarding the benefits after birth, although one sees the Buddha’s body among the various marks and signs, the mind is not yet clear;

it is only after the twenty-one days have passed that one sees it with perfect clarity. This is because the stage of the person in this chapter corresponds to the stage of the "Practicing Seed" (śikṣā-bīja), where such vision occurs.
Although contemplation has shattered the sands of phenomena (*reṇu-saikatā*), because it has not yet been eliminated, the mind is not clear regarding the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

After twenty-one days have passed, one enters the *prakṛti-bīja* (nature-seed) stage, where the sands of phenomena are invaded and severed; thus, each of the eighty thousand marks becomes clearly manifest.

From this point, throughout three *kalpas*, one travels through the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma, thereby entering the *mārga-bīja* (path-seed) stage and ascending to the first ground (*bhūmi*). This is that ground.
One immediately attains the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas. Regarding the "Hundred Dharmas," their enumeration is as set forth in the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.
Now, within these dharmas, one realizes the Three Truths; thus, the hundred dharmas serve as the gate for penetrating and illuminating the Three Truths.
If the Three Truths are illuminated, then all things are fully understood. Therefore, the treatise says: "It increases wisdom and is the seed of contemplation."
Because the meaning of these various dharma-gates clarifies this principle, the mind is filled with great joy; therefore, it is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is termed "superior-grade lower birth," and the conceptualization of this superior birth is called the Fourteenth Meditation.
[Commentary] Regarding the fifteenth section, the contemplation of birth in the middle grade, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation from "If there are sentient beings...
onwards; and third, the concluding summary from "This is called... onwards. Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, clarifying the causes for birth;
second, encountering the conditions from "At the time of the end of life, Amitābha Buddha... onwards; [third, the duration of stay; and fourth, the subsequent rebirth].
Third, from "The practitioner, having seen this... downwards, it explains the birth in the fourth [stage]. From "At the time when the flowers bloom...
onwards, it clarifies the benefits after birth.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Those who attain birth in the middle grade, the superior level... [and so forth].
If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold the five precepts, observe the eightfold fast, and practice all the various precepts,

refraining from committing the five heinous crimes and remaining free from all faults and afflictions, they dedicate these roots of goodness with the vow to seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary: The five precepts consist of not killing, stealing, engaging in sexual misconduct, speaking falsehoods, and drinking intoxicants. The eight precepts add to these:
not sitting on high beds; not wearing flower garlands, necklaces, or applying perfumes to the body or scenting one's clothes;
and not performing or attending dances, songs, or musical performances.

[Commentary]: In the section on "Birth in the Middle Grade," the mention of "various precepts" among the causes for birth merely provides a brief enumeration of the beginning of the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*).

If one were to rely solely on this, it would suggest that upon hearing the praise of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) in that realm, one immediately becomes an Arhat endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).

However, inferring the cause from the fruit, it is not the case that one exclusively maintains the precepts; rather, one must practice both the principle-contemplation (*li-guan*) and the phenomenal meditation (*shi-chan*) of the Hīnayāna, yet has not yet attained realization.
If one remains in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) at the time of death, hears praise of the Vaipulya sutras, turns the mind toward the Mahāyāna, and vows to be reborn in a Pure Land—

provided that this mind of dedication reaches at least the seventh stage of faith in the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddhayāna), or the fourth or fifth of the ten stages of practice-and-observation (kuan-hsing) in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)—
then such a person belongs to the highest grade of the middle level of rebirth. This applies even if their minor practices have already reached the stage of patience (kṣānti).
Furthermore, regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), if one simply shifts according to the [nine] stages, it corresponds to this very category.

However, for those at the levels of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), or those who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they must undergo a sharp and intense transformation to transcend into this category.
Generally speaking, both the Śrāvaka vehicle and mundane wholesome states are classified into nine grades based on the depth and height of the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, will emit golden light that reaches the person.
He will proclaim suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praise the renunciation that allows one to be free from all sufferings.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner’s heart will rejoice greatly; they will see themselves sitting upon a lotus pedestal, kneeling with palms joined.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, before his head had even been raised, he attained rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss; as soon as the lotus flower opened,
he heard various voices praising the Four Noble Truths, and at that very moment, he immediately attained the path of Arhatship,
endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernatural powers, and the eight liberations.
[Commentary] Regarding the benefits after birth, the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) has two parts; first, the direct explanation of the scriptural text.

[Exegesis] The Four Truths are suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. An Arhat is one who is worthy of offerings (*arhat*), one who does not give rise [to further existence], and a slayer of the thief [of defilements].

The Three Clarities (*trividyā*) are the clarities regarding the past, present, and future. The Six Supernormal Powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are the divine eye, the divine ear, and knowledge of others' minds.
Knowing past lives, the exhaustion of outflows, and the attainment of mastery over the body—these six are all unobstructed; therefore, they constitute the "pervasions. The eight liberations are:
first, possessing the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; second, lacking the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms;

third, the liberation of pure form; fourth, the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the cessation of perception and feeling.
The eighth is the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*). Among these eight, the first three are subtle and free from defilement or attachment to the five sensual desires;
the middle four involve detachment from the lower realms; and the last one is able to liberate the mind and its deliberations, and is therefore called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).

It is also termed "reversal and relinquishment" (*prātikūlya-utsarga*). "Reversal" (*prātikūlya*) means turning away from those pure and clean five sensual desires; "relinquishment" (*utsarga*) means abandoning this attached mind.
[Commentary] Since the Four Noble Truths are practiced in common with the Two Vehicles, due to the influence of past habituation, one hears of two kinds of Four Noble Truths:

those of arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) and those of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Regarding the arising-and-ceasing [truths]: suffering (*duḥkha*) involves the shifting of the three characteristics;

origination (*samudaya*) involves the movement of the four mental states; the path (*mārga*) involves being easily overturned by its opposites; and cessation (*nirodha*) involves the extinction of existence and returning to non-existence. As for the non-arising [truths], the first is suffering...

The mark of non-oppression is the accumulation; the mark of non-aggregation is the path; the mark of non-duality is cessation; and the mark of non-arising is the subsequent three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*):
the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows in the present, and the clear knowledge of the divine eye regarding the future.

These three are called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*) and are also termed "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*). As for why the other three are only termed "supernormal powers," the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the supernormal power of the body is merely...
The divine ear of the *śilpasthāna-devas* merely hears sounds; the knowledge of others' minds merely perceives their distinct thoughts. Therefore, these are not "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*).
Knowledge of past lives brings about great revulsion toward past suffering; the divine eye brings about great revulsion toward future suffering;

and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) involves the correct contemplation that severs delusions. For this reason, these three are called "clear knowledges. [End of] Great Treatise on the Questioning of Supernormal Powers.

What is clarified? The direct knowledge of the past and so forth is called "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*); the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past and so forth are called "clear knowledge.
Next, the eight liberations are explained: first, regarding "internally possessing form," "internal form" refers to the skeletal person (the internal body).

This is because one maintains the skeletal person for the sake of cultivating the eightfold flow of light; furthermore, because the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm are difficult to sever, [one relies on this].
Contemplating external forms with an impure mind occurs at the stage of the first dhyāna; it can liberate one from both its own level and the lower realm of desire.

Second, the lower stage refers to the second dhyāna; because the internal purity of the second dhyāna makes it difficult to sever the delusions of desire regarding the internal body, one continues to contemplate the signs of external impurity.
Third, the lower stage involves setting aside the signs of external impurity.
However, because within meditative concentration one refines the eightfold radiant light so that it is pure and brilliant, it is called "pure" (*śubha*).

Regarding its placement in the third dhyāna and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*): if one extinguishes the fundamental fourth dhyāna and the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) involving form, and enters concentration by taking infinite space as the single object of focus, one then contemplates that this concentration exists based upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*); therefore, it is [said to be] non-existent.
Constantly perceiving the five bases of consciousness as suffering, empty, void, deceptive, and unreal, one gives rise to a mind of revulsion and does not cling to them.

As for the sixth base, the sphere of nothingness: when one abandons the object of consciousness and enters meditative absorption by focusing on nothingness, one likewise contemplates this absorption as void, deceptive, and unreal, and does not cling to it. Even until... [the seventh sphere].
Regarding "not being attached to the seven [levels], including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception":

when one abandons the sphere of nothingness and enters meditative absorption by taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as an object, one does not even become attached to the eighth, which is cessation (*nirodha*), etc. This refers to turning away from and ceasing the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) such as feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Disciples of the Buddhas, weary of and disgusted by a distracted mind, desire to enter meditative absorption for the sake of rest.
Because the *nirvāṇa-dharma* is firmly established within the body, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*), wherein perception and feeling are extinguished.

Regarding the first three [categories], their stage is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), where they are able to abandon the five desires of their own level. Regarding the middle four, their stage is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
all of them successively abandon the lower stages. Furthermore, the first three also abandon the lower [levels], while the middle four also abandon their own [level].

The mutual manifestation of the stages has been explained; by means of this, the subsequent [stages] can be known. This is also called "lower liberation" (*adho-vimokṣa*); it is designated as the cause by the name of "liberation" (*vimukti*), which is the fruit.
○ Second, the explanation and reconciliation of doubts and obstacles below. Part three: First, reconciling the doubt regarding the non-arising of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the assembly: the treatise clarifies that those of the Hīnayāna who are "not born" are definitively not born [in this realm].

Here, however, those who have attained birth and subsequently regressed from the Bodhi-mind can attain birth; once they reach that place and their untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) has matured, they realize the fourth fruit.
The *Mahā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) is likewise. Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of guiding those of the Hīnayāna, yet in reality, such [Hīnayānists] do not exist there.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* and the *Vyākhyā* interpret the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* in light of the present sūtra and the *Treatise on Rebirth*.

Regarding the statement in the *Treatise* that there is "no birth," this refers to the definitive nature of those who have entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The present sūtra states that "birth" refers to those who have regressed from Bodhicitta and taken up the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

The preceding section of the *Śāstra* explains: "While one is currently engaged in the practices of the Lesser Vehicle, non-birth is essential; it must depend upon the arousal of the Great Vehicle [mind] at the end of life."
Because it arises from the mind, if there were no prior seeds, how could one turn from the Small toward the Great at the very end of life? Thus, we know this does not contradict the previous meaning.
Furthermore, to resolve lingering doubts: since birth is attained by turning the mind toward the Great, why is it that upon reaching that [heaven], one instead realizes the fruits of the Small?
To explain this, it is said: "The untainted path has matured," and so forth; for although one has long practiced the Great, one may regress from it.

Because the stage of *kṣudraka* (minor) is profound, that Buddha speaks of practicing the minor [vehicle] and causes them to realize its fruits; this is intended to provide further access for those who follow after.

When the sutras and śāstras cite the intent of the "minor," and when the present sutra and its commentary state that those who realize the fruits of the minor vehicle in that land do so, the intention is to separately provide access for those of the Hīnayāna who seek rebirth there.
Once they have been born there, they will all yearn for the Mahāyāna and will certainly not [remain fixed in] realization [of the minor].

Although Xiao Ran expresses this intention, the former interpretation remains correct. Regarding the second point, the lower section of the commentary addresses the objection that those of middle capacity would not reach the level of the lower [nine grades].

[Commentary]: One might ask, "Since those of middle capacity should attain Arhatship immediately upon reaching the appropriate time, why do they not reach the nine grades? The explanation is that these are cases of regression (parihāṇi).
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who are reborn in that land, once their untainted path has matured, realize the minor fruits;
yet, rather than remaining fixed in those minor stations, they again give rise to the great mind and advance with even greater speed.
Whether in five kalpas or ten kalpas, they attain the first bhūmi. Such stages are indeed superior.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question—why is it that those born there with lower grades attain the Bodhicitta immediately upon hearing the Dharma at the appropriate time, whereas those born there with middle and upper grades only realize the fruit of Arhatship?—the difficulty lies in the disparity between the small and great capacities.

The fourth grade cannot match the ninth grade. The explanation states: the "lower" refers to the answer given by way of the swiftness of attaining the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), while the "middle and upper" follow their habitual practice.
Although one may realize the small fruits [of the śrāvaka path], it takes no more than ten kalpas before one must enter the first bhūmi;

yet for those with heavy, nine-grade evil karma, it takes twelve great kalpas before they can emerge from the womb. Furthermore, even after generating the Great Mind (bodhicitta), one must pass through many more kalpas before attaining the stage of dharmakṣānti.

Therefore, by comparison, rapid realization is considered superior to that. Third, the section on the "Three Great Roots" addresses the difficulty of not leaving the household life within the intermediate [path].
[Commentary]: The *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Text) clarifies the superior grade [of the bodhisattva] who leaves the household life, but does not clarify the middling grade who leaves the household life.

What is clarified here is precisely that middling grade. If one does not leave the household life, the Sūtra states that one observes the śrāmaṇera precepts for one day and one night; thus, we know it exists.
However, the *Mahāvaipulya* does not clarify this, as its discourse is based on the long-term beginning and end [of the path]. Here, it is stated that one leaves the household life.
Regarding the "householder" (gṛhastha), this is discussed from the perspective of a short duration.

[The *Chao*] explains that while it is said one cannot practice as a śramaṇa, this refers to not clarifying the beginning and end of the long duration of leaving home—that is, for one who leaves home for life.
"From the perspective of a short duration" refers to a single day or a single night.
At night, one also knows that if based on a short period, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] also has it according to its meaning;
yet if discussing a long period, this sūtra does not mention it. Thus, the matters in these two sūtras are the same.
This is called the "middle-grade superior rebirth.
[Commentary] Regarding the middle-grade intermediate rebirth, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "If there are sentient beings...

and so forth; third, the concluding summary beginning with "This is called...". Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, clarifying the causes for rebirth; second, from "As... and so forth...
This practitioner, below, clarifies the third [stage], "meeting with conditions"; from "the practitioner sees for himself" below, it clarifies the fourth, "attaining birth";
and from "in the jeweled pond" below, it clarifies the benefits after being born.
Regarding those born in the middle grade of the middle level:
if there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts, or for one day and one night, observe the śrāmaṇera precepts,
or for one day and one night, observe the full set of precepts with perfect dignity and without deficiency, they dedicate this merit...
"I formerly vowed to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, perfuming my cultivation with the fragrance of the precepts.

[Commentary: The "ten precepts" refer to the aforementioned eight precepts, further supplemented by the prohibitions against handling gold, silver, or raw silk, and against eating past midday, thus constituting the ten precepts.
The "complete precepts" refer to the two hundred and fifty precepts, the five hundred precepts, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding "middle birth in the middle grade" (*zhōngpǐn zhōngshēng*), the *Shū* (Exegesis) on the section concerning the cultivation of causes states: "The 'ten precepts' (*shíjiè*) explain the scripture’s reference to maintaining the śrāmaṇera precepts.

Regarding "raw gold and silver" (*jīnyín shēngxiàng*), Nanshan says that there are two designations, Hu and Han; "Hu" refers to "raw image" (*shēngxiàng*), which is translated here as "gold and silver.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (*Shànjiàn lù*) states: "Raw color (*shēngsè*) and similar color (*sìsè*); 'similar' means 'image' (*xiàng*). This refers to gold.
When raw silver is produced, it can be dyed to resemble gold; therefore, it is called "raw image" (*jìngxiàng*).

If this is so, what is the foreign term for this local expression "raw image"? The answer is that in the northern Hu regions of the Five Indias, there are linguistic elements that overlap with Chinese.
Thus, when the Hu people translated [the term], they used the word *jìngxiàng*, which was then re-translated back into Chinese while retaining its foreign phonetics.

When the life of one who practices in this manner is about to end, they will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue emitting golden light and holding seven-jeweled lotus flowers, approaching before the practitioner.
The practitioner will personally hear a voice from the air praising them, saying:
"O son of good family! Because you, a person of virtue, have followed the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I have come to welcome you."
The practitioner sees himself sitting upon a lotus flower, which then closes; he is born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss within a jeweled pond.
After seven days have passed, the lotus flower unfolds. Once the flower has opened, he opens his eyes, joins his palms, and praises the World-Honored One.
Hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and attains the stage of Srotāpanna. After half a kalpa, he becomes an Arhat.
[Commentary]: *Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated as "cultivating the outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) or "flowing against the current.
This is called "being born among those of middle grade within the middle grade. [Commentary]:

Regarding "being born among those of lower grade within the middle grade," there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "If there is... and so forth; and third, [the conclusion].
This is titled "Explanation of the Subsequent Summary," which contains four sections: first, clarifying the cause; second, from "When this person’s life ends" onwards, clarifying the conditions;
third, from "Upon hearing of this matter" onwards, attaining birth; and fourth, from "After seven days have passed" onwards, the benefits after being born.
Regarding those born in the lower grade of the middle class:
if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice benevolence and compassion in the world.

[Commentary: Regarding the cultivation of causes for birth in the lower grade of the middle class, the Sūtra says: "They filially support their parents and practice benevolence and compassion in the world."

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot subdue their afflictions through mundane goodness; how then could they be included among those of the middle grade? Having previously analyzed the stages [of the three grades], one should understand that persons of the middle grade correspond to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-yāna*), which is equivalent to the five ranks (*pañca-varga*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).

This is because, at the end of their lives, they were extensively instructed by virtuous friends regarding Amitābha Buddha, enabling them to accord with their own fundamental nature to take rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), and because they spoke of Dharmākara’s vows and made aspirations in accordance with principle.
Having heard this, one attains realization of the Mahāyāna and gives rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) to seek birth in the Pure Land.

Although the sutra does not explicitly state that one gives rise to the mind of dedication, since it has extensively explained [the path], how could one not turn the mind? This is merely an elliptical expression;

because the mind generated at the moment of death is sharp and powerful, one is able to enter the initial stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the Separate or Perfect Teachings. Consequently, the delusions common to the world are suddenly suppressed, thereby enabling [one to transcend] the mundane.
It is well that this Great Master, regarding these nine grades within the three stages of the Mahāyāna, possesses profound significance.
When such a person is about to pass away, they encounter a virtuous friend who extensively expounds for them the land of Amitābha Buddha.
He also spoke of the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Having heard this matter, he immediately passed away; like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, he was reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

After seven days had passed, they encountered Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; hearing the Dharma with joy, they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, and after the passing of one small kalpa, they became *arhats*. [Commentary]:
Regarding the benefits after rebirth, it is asked: "How does one reach that realization of the Small [Vehicle] after the passing of one small kalpa? and it is answered: "One becomes an *arhat*."

Question: All follow their original habitual tendencies; how then can this practitioner, whose original habituation was to worldly goodness—the cause for rebirth as a human or deva, and not the path of a śrāvaka—attain arhatship upon reaching that state?
Answer: Filial piety, benevolence, and compassion are the foundation for both the great and the small;
what teaching does not discuss them? Yet the Āgamas specifically treat these virtues, verifying the cause by means of the fruit; thus, they rely upon the Tripiṭaka.

Although one practices filial piety and other worldly virtues, the mind remains focused on impermanence; because this has been maintained for a long time and the mind is directed toward the untainted path until it matures, one realizes the Lesser Fruit.
This is called "middle-grade lower birth," which refers to the perception of birth in the Middle Class, and is named the Fifteenth Meditation.
[Commentary] Regarding the sixteenth [section], the lower grade of birth through contemplation (*adhimukti*), there are three parts:

first, the heading; second, the explanation from "Or there may be sentient beings... onwards; third, the concluding summary from "This is called... onwards. Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, clarifying the cause;
second, the explanation from "At that time, that Buddha... onwards, clarifying the conditions (*pratyaya*); third, from "Having spoken these words... onwards...
The section "Clarifying Birth" (from the fourth fascicle, following the seventh seven-day period) clarifies the benefits after birth.

[Commentary] Regarding the sixteenth [section], it should be understood that the intent of the sutra—stating that those of the three lower grades who have committed light or heavy sins may extinguish them upon encountering favorable conditions as a cause for rebirth—is expressed through the extinction of the evils of the three karmas and so forth, in order to facilitate easy understanding; thus, they are designated as the three lower grades.

Dedicating [merit] toward ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle constitutes the middle three grades of cause; taking the various virtues of the Mahāyāna as the cause constitutes the upper three grades of cause.
Thus, the upper and lower [grades] mutually reflect one another as the objects of contemplation.

If one contemplates according to reality and speaks based on the meaning, then the great and small, the good and evil, follow the mind of dedication and the power of the destruction of offenses, with each having its respective stage of depth.

Regarding the nine grades discussed here: although the three types of people mentioned now have extinguished their karmic obstructions upon hearing the Dharma and praising the Buddha, they have not yet subdued their afflictions;

therefore, they belong to the lower three grades, as they are at the stage of the "name-and-characteristic" (naming) level. If their resolve to extinguish sin is sharp, they enter the outer stages of the Separate and Complete Teachings, which corresponds to the middle three grades;
if they can reach the inner stages of the ordinary person (ārya-mārga), they correspond to the upper three grades. King Ajātaśatru repented for his patricide and attained rootless faith.
This is of that same category.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Among those who are reborn in the highest grade of the lowest level, there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds;
though they do not slander the Vaipulya sūtras, they are like such foolish people."

Having committed many unwholesome deeds without shame or remorse, when their lives were about to end, they encountered a virtuous friend who recited for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Because of hearing the names of these various sūtras, their extremely heavy evil karma from a thousand kalpas was eliminated.
Furthermore, the wise one instructed them to join their palms, pay homage, and recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha."
"By the power of the Buddha’s name, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas.

[Commentary] The *Sūtra on the Superior Birth in the Lower Grade* states: "Although one does not slander the Vaipulya sūtras," this indicates that in this grade, the offense of slandering is still light.
Reaching the lowest of the lower grades, it says: "If one commits the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, possessing all manner of unwholesome acts, then one slanders [the Dharma]."

Because there is no evil karma among the sūtras and other teachings that one has not committed, they are said to be "complete. The Complete and Sudden Teaching (Yuan-dun jiao) states that regarding offenses, there is neither light nor heavy;
if one repents, they are all extinguished. For example, when the seer Śyāma killed various Brahmins, he realized in three moments of thought that he had slandered the Vaipulya sūtras;
his mind underwent repentance, and he was immediately reborn in the Buddha-land.
At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatched an emanation of a Buddha, an emanation of Avalokiteśvara, and an emanation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta to the practitioner’s presence, praising him, saying:
"Good son, because you have invoked the name of the Buddha, all your sins have been extinguished; we have come to welcome you."
Having spoken these words, the practitioner immediately sees the radiance of the transformation Buddha filling his room;
having seen this, he rejoices and passes away, riding upon a precious lotus flower behind the transformation Buddha to be reborn within a precious pond.

After seven times seven days, the lotus flower shall finally bloom. At the time the flower blooms, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall emit great radiance, stand before that person, and preach the profound twelvefold scriptures for them.

Having heard this, they will believe and understand it, giving rise to the mind set on the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). After ten minor kalpas, they will be fully endowed with the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas.
"Entering the First Ground;
this is called 'the superior birth of the lower grade.

[Commentary] Regarding "the middle birth of the lower grade," there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are four sections; first: [The text continues with the specific details of the explanation.]
The second section, from "Manifesting the Causes" (*mingyin*), clarifies the conditions (*pratyaya*) through the passage beginning with "blowing down the celestial flowers.

The third section, from "As in the space of a single thought-moment" (*ru yī niàn qǐng*), clarifies the attainment of birth (*shēng*). The fourth section, from "Having passed through six kalpas," clarifies the benefits obtained after birth (*shēnghòu huòlì*).

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Among those reborn in the middle grade of the lowest class, there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of precepts.

Such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha or the property of the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the assembly present), preach the Dharma impurely, and lack any sense of shame or remorse; by means of such evil karmas..."
Thus adorned, such a sinner, on account of their evil karma, was destined to fall into hell; yet as their life was about to end, the various fires of hell simultaneously approached them.

Encountering a spiritual friend who, with great compassion, immediately praised for them the ten powers and majestic virtue of Amitābha Buddha, extensively extolling that Buddha’s radiance and supernatural power, and also praising his precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

Upon hearing "Liberation, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation," this person eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas, and the fierce fires of hell are transformed into a cool, refreshing breeze.

[Commentary] Regarding those who stole the property of the *saṃghāṭī* or the property of the *saṃgha* present before them, as described in the *Xiapin Zhongsheng Jing* (Sūtra on the Middle Rank of the Lower Grade): the stolen items...
Objects do not exceed four kinds of permanent property (*nitya-dharmas*).

First is the "permanent property of the permanent," which refers to the monastic community’s kitchens, storehouses, temple buildings, utensils, flower and fruit orchards, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, and so forth. Because their substance pervades the ten directions and cannot be partitioned for individual use, they constitute the "permanent property of the ten directions.
As in the case of the constant food provided by a monastery to the Sangha, its substance likewise pervades the ten directions; it is exclusively...

Regarding the three types of "presence" (*pratyakṣa*)—the local, the original site, and the third type of presence—"presence" refers to property acquired by the Saṃgha that is present before them from the ten directions.

For example, regarding the light belongings of the five classes of deceased monastics: if they have not yet been formally consecrated (*karmavācanā*), one incurs an offense against the Saṃgha of the ten directions;

if they have already been consecrated, one incurs an offense with respect to the Saṃgha present before one. Thus, this belongs to the third type of presence. Stealing from these first two types constitutes theft from "presence."
It is called stealing the property of the Saṃgha; the latter two types are termed stealing the property of the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the present community).
One who preaches the Dharma impurely seeks only fame and profit rather than benefiting sentient beings.

One who lacks shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) commits evil in private without feeling shame before the heavens, and commits evil in public without feeling dread of blame before others. "Shame" (*hrī*) refers to modesty and remorse.
Various celestial flowers are blown [toward him], and upon each flower there is a transformed Buddha and Bodhisattva to welcome this person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, they immediately attain rebirth within a lotus flower inside a pond of the seven treasures.
After six kalpas had passed, the lotus finally blossomed; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of Brahmā, comforted those people and preached for them the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Having heard this Dharma, they immediately gave rise to the aspiration for supreme enlightenment.
"This is called the middle birth of the lower grade.

[Commentary] Regarding the lower birth of the lower grade, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are four sections: first, clarifying the causes;
second, from "seeing the golden lotus flower" downward, clarifying the conditions; third, from "in the space of a single thought-moment" downward...
It clarifies that one attains birth in the fourth stage by descending from within a lotus flower, thereby clarifying the attainment of benefit.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī:

"As for those of the lowest grade of the lowest birth—there may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds, such as the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts, being fully possessed of all manner of unwholesomeness; such are these foolish people."
Due to their evil karma, they ought to fall into the evil realms and experience endless suffering for many kalpas;

yet such foolish people, at the moment of death, may encounter a spiritual friend who comforts them in various ways, preaching the sublime Dharma and instructing them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

However, being oppressed by suffering, those people have no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The virtuous friend then says to them: "If you are unable to mindfully recite the name of that Buddha..."
One should recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha with such a sincere mind that the sound does not cease, performing ten full recitations.
By reciting the name of the Buddha, "Namo Amitābha Buddha," in every thought-moment, one eliminates the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.

[Commentary] In the sub-commentary on the "Lower Grade, Lower Birth," regarding the section on cultivating the causes, there are two parts; first, it clarifies that reciting the name eliminates transgressions.
[Treatise] "Reciting the Name of Amitāyus Buddha up to ten recitations" means that the virtuous mind continues in succession for ten recitations.
Alternatively, one may achieve rebirth through a single thought-moment because mindfulness of the Buddha eradicates karmic obstacles;
thus, mindfulness of the Buddha serves as the supreme condition. If it were not so, how could one attain rebirth?
[Commentary] Second, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da lun) in a question-and-answer format. First, the question:

"How can a practitioner, by means of the mental power of a short duration, surpass one who has committed evil throughout their entire life? This censure is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. [Sub-commentary] Question: How is it that a practitioner, through the power of the mind for a brief period, is able to overcome those who have created evil throughout their whole lives?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains this censure.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding the mind being "low," this is answered from the perspective of a fierce mind.
[Sub-commentary]: Although this mind lasts for only a brief moment, its power is fierce and sharp—like a person on the verge of death who knows they will certainly not escape.
Because its resolute determination is superior to the power of a hundred years of vows, this mind is called a "great mind" (mahācitta), as it involves the relinquishing of the body.
Because of this urgency, it is like a person entering battle who does not spare their own life; such a person is called a "valiant one.
[Commentary] This fierce and sharp mind arises from two conditions: first, encountering a virtuous friend; second, being oppressed by suffering so that the mind fears the evil realms.

Hearing the name of the Buddha with one's ears, one thus recites and contemplates it with firm resolve and utmost sincerity. Since the object is supreme and the mind is fierce, [the merit is immeasurable].
Therefore, when there is little time but much work to be done, yet one can transcend a hundred years through such vast and enduring vows of power—
should these two conditions exist and yet a fierce resolve not arise, this person is destined to fall into hell.
At the time of death, one will see a golden lotus flower, like a solar disc, appearing before that person;
in the space of a single thought-moment, they shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Within the lotus flower, for a full twelve great kalpas, the flower finally opened;
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, extensively expounded for them the true mark of all dharmas and the methods for extinguishing sinful karma.
Having heard this, they rejoiced and immediately gave rise to the bodhicitta.
This is called "inferior birth in the inferior grade"; this is called the perception of birth in the inferior grade, and it is named the sixteenth contemplation.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the benefits; first, the outline of the commentary.
[Commentary] In the second section on benefits, there are two parts: first, clarifying that the lady attained realization of non-arising;
second, clarifying that the handmaidens resolved their minds [on enlightenment]. [Sub-commentary] Second, explaining the sutra: first, the lady’s realization of the Way.
When these words were spoken, Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants, upon hearing what the Buddha had said, immediately beheld the vast and expansive features of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
they saw the body of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas, their hearts filled with joy at this unprecedented marvel.
They attained a sudden and great awakening, reaching the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
[Commentary]: The Sūtra states that one attains the realization of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through a sudden, great awakening.

This means that by hearing the sixteen contemplations with the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one hears them and practices them immediately, entering suddenly into the perfect stage of abiding. This is because one understands that the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), are themselves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
They are neither vertical nor horizontal; the three bodies are fused and wondrous. One's entire mind is the Buddha, and the entire Buddha is one's mind; thus, the subject and object are one.
Since conceptual thought has been forgotten and the secret treasury of the three virtues has been merged into cessation, one should contemplate that it is now suddenly opened;
for this reason, it is called "sudden and great awakening. This awakening extends through the stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*).

Therefore, it is specifically said that one "attains the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), which reveals that this great awakening definitively resides in the stage of partial truth (*fenzhen*). If the sixteen contemplations were not the sublime essence (*miaozong*), how could they cause [the practitioner] to...?
The scriptural passage on "the sudden entry of the faculties into the perfect stage" concludes by demonstrating that this contemplative gate is neither partial nor gradual;

thus, it is clear that one cannot use phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to explain away the text. Second, the explanation of the maidens' arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*).
Five hundred female attendants resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and vowed to be born in that land;
the World-Honored One prophesied that they would all go there and, having been born in that land, would attain the Samādhi of the Presence of All Buddhas.
Immeasurable devas likewise resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.

[Commentary]: The sutra text merely states, "one gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. At what stage does this occur? The sutra indicates that after the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it separately mentions the "giving rise to the mind.

This proves it is not the true [initial] arising of the mind. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Only when a bodhisattva attains the 'patience of compliance' (*anuloma-kṣānti') is there the meaning of 'giving rise to the mind.
Therefore, for the most part, the stage of giving rise to the mind is explained in terms of its semblance (*pratibimba'), and is designated as the 'contemplation of names.'"
Regarding "practice" (*caryā*), it also carries the sense of "setting forth," but because it is far removed from "arising" (*utpāda*), it cannot be discussed [in this context].

The third major section, the *Parīndanā* (Circulation) chapter, states in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-ṭīkā*: "Circulation" (*parīndanā*) means "downward pouring," and "circulation" (*saṃtati*) means "unobstructed.
It is intended that the waters of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) shall pour down from now on, so that the fish-trap of the holy teachings will not be blocked in future ages. For this reason...
The following section cites titles and enumerates benefits to encourage people to practice; otherwise, how could one ensure that the water of the Dharma flows downward without obstruction?
[Commentary] Part Two: First, the general and specific division of the sections.
[Commentary] Third, the Propagation, which also has two parts: first, the propagation within the royal palace; second, at that time, the World-Honored One...
The Blessed One descended from Mount Mingju (Vimalaśikhara) to propagate [the teaching]. This section has four parts: first, listing the names and instructing on their retention;

second, explaining that practicing these [teachings] below has benefits and exhorting others to accept and believe them; third, from the address to Ānanda onwards, the entrustment to him to maintain [the teaching];
fourth, from "He spoke this" onwards, Maudgalyāyana and the others hearing it with joy.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the topical divisions (*ko*). Now, regarding the two instances where the path of practice for the circulation of this sutra is taught: first, in the royal palace, the Buddha himself exhorted [Ānanda];

second, upon returning to Gṛdhrakūṭa, Ānanda recounted it in full. Regarding the first passage, there are four sections. First, listing the names and instructing on their upholding. Within this, first is Ānanda’s question.
Within this, first is the inquiry concerning the title of the sutra, beginning with the words "What should it be called... and so forth.
[Commentary]: At the beginning, Ānanda first asks what the title of the discourse shall be; this is the lower question regarding the name of the scripture.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what name should this scripture be known?"
[Commentary] The words and meanings explained above are not uniform; under what meaning should this sutra be named?
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "the words and meanings are not uniform" in the Commentary: the sutra text has separately presented three kinds of pure karma and sixteen subtle contemplations;
it is not yet clear by which of these it should be given its general title. 2. From "This Dharma" onwards, the question concerns the upholding of the Dharma.
[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "How should this essential dharma be received and upheld?"—this asks about the method for receiving and upholding it. [Sub-commentary]:
Second, the two Tathāgatas provide their answers; first, the initial Buddha answers the preceding question.

[Commentary]: The Buddha’s answer—namely, the visualization of the Land of Utmost Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta—is also called "Pure Karma Born Before All Buddhas," corresponding to the first question.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This sutra is titled 'Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva';
it is also titled 'Purifying Karmic Obstructions and Being Born Before All Buddhas.'"

[Commentary] The single character "contemplation" (guan) is the wondrous essence of mental contemplation; it is the perfect reality (dharmatā) of the three sages of Sukhāvatī. This name is established based on its essence (tǐ).
"Purifying karmic obstacles to the utmost degree" refers to those who have committed the five heinous crimes yet are born before the Buddhas;

this encompasses all nine grades. This name is derived from its function (yòng). These four meanings—essence, substance, function, and name—are collectively the explanation of the title. These four [aspects].
Since the perfection [of the title] corresponds precisely to the characteristics of the teaching, the two names are presented; thus, the intent of the five chapters is fully realized.
Believing that my current explanation of the title accords with the Buddha’s own intention, I now proceed. Second, "You should next" answers the subsequent question.
[Commentary]: "You should receive and uphold [this] so as not to let it be forgotten" is said in response to the subsequent question.
"You should receive and uphold [this] so as not to let it be forgotten.

[Sub-commentary]: "So as not to let it be forgotten" refers precisely to the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*). It is because the mind of mindfulness is able to accomplish the four dharmas, beginning with desire (*chanda*).
If one wishes to advance in skillful wisdom and single-mindedness, yet forgets them, none shall be accomplished. The Buddha ordained that by not forgetting, one possesses five dharmas;
thus, the merit of upholding [the teachings] is fully realized therein.
One who practices this samādhi will, in their present body, behold Amitāyus Buddha and the two Great Beings.

[Commentary] Second, citing the benefits to encourage practice. Third, first clarifying the production of goodness and the extinction of evil; second, first clarifying the lower level by directly clarifying the production of the goodness of seeing the Buddha.
[Commentary] Next, it is explained that through the sixteen contemplation gates which are beneficial practices, one obtains great benefit,

such as being able to see that Buddha and Bodhisattvas in this very life. [Sub-commentary] Being able to see Amitābha and the two Bodhisattvas— their true Dharma-bodies— is the ultimate limit of generating wholesome roots, because it is profound.
Compared to this, what good would not arise?

If even a son or daughter of good family merely hears the name of the Buddha and the names of these two bodhisattvas, they will eliminate the offenses of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas;
how much more so if they bring them to mind!
[Commentary] "The two good men" and below illustrate by contrast the extinction of the sins of birth and death.
[Sub-commentary] "Good sons and good daughters who hear the name" and below clarify the benefits of mindfulness of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
it shows that merely hearing their names eliminates immeasurable sins, let alone recollecting them, thereby clarifying that mindfulness of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas brings great benefit.
Furthermore, the inferior is cited to illustrate the superior.

[Commentary]: Hearing the name is the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), while recollecting it is the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). By citing the inferiority of hearing, one should understand that this illustrates the superiority of the practitioner’s cultivation.

One should know that the previous state of non-forgetfulness is also a form of recollection; however, that belonged to the stage of preparation (prayoga), whereas the present recollection belongs to the stage of realization.
Mindfulness is precisely what is meant by "right cultivation"; though the names are identical, their meanings differ, and one must distinguish them well.
If one practices mindfulness of the Buddha, it should be known that such a person is a *pundarīka* lotus among men.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the excellence of the body and the excellence of the spiritual friend. First, from "recalling the Buddha" onwards, the white lotus serves as a metaphor to clarify the excellence of the body.
[Sub-commentary] "Recalling the Buddha" means that among humans, he is a *pundarīka* (white lotus) flower, clarifying the excellence of his body.
[Commentary]: *Puṇḍarīka* is translated here as "white lotus.

Nirvāṇa is described as the white lotus among all water-born flowers, signifying that the cultivation of the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) surpasses all other practitioners on the path—that is, those at the seven stages of expedient means (*qifen*).
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva serve as his supreme friends.
[Commentary] The section beginning with "The two Avalokiteśvaras" clarifies the excellence of the friends who are comparable to those in the stage of the final birth before Buddhahood.
[Sub-commentary] Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve as his supreme companions and associates.

[Commentary]: The two sages originally cultivated the samādhi of nianfo (Buddha-recollection) of the Perfect Teaching; now, for the practitioner who is a candidate for the position of Heir Apparent (Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage), the cultivation of this very samādhi is likewise required.
Although their levels differ, the dharma they cultivate is identical, and thus they may serve as companions.
This is like the mutual exchange of practitioners of worldly arts and techniques—how could one distinguish between noble and base?
"One shall sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and be born into the family of all Buddhas.
[Commentary] Third, "sitting at the site" clarifies attaining the fruit and initiating practice.

[Sub-commentary] "Sitting at the site of enlightenment" refers to the place where one attains supernormal powers; it is called the *bodhimaṇḍa* because one attains the Way (*bodhi*) beneath the Bodhi tree.

Therefore, it is called "sitting" in the sense of attaining the fruit by relying [on this seat]; it is called "arising in practice" by relying on this seat, which is named "being born into the Buddha-family.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the phenomenal characteristics: sitting beneath the Bodhi tree upon the Vajra-throne at this place and attaining Buddhahood is what is meant.
The affairs of the *bodhimaṇḍa* fundamentally express the principle; now, contemplating the original nature, one realizes the awakened body of Amitābha.

This very body is the *bodhimaṇḍa* upon which one sits. It is the family from which Buddhas are born. "Principle" (*li*) is one, while "meaning" (*yi*) differs; "field" (*chang*) is named for the place, and "family" (*jia*) is named for the source.

Taking this principle as the field, one must attain the fruit by sitting; taking this principle as the family, one must initiate practice by being born. The fruit is the partial fruit, and the practice is the true.
The original aim of cultivating this contemplation is to realize the fruit of partial enlightenment through effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

Because one desires to deliver sentient beings through the "practice of illness" and the "practice of an infant," one cultivates the contemplation of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land; since one will swiftly attain [enlightenment] upon being born there, it is said that "one shall sit."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You should well uphold these words; to uphold these words is to uphold the name of Amitāyus Buddha.
[Commentary] The third section concludes the names and concludes the entrustment of the names.
[Commentary] The title is summarized as "Entrustment," also called "Contemplation of Amitāyus Buddha," and also called "Elimination of Karmic Obstructions.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "one who is skilled at upholding": "skilled" (hǎo) means "sublime" (miào). It is only by means of a mind that is neither horizontal nor vertical and transcends conceptual thought that one can receive and uphold the chapters and phrases of this sutra.
Since the specific text is sublime, it is therefore able to uphold the general title of the sutra mentioned above.
The intent behind explaining this through the subtle fusion of the three and one lies herein; this was entrusted to Ānanda for the sake of people today.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, the Venerable Ānanda, Vaidehī, and the others who heard what the Buddha had said were all filled with great joy.
[Commentary]: Regarding "four kinds of joy," the assembly below rejoices upon hearing [the teaching].
[Treatise]: There are three meanings for "joy": first, the purity of the speaker; the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom is free from error, which is termed "purity.
Second, the purity of the Dharma taught; it enables sentient beings to attain realization.
The fruit obtained through reliance on the three bases of samādhi is the purity of the body-attestation resulting from the fulfillment of practice in reliance upon the Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding the "three meanings," they are: first, meeting a person; second, hearing the Dharma; and third, attaining the fruit. This passage appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Those who take refuge in this sutra are, as it were, Buddhas; for a Buddha must necessarily possess the four types of unimpeded knowledge—namely, those regarding phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Because they explain and contemplate the Buddha-dharma free from error, they are called "pure. Now that we have encountered such a person, how could we not rejoice?
This Dharma is the contemplation of phenomena through sixteen gates, which exhaustively perfects its subtlety and is able to...
When the mind enters deep samādhi, it is free from all that is merely provisional; therefore, it is called "pure. Upon hearing such a Dharma, how could one not rejoice?

As for the fruit, it is the fruit obtained through the diligent cultivation of contemplation. When Vaidehī and the others heard the Dharma, they immediately practiced and attained the fruit of the "True Part" (bhūta-koṭi).
The handmaidens and the devas attained the fruit of "semblance" (pratirūpa). Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda, like the Buddha himself, performed transformations.
The capacities of sentient beings may increase their progress on the Path, yet its depths remain unfathomable; each attains what is called "purity" by means of abandoning delusions.

Having attained such a fruit, how could they not rejoice? These three characteristics arise from the attainment of the fruit, the fruit arises from the Dharma, and the Dharma is proclaimed by a person.
Since the assembly rejoices while possessing these three meanings, although I do not behold the golden countenance [of the Buddha] with my own eyes this day, I act [on his behalf].
Although they were covered by sublime wisdom and further obtained this subtle and wondrous method of contemplation, they had not yet attained the fruit;
therefore, they lacked the third joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One stepped through the void and returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
[Commentary]: Regarding the second section on the circulation [of the teachings] at Vulture Peak, first, the Buddha returns to Gṛdhrakūṭa by walking through the air.
[Sub-commentary]: Within the section on the circulation at Gṛdhrakūṭa, first, the Buddha walks through the air back to Gṛdhrakūṭa;
this manifestation was displayed because he wished to increase the people's reverence and to comply with their words.
[Commentary]: When he previously went to the invitation, he vanished from Vulture Peak and emerged in the royal palace; now, he walks through the void and returns to Vulture Peak.

In both instances, he employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), yet in the former case he was hidden and in the latter revealed. This is because in the former occasion, he intended to perform a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) but the transformative method had not yet been perfected, so he went secretly.
Now, as he proclaims the *Sūtra of the Wondrous Contemplation*, those of appropriate capacity have already received benefit; he wishes to cause them all to follow this Dharma together.
Therefore, he returned after manifesting these transformations so clearly.
At that time, Ānanda extensively recounted the aforementioned events for the great assembly. Having heard what the Buddha had said, immeasurable devas, nāgas, and yakṣas were all greatly rejoiced;
they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.
[Commentary] Second: Ānanda repeats [the teaching].
[Sub-commentary] Next, Ānanda, along with the devas, nāgas, and others, having heard the Dharma with joy, prostrated and departed.
The Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.

[Excerpts: Because the awakening of the faculties within the royal palace was not yet known at Vulture Peak, [the Buddha] dispatched [Ānanda] to proclaim it again so that all might believe and accept it.
What Ānanda recorded is thus the very word of the Buddha; therefore, the text says: "Having heard what the Buddha spoke, they were all greatly rejoiced. This is the principle.
Joy arises from the three preceding meanings of the contract.
*The Sublime Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, Compiled Edition, Volume Five (End).
